text:
GW Law student attorneys in the Immigration Clinic helped a client and domestic violence survivor obtain asylum in the Annandale Immigration Court in October, marking a second major win for the clinic in a single semester.

Current and former student attorneys Mikaela Black, Caroline Peters, Olivia Russo, Angelica Salazar, and Maria Villalobos, wrote a 46-page brief, compiled over 1,200 pages of documents, and argued the client’s case in court.

The Immigration Clinic, led by Clinic Director Paulina Vera, JD ‘15, Distinguished Professorial Lecturer in Law, is one of 21 clinics offered through GW Law’s Jacob Burns Community Legal Clinics Program. The asylum result follows another success in which the clinic helped a 72-year-old grandmother avoid deportation by obtaining a rare writ of coram vobis to waive decades-old shoplifting convictions.

“Professor Vera and the student attorneys in the Immigration Clinic are truly living out GW Law’s mission to make an impact on the law,” said Dean Dayna Bowen Matthew. “Not only did they gain invaluable real-world experience in these two cases, they were able to make an undeniable difference in the lives of their clients, using law as a tool to achieve impactful results.”

The client in the asylum case is originally from Pakistan and a mother of two children, both United States citizens. She moved to the U.S. with her now ex-husband. For over 10 years, the client endured psychological and physical abuse from her ex-husband, leading to multiple hospital visits, Vera said. After initiating a divorce, which came with social and familial stigma, the client feared for her life if she were to return to Pakistan.

Student attorneys in the clinic wrote a 46-page brief and compiled over 1,200 pages of documents in support of the claim for asylum. Their work culminated in a hearing at the Annandale Immigration Court in Annandale, Virginia. After hours of testimony, led by Peters, Class of 2027, the Department of Homeland Security attorney waived appeal and the immigration judge on the case granted humanitarian asylum.

According to research from the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, the national asylum denial rate reached 94 percent over the summer with just 771 people obtaining asylum in June.

“I cannot emphasize enough how hard it is to get a result like we did,” Professor Vera said. “By design, asylum cases, especially gender-based asylum cases, are very difficult to win these days.”

From Briefing to Trial

The case required an all-hands-on-deck approach from a team of five student attorneys across two academic semesters. Professor Vera directed the student attorneys to try three approaches at once: applying for a U visa, which is granted to victims of crimes in the U.S. who cooperate with law enforcement; applying for a T visa, which applies to victims of trafficking; and applying for asylum. Villalobos and Black, both JD ‘26, worked to apply for the U and T visas in October of last year.

“Our client came to us and told us her story involving domestic violence and how she ended up in the United States,” Villalobos said. “We were starting from scratch. We sat down–me and [Black] with Professor Vera–and she laid it out and said, ‘We’re going to try absolutely everything that would be applicable, that would fit her situation, and it’s going to be a lot of work.’”

Ultimately, it was the asylum case that ended up being the quickest path to success. Last Spring, Peters and Salazar, class of 2027, took on the mantle to prepare for the client’s hearing in immigration court. Peters and Salazar compiled the 46-page brief and an affidavit for their client with the help of Professor Vera’s guidance and feedback. Peters then practiced the case in moot trial sessions with her client, honing her oral argument skills.

Prior to the trial on Tuesday, October 6, Peters sat in on other cases presided by the judge in the case.

“[The judge] was tough to say the least,” Peters said. “I was really confident and prepared when I walked in but also a little bit nervous because I didn’t know how the judge and opposing counsel would react to my arguments. I didn’t know how my opposing counsel was going to react to my arguments”

When the Immigration Clinic team received their decision that afternoon, they were thrilled.

“For me, it was especially rewarding because I wasn’t simply researching a hypothetical legal issue for class,” Salazar said. “The work I was producing was being an advocate for a person whose future depended on the outcome.”

Combining Passion with Legal Education

All of the students involved in the Immigration Clinic said they first became interested in doing this work because of a passion for helping others.

Both Salazar and Villalobos have personal experiences with the immigration system. For them, working in the clinic was not only an opportunity to improve their legal skills; it provided the means to make a real difference for clients who have had similar life experiences.

“I was born in Colombia and I immigrated to the United States with my family when I was 7 years old,” said Villalobos, adding that her experience filing her citizenship application and becoming a citizen when she was an undergraduate student made her want to go to law school. “I was really excited when I got accepted [into the clinic]. It felt like a full circle moment to represent clients that went through similar things that my family and I did.”

Professor Vera’s mentorship has also been an extremely valuable experience, the students said.

“I was super very intimidated by this whole process–by doing a trial on my own,” Peters said. “But Professor Vera was so knowledgeable and really supportive the whole time.”

Professor Vera is not just a mentor, Salazar said, she is a role model.

“I’ve never had a Latina professor,” Salazar said. “Seeing her and learning from her, and then also seeing how she is as a lawyer and trying to be more like her, it made a really big difference for me.”

The case is just one example of how experiential education offered to students through GW Law's clinical program serves the strategic goals of both the university and GW Law, fulfilling the mission to be a global law school that exists to have an impact on the law.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security is expected to face reinvigorated oversight and scrutiny in the next Congress, as top Democrats pledge to pursue investigations into the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement approach, allegations of corruption and other issues at DHS.

With their new majorities in the House and Senate following Tuesday’s midterm elections, Democrats are previewing plans to pursue aggressive oversight and investigations at DHS, ranging from Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s rapid expansion to staffing cuts at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-Miss.) will seek the chairmanship of the House Homeland Security Committee, a position he previously held from 2019 through 2023. In a statement, he said the Trump administration “will finally be faced with real oversight” next year.

“We will have much on our plate after congressional Republicans have sat on their hands doing nothing for two years, but we will not shy away from what the American people demand of us,” Thompson said. “We will investigate the administration weaponizing DHS against Americans, its out of control immigration policies, and its blatantly corrupt self-dealing. The American people expect nothing less, and we will deliver.”

In a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Wednesday, Thompson demanded written confirmation that DHS would comply with records preservation requirements. He also pushed DHS to provide by Dec. 2 all information and documents sought by the committee over the last two years.

Meanwhile in the Senate, with Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.) retiring, Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) is anticipated to take the gavel at the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.

“The new majorities in Congress must focus on affordability and accountability for the American people,” Hassan said in a statement. “We must use every tool at our disposal to rein in this President, end this illegal war in Iran, and reverse his tariffs. And as part of my new role on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, we will investigate and expose the corruption that is hurting taxpayers and Americans.”

Hassan has already posted job openings seeking “investigators and oversight counsel to lead investigations” at the homeland security committee. Open positions include an anti-corruption counsel and a policy advisor for AI security and safety issues.

Democrats’ oversight activities in the minority over the last two years offer a preview of what they may do next year with the power to call hearings, issue subpoenas and advance legislation.

Immigration enforcement is expected to be the top issue. Democrats on the House Homeland Security Committee have repeatedly pushed back against the Trump administration’s aggressive deportation agenda.

Democrats, including those on the appropriations committees, have raised repeated questions about how DHS is spending an influx of funds from the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act, as well as this year’s Secure America Act. Much of that funding went to ICE and Customs and Border Protection.

Thompson and Democrats on the homeland security committee have also sought investigations into ICE’s hiring practices, as the agency has more than doubled in size by hiring 12,000 new personnel under the Trump administration.

Democrats on the house committee have also pledged to investigate what they have called “the weaponization” of DHS, including reports on the department’s use of watchlists, biometric tools, data collection, social media monitoring, and other intelligence capabilities.

Kristina Moore, a former congressional investigator who now advises companies as partner at Womble Bond Dickinson, said “it’s pretty predictable” that ICE will be at the top of list of targets within DHS.

“In terms of, how are decisions made, who facilitated in making those decisions, who was hired, and then within that, is there any waste, fraud, and abuse?” Moore told Federal News Network. “Was a contract obtained because of a kickback? Was a contract obtained because of a relationship? Was it a no bid contract?”

Democrats are expected to target companies tied to allegations of corruption, including at DHS. Lawmakers have raised repeated questions about spending decisions at DHS, including many issues stemming from former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem’s tenure at DHS. In October, for instance, Thompson and his colleagues sent a letter to DHS seeking more information about the department’s purchase 10 luxury jets from a company owned by a political donor connected to Noem.

Moore said she advises companies that believe they might be swept up in any DHS-related inquires to be prepared to respond to congressional investigators and engage before lawmakers feel compelled to flex their subpoena powers.

“I would advise clients that you don’t want to be that company that Congress feels like they have to make the example out of,” Moore said.

Beyond ICE and immigration enforcement, meanwhile, House and Senate Democrats have also put a spotlight on staffing cuts at other DHS components, in particular CISA and the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

Democrats and Republicans have also introduced a slew of bills in recent months aimed at strengthening the government’s approach to AI security, including efforts within DHS.

Tonya Ugoretz, a cybersecurity leader at consulting firm PwC and former senior cyber official at the FBI, said she expects lawmakers in the new Congress to closely examine cybersecurity capacity across the federal government, not just at CISA.

“We’ll see more congressional scrutiny overall, both on the cybersecurity resourcing and preparedness within the federal government, as well as clarity around which government agencies will have a role when it comes to being the main interfaces with some of the developers of the new frontier AI capabilities,” Ugoretz told Federal News Network.

text:
As previously reported, the FY 2027 DV Lottery will remain on pause once more. On October 29th, 2026, the Ninth Circuit stayed a lower court’s order requiring the State Department to open DV-2027 registration and administer the DV Program. The appeal remains pending, but for now the government does not have to do anything.

Background

In August 2026, Red Eagle Law, L.C. filed suit against Secretary of State Marco Rubio for failing to open the FY 2027 DV Registration period. Red Eagle Law is a San Diego County law firm that specializes in helping DV winners. They alleged that by not opening the DV Program, they were losing money because many of their clients are DV Winners.

Judge Jinsook Ohta of the US District Court for the Southern District of California entered a Preliminary Injunction requiring the State Department to open DV-2027 registration and adjudicate DV-2027 cases. The order included several deadlines, including notifying DV Winners by December 3rd. The Government quickly filed an appeal.

Ninth Circuit Stays Lower Court’s Decision

A panel of judges consisting of Judge McKeown, Judge Smith, and Judge Thomas determined that the government was likely to prevail on appeal. One reason why was who filed the lawsuit. Congress created the Diversity Visa program to encourage immigration from countries with low admission rates, and the panel found that a law firm’s revenue from representing selectees falls outside the interests the statute protects. Notably, the only Plaintiff was Red Eagle Law. There were no prospective applicants or DV winners who filed suit. Judge Smith concurred that the law firms’ injuries were too hypothetical to file a suit.

The panel did make one thing clear. Granting the stay doesn’t mean it endorses the State Department’s decision to leave the program closed.

What Happens Next?

The DV-2027 registration will remain closed until further notice. There is currently no ETA for when the DV Program will be reopened. The injunction deadlines will be paused until the appeal is resolved. Red Eagle Law stated they will continue to fight and can petition the entire Ninth Circuit or the Supreme Court to hear their case. We may also see more lawsuits filed against the government.

No one can apply for the FY 2027 DV Lottery since registration has not opened. If any website or person tells you that they applied for you, please be aware this is not true. Keep an eye on the travel.state.gov website for updates.

text:
(The Center Square) — New York can continue restricting county sheriffs from cooperating with federal immigration enforcement crackdowns while a legal challenge over the law plays out in court, a federal judge has ruled.

The ruling by U.S. District Court judge Mae A. D'Agostino rejected a request from 15 New York county sheriffs for a preliminary injunction to block the restrictions with Attorney General Letitia James's office pursuing separate legal challenges to force sheriffs to cancel so-called 287(g) agreements and federal housing contracts with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

A lawsuit filed in August by Rensselaer County Sheriff Kyle Bourgault and 14 other sheriffs alleges that a provision of the newly enacted "Local Cops Local Crimes Act" banning 287 (g) agreements with ICE is an illegal overreach by the state government that interferes with contractual agreements between counties and the federal government.

The sheriffs claimed in court filings that the new restrictions would "go further" than limiting immigration cooperation to "nullify the ability of independently elected constitutional officers to enter into contracts authorized by federal law" and have asked the court to declare them unconstitutional.

"Local law enforcement should be focused on keeping New Yorkers safe, not carrying out the administration's cruel mass deportation agenda," James said in a statement in response to the latest ruling. "We will continue to defend our laws in court."

But D'Agostino ruled that the sheriffs had not proven they have legal authority to bring their constitutional claims against the state, citing a New York law that restricts the ability of local governments to challenge state laws on constitutional grounds.

"Although some scholars have called for a reform of the legal landscape to allow local governments to sue their parent state, the current state of the law does not appear to allow for such a suit," D'Agostino wrote in the 28-page ruling. "Indeed, Plaintiffs have not presented a single case which states that an independently elected sheriff may indeed sue in his official capacity to protect the duties of his office."

In a statement, Bourgault vowed to press on with the legal challenge and defended sheriffs' use of immigration screening at county jails, saying it gives law enforcement "important information" about individuals in custody.

"'We are reviewing the ruling and determining the next course of action," Bourgault said in a statement. "This screening is an effective tool for law enforcement. We utilize this screening to gather information on those brought to our facility and their past crimes and whether they are wanted here or abroad."

"That is basic but very necessary information, and the state has yet to tell us how they are improving safety by not allowing screening of illegal migrants," he added.

The legal fight over the ICE agreements is part of a mountain of litigation surrounding the Local Cops, Local Crimes Act, which also bans ICE agents from wearing masks and restricts ICE's access to schools, churches, courthouses and other "sensitive" locations. A federal judge in August temporarily blocked the ICE mask ban.

New York is also being sued by the Department of Justice over the new law, and federal prosecutors secured an injunction temporarily blocking a ban on ICE agents from wearing masks during immigration enforcement operations while legal fight plays out in court. James has filed a countersuit to uphold the law.

The issue was featured in the governor's race with GOP gubernatorial nominee and Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman and his running mate, Madison County Sheriff Todd Hood, in support of the ICE agreements. Blakeman was defeated in Tuesday's election after Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul won another four year term in office.

text:
The day after a blue tsunami swept across the United States in the midterm elections, The View cohost and former Trump White House communications director Alyssa Farah Griffin weighed in on the Republican Party’s crushing defeat, pointing to President Donald Trump‘s aggressive immigration policies and controversial ICE enforcement tactics as one of the reasons even longtime conservative voters had turned against his administration.

On the Behind the Table podcast with producer Brian Teta, Griffin, who has been an outspoken critic of her former boss, argued that the administration had taken its immigration agenda too far, mistaking Americans’ desire for a secure border for support for increasingly extreme enforcement measures.

“When you see deep ruby red pockets of the country rejecting this presidency, it’s because of policies he chose to put in place, which are not traditionally Republican policies. And then I would add the ICE enforcement,” explained Griffin. “I did not grow up in a Republican party where we basically betrayed immigrants, and we wanted them out of this country, and we hated the ones who were here illegally.”

“That is not what George Bush stood for. That’s not what John McCain stood for. That’s not what Mitt Romney stood on,” explained Griffin. “They overreached, and they thought that this sort of casual, frankly, racism that permeates a lot of this administration was how a lot of the country feels. And we don’t. And we sent a message. We wanted the border secured. We do not want to see the ICE enforcement that we’ve seen.”

“And one of the most striking images that I saw from last night, I forgot to pull it up on the show, was people putting their ‘I voted’ stickers at the spot where Alex Pretti was killed and at the spot where Renée Good was and others. It was literally saying they are not here to vote, but we are voting for you and for what your death represented,” said Griffin.

Griffin went on to state, “Politicians take this idea of ‘I was elected,’ and then they want to go to the most extreme version of what that could mean. And this is Donald Trump’s legacy now. There’s no coming back from this.”

text:
​​​​​​​​​​​FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

Media Contacts

press@oag.maryland.gov

410-576-7009

BALTIMORE, MD – Attorney General Anthony G. Brown and a multistate coalition of 22 attorneys general and Pennsylvania’s governor secured an important victory in court that stops the federal government’s imposition of unlawful immigration-enforcement conditions on congressionally authorized public safety grants, including grants dedicated to juvenile justice and grants intended to keep law enforcement officers safe and fight crime.

District of Rhode Island Chief Judge John J. McConnell, Jr. declared the Trump administration’s actions unlawful and permanently enjoined any implementation or enforcement of these conditions.

“By threatening to pull funding from police and violence prevention programs, the Trump Administration risked Marylanders’ safety to pressure our State into doing Washington’s immigration work,” said Attorney General Brown. “This ruling secures the resources that keep Maryland law enforcement and the communities they serve safe from crime.”

Last year, the Trump administration, disregarding the clear letter of the law and intent of Congress, declared that states would be unable to access Victims of Crime Act (VOCA) funds unless they agreed to the administration’s extreme immigration demands. The multistate coalition succeeded in getting the federal government to remove those conditions on over $1.3 billion of VOCA funds.

The Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Formula Grants (known as the Byrne JAG Program) was affected by these unlawful conditions. For decades, regardless of which political party held power, the Byrne JAG Program has been the leading federal source of criminal justice funding to state and local governments.

In Maryland, DOJ grants fund a broad range of programs and services supporting public safety, victim services, and the administration of justice. For example, the Baltimore City Sheriff’s Office Safe Pathways project uses Byrne State Crisis Intervention Program funds, which is separate from the Byrne JAG Program and would also have been affected by these conditions, to support firearm safe-storage education, community outreach, behavioral health referrals, and violence prevention. The program has served more than 17,000 individuals, engaged over 10,400 participants, conducted 97 outreach events, delivered 890 firearm safety trainings, and made 173 referrals for supportive services.

Civil immigration enforcement is a federal responsibility and not a state government responsibility. The Trump administration’s unlawful attempts to coerce states into doing their bidding conflict with core principles of American governance: the separation of powers and federalism. The administration’s actions violated laws passed by Congress as well as the Spending Clause of the U.S. Constitution.

Joining Attorney General Brown in this lawsuit were the attorneys general of California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Hawaiʻi, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin, as well as the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.

authors: MICHAEL KUNZELMAN, REBECCA SANTANA and SAFIYAH RIDDLE, Associated Press, MICHAEL KUNZELMAN, REBECCA SANTANA, SAFIYAH RIDDLE
description:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's administration held secret talks with Iran on deporting Iranians even as the war there dragged on, court documents obtained by The Associated Press show.
A legal group representing Iranians held by Immigration and Customs Enforcement said a dozen Iranian detainees had been given notice over the past week that they would be deported to Iran.
The legal group, the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund, brought the lawsuit in which the transcript was released.
None of the detainees who have been contacted have been provided any information in writing from immigration authorities, the legal group said.
Follow the AP's coverage of the Iran war at https://apnews.com/hub/iran.
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's administration held secret talks with Iran on deporting Iranians even as the war there dragged on, court documents obtained by The Associated Press show.

The court documents unsealed Thursday show the Republican administration as recently as mid-October said it had plans to deport the Iranians through an unnamed third country, although it was unclear when it intended to do so. The judge in the case ordered the government to give the court 24-hour notice of any finalized plans to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country and five days' written notice before any such deportation is carried out.

“We are at war with a country where the President of the United States has said, as recently as two or three days ago, if not yesterday, that it is essentially lawless ... A country that is an enemy of the United States, according to the current president. A country that, according to our president, murdered tens of thousands of protestors,” Judge Ana Reyes said according to the Oct. 15 transcript.

“And what you’re telling me is that the United States of America is going to send individuals back to that region, facing what you and I and everyone who would ever look at this would know would be, at a minimum, a serious threat of certain death.”

“Yes, your honor,” Justice Department attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel said. “The government is executing lawful orders of removal.”

Georgiev-Remmel told the court there was no specific date set to carry out any removals. A legal group representing Iranians held by Immigration and Customs Enforcement said a dozen Iranian detainees had been given notice over the past week that they would be deported to Iran. The legal group, the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund, brought the lawsuit in which the transcript was released.

The court documents show that the administration maintained contacts with Iranian officials during the war over the removals, specifically for submitting travel documents and figuring out “possible avenues for removal.”

The Department of Homeland Security and the State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Lawsuit has been challenging deportations of Iranian asylum seekers

The development emerged from an ongoing lawsuit that alleges the Trump administration’s immigration agencies have been sharing confidential information about Iranian asylum seekers with the Iranian government, violating national immigration regulations and endangering countless Iranians, court filings argue.

The Iranian American Legal Defense Fund said Thursday at least 12 Iranian detainees have been contacted by the Iranian Interest Section, an Iranian representative office in the Pakistani Embassy in Washington that handles consular affairs, in the past week and notified of an upcoming deportation flight to Iran through Pakistan. The group did not say when the deportation would occur.

One of those detainees attempted suicide once he learned he might be returned to Iran, according to Yasmine Chubin, the executive director of the organization. He was one of two people who were subsequently moved across state lines to a detention center in Texas, where detainees are often relocated immediately preceding a removal.

None of the detainees who have been contacted have been provided any information in writing from immigration authorities, the legal group said.

Activists abroad have expressed concern about deportees returning to Iran, whose theocracy has been cracking down on intellectuals and where the government vociferously cracks down on any dissent.

The lawsuit depicts a coordinated campaign between the U.S. and Iranian governments to identify Iranians in ICE custody and pressure them to return to Iran — a marked departure from decades of diplomatic hostility between the two governments. DHS has denied that it is sharing asylum application records with the Iranian government.

Hundreds of emails exchanged between U.S. immigration officials exposed how the two countries worked together to arrange for more than 100 Iranians to be flown back to Iran on three immigration flights in September and December 2025 and January 2026.

Deportations of Iranians have been historically rare

During the Oct. 15 hearing, Reyes warned government attorneys that she would initiate contempt proceedings if the administration violated her order to give the court advance notice of any planned deportation flights.

“We are talking about sending individuals in our care and custody to a country that we have bombed and we may continue bombing, and is a declared enemy of this country,” Reyes said.

In a court filing Wednesday, the Justice Department said the judge’s order effectively served as an injunction against the government “given the possibility of sanctions and contempt dangling overhead.”

Deportations of Iranians back to their home country are historically rare, owing to the lack of diplomatic relations between the U.S. and Iran and the possible persecution they could face if they were sent to Iran.

But under the Trump administration, which is carrying out a broad immigration crackdown, ICE has aggressively pushed to deport people even from countries that have typically been reluctant to take people back or with whom the U.S. has had icy or no diplomatic relations.

Sometimes that has meant sending people back to their home country, but it has also meant deporting people to other countries they have no connection with.

The Trump administration has deported people, including Iranians, to countries other than their own in an attempt to circumvent diplomatic hurdles with governments that won’t take their people back. During Trump’s second term, countries including El Salvador, Costa Rica and Panama have accepted noncitizens from the U.S.

In June, an Iranian woman was among two dozen migrants the U.S. deported to the Central African Republic.

text:
A federal judge has denied a request from 15 New York county sheriffs seeking to temporarily block enforcement of a state law restricting cooperation between local law enforcement agencies and federal immigration authorities.

In a decision issued Wednesday, Nov. 4, U.S. District Judge Mae A. D’Agostino denied the sheriffs’ motion for a preliminary injunction against New York’s Local Cops, Local Crimes Act.

The law, signed by Gov. Hochul on May 27, 2026, prohibits local law enforcement agencies from entering into or maintaining certain agreements with federal immigration authorities, including agreements under Section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act.

Those agreements allow trained local officers to perform certain federal immigration enforcement functions under federal supervision.

The lawsuit, led by Rensselaer County Sheriff Kyle Bourgault, challenges the law on constitutional grounds, arguing that it interferes with existing federal agreements and the authority of independently elected sheriffs.

The sheriffs sought to prevent the state from enforcing the law while their legal challenge proceeds.

However, D’Agostino ruled that the sheriffs had not demonstrated they were likely to have the legal authority to bring their constitutional claims against the state.

Under New York law, local governments and their officials generally cannot challenge state legislation on constitutional grounds unless they qualify for certain limited exceptions.

The judge determined that the sheriffs had not sufficiently established that those exceptions applied to their request.

The court did not resolve the underlying constitutional arguments.

Following the ruling, Bourgault said his office was evaluating its options.

We are reviewing the ruling and determining the next course of action.

The sheriff defended the use of immigration-related screening at the county jail, arguing that it provides law enforcement with important information about individuals in custody, saying,

This screening is an effective tool for law enforcement. We utilize this screening to gather information on those brought to our facility and their past crimes and whether they are wanted here or abroad. That is basic but very necessary information, and the state has yet to tell us how they are improving safety by not allowing screening of illegal migrants.

According to court documents, Rensselaer County entered into its first 287(g) agreement with federal immigration authorities in 2018, with its current agreement signed in March 2020.

Under the agreement, trained correction officers assist federal immigration authorities in identifying and processing individuals already in custody.

Bourgault argued that terminating the agreement would limit his office’s law enforcement capabilities and could result in additional enforcement action by the state.

Rensselaer County Executive Steve McLaughlin also criticized the restrictions, saying,

We are committed to protecting common-sense law enforcement tools, such as screening of all brought to our county jail, including citizens and illegal migrants. We want the ability to know whether a person is wanted on charges elsewhere before they are released back into our communities.

McLaughlin also criticized Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James, saying he would hold them responsible if someone released from custody harmed a resident, saying,

Any illegal that is released and harms one of our citizens, as has already unfortunately happened, I will as County Executive hold Kathy Hochul and Letitia James personally responsible.

In a social media post, the Attorney General stated:

Legal challenge remains ongoing

The court’s decision also details efforts by the New York Attorney General’s Office to obtain information about Rensselaer County’s compliance with the law.

According to court documents, the state sought an order in August compelling the Rensselaer County Sheriff’s Office to terminate its 287(g) agreement.

Bourgault also raised concerns about potential impacts on state funding for law enforcement equipment.

The sheriffs argued that the law violated several provisions of the U.S. and New York constitutions, including protections related to existing contracts and the authority of local officials.

However, D’Agostino concluded that the plaintiffs had not established a sufficient legal basis to obtain the requested injunction.

The ruling leaves the state’s restrictions in place while the broader legal dispute remains unresolved.

The decision does not dismiss the lawsuit or make a final determination on whether the challenged law is constitutional.

text:
Harmeet Dhillon stepped down as head of the Department of Justice's (DOJ) Civil Rights Division after Democrats' sweeping midterm victories, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced on Thursday.

"Today, I accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who led the Civil Rights Division with conviction the past 18 months," Blanche wrote on X.

"She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor," he added. "The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors."

Dhillon, a longtime ally of President Donald Trump, was confirmed by the Senate in April 2025 to lead the division, which enforces federal civil rights laws. During her tenure, the division shifted its priorities toward issues, including religious liberty and Second Amendment rights, while also pursuing cases involving voter rolls, immigration, and alleged antisemitism on college campuses.

The division also saw departures among career attorneys, followed by recruitment of lawyers with backgrounds in conservative advocacy, according to reports.

Dhillon's departure makes her the first senior DOJ official reported to be leaving after the election, as the administration prepares for a change in congressional control. Bloomberg Law reported that other political appointees could also leave before the end of the year.

Dhillon previously said she intended to return to private practice after her government service. She founded the Dhillon Law Group, a California-based firm focused on civil rights, free speech and election law.

title: Trump Squandered the GOP's Immigration Advantage - City Journal
description:
The Trump administration severely misunderstood this immigration mandate, confusing America’s desire for a strong border policy and nationwide immigration enforcement with a wish for a dramatic expansion of the enforcement duties of the federal government.
Democrat James Talarico’s Senate win in Texas was especially striking along the border, where immigration enforcement has been particularly visible.
George H. W. Bush, for example, signed the Immigration Act of 1990, which expanded lawful admissions while strengthening nationwide immigration enforcement.
The Trump administration also erred in allowing images of masked agents making arrests in public to define its enforcement agenda.
The Trump administration could have instead ramped up tracking of visa overstays by verifying departures, or pursued legislation to punish employers who knowingly hire illegal aliens.
text:
0:00To use this feature you must register.

Tuesday’s midterm election was a bloodbath for the Republican Party. Democrats captured both chambers of Congress and flipped both the governor’s office and a Senate seat in Texas for the first time in more than three decades, among other stunning gains.

While the results may have been a shock, they should not come as a surprise. In 2024, voters gave Republicans a mandate to restore control over America’s borders and reverse the failed immigration policy of the Biden administration, which had stood by as illegal border encounters surged by nearly 11 million over four years.

The Trump administration severely misunderstood this immigration mandate, confusing America’s desire for a strong border policy and nationwide immigration enforcement with a wish for a dramatic expansion of the enforcement duties of the federal government. By doing so, they squandered Republican’s long-standing messaging advantage on immigration and lost one of the largest voter demographics that helped Trump and the GOP cruise to victory in 2024: Hispanics and Latinos, who now make up one in five Americans.

Trump won 43 percent of the Latino vote in 2024, up from 35 percent in 2020. Two years later, Republicans wiped out these gains and then some. Only about one-third of Latino voters backed Republican House candidates in this week’s midterms; roughly six in ten supported Democrats. Exit polls imply that Latino men, in particular, swung 25 points toward Democrats—a decisive shift.

The effect was palpable in specific races. Democrat James Talarico’s Senate win in Texas was especially striking along the border, where immigration enforcement has been particularly visible. Cameron County, home to Brownsville, Texas, backed Trump with 52.5 percent of the vote in 2024. On Tuesday, Talarico took 68.4 percent of the county’s vote against Ken Paxton’s 29.9 percent.

In South Florida, Congresswoman María Elvira Salazar, a Republican who criticized the Trump’s administration overreach on immigration, won by nearly 21 points in 2024. On Tuesday night, she barely survived Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez by less than 100 votes (and those results may change as the race heads into a recount). The race of Representative Mario Diaz-Balart, another Cuban-American Republican, also remained too close to call as of Wednesday morning.

The warning signs began to appear well before Election Day. Among Hispanics who voted for Trump in 2024, the president’s approval fell from 93 percent early in his second term to 57 percent this fall.

Did the GOP lose with Hispanics because it followed through on its immigration enforcement promises? Not at all. Hispanics and Latinos still favor enforcement. In an April survey, for example, 62 percent of Hispanic voters supported strong border enforcement. And last November, more than two-thirds of Hispanic Americans said they supported deporting at least some illegal immigrants.

But these views are nuanced. In the April poll, 85 percent backed creating more pathways for people seeking to immigrate legally. And eight in ten said that Trump should focus on deporting those who committed serious crimes. Many Hispanic voters, in other words, favor enforcement, but not indiscriminate enforcement, and want it alongside expanded immigration.

There’s reason to believe these views drove Hispanics’ leftward shift. In a poll from just before the election, “immigration policy, deportations, and ICE” were the top priority for Latino voters—40.7 percent of respondents put these issues among their top three concerns, compared to 39.6 percent who identified combating corruption and 37.8 prioritizing abortion.

Republicans used to understand better the delicate politics of immigration. George H. W. Bush, for example, signed the Immigration Act of 1990, which expanded lawful admissions while strengthening nationwide immigration enforcement. Though Republicans have traditionally sided with immigration restrictionists, they have also recognized that America benefits by welcoming legal immigrants. The American people get to choose whom to admit, and those admitted will get a fair shot at building a new life in the greatest country on earth.

The Trump administration’s narrow immigration vision has damaged that bargain. In January, it paused immigrant visa issuance for dozens of countries, including Venezuela and Cuba, whose people overwhelmingly vote Republican after achieving citizenship. (A court order ended the pause in August.) Republicans in the House and Senate had a hard time selling the message to their Hispanic constituencies that immigrants should get in line and wait their turn while the White House was essentially proposing to stop the line from moving at all.

The Trump administration also erred in allowing images of masked agents making arrests in public to define its enforcement agenda. Sixty-three percent of Americans considered identity-concealing face coverings unacceptable for immigration officers. Public support for law enforcement depends on public confidence, and a government that demands accountability from immigrants should also ensure that its own agents are held accountable for their actions.

Moreover, while deportations are a legitimate and necessary enforcement tool, the White House’s reliance on public roundups as its principal approach has undermined that legitimacy. The Trump administration could have instead ramped up tracking of visa overstays by verifying departures, or pursued legislation to punish employers who knowingly hire illegal aliens. There was plenty of room for improvement on visa overstays when Trump took office: between 2021 and 2024, more than 21,885 visa overstays had produced just 496 investigations and eight arrests.

Republicans can win back Hispanic Americans’ trust on immigration policy by returning to the original bargain. That means combining secure borders with a legal immigration system that prioritizes immigrants who are likely to be a net economic benefit. It also means enforcing final removal orders with due process, prioritizing public safety, and no longer imposing sweeping barriers on eligible visa applicants.

The Hispanic voters who supported Trump and the GOP in 2024 were entitled to expect competent government. Making lawful immigration harder was no substitute for delivering it.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security is more heavily scrutinizing immigrants’ tax records, issuing denials of citizenship for those on IRS payment plans or who have sought filing extensions.

It’s a stark departure from past practices for evaluating whether would-be citizens meet the agency’s “good moral character” standard, where an applicant’s willingness to pay taxes, including through payment plans, was previously considered positive evidence in an applicant’s case for naturalization, attorneys said.

But the policy shift at US Citizenship and Immigration Services makes those circumstances a new hurdle for would-be citizens amid plummeting naturalization rates in President Trump’s second term.

Tax payments came under sharper review after a policy memorandum issued last year directed officers to take a “holistic” approach to evaluating good moral character, including evidence of community involvement, educational background, and compliance with tax obligations. Prior to the memo, unless there was a tax-related charge or conviction, they weren’t used against applicants, attorneys said.

Bloomberg Law reviewed multiple naturalization denials shared by attorneys based solely on participation in a payment plan or request of a filing extension.

Citing agreements with the IRS to file taxes later or pay in installments in citizenship denials goes well beyond the intent of federal immigration statute and the language of USCIS regulations, said Doug Rand, a former senior official at the agency.

“It’s completely looney tunes,” he said, predicting attorneys would successfully appeal the denials. “It’s a waste of time, especially when the agency has all these big backlogs. But the political leadership doesn’t care.”

The administration, meanwhile, defended its ability to review all factors.

“Ensuring tax compliance is a long-standing legal requirement this administration will not overlook,” said Zach Kahler, a spokesman USCIS.

The IRS didn’t respond to a request for comment.

More Time to File

It’s a common misconception that a filing extension defers the deadline to pay, but taxpayers must still make an estimated payment of what they owe. Not doing so results in a civil penalty.

Those who requested a filing extension but didn’t pay by the deadline are having their naturalization applications denied, as are those paying taxes on installments.

For example, Lily Axelrod, an immigration attorney in Memphis, said one such client was denied for naturalization last month shortly after her husband took the citizenship oath.

“She’s not had a single immigration violation,” Axelrod said.

USCIS’ rejection stated her request for a filing extension and failure to pay on time without extenuating circumstances was “an unlawful act that adversely affects your moral character.” That language is typical in recent denials, even for applicants with no criminal records or history of sanctions by the IRS.

“USCIS is being more harsh than the IRS itself,” said Michelle Marty Rivera, an immigration and tax lawyer based in Miami.

Moral Character Test

Demonstrating good moral character has been a requirement for citizenship since the passage of the first naturalization law in the 18th century.

Evaluations focused on criminal histories, although the USCIS policy manual statesthat an immigrant who fails to file or fully pay their taxes may be precluded from meeting the criteria.

Examples cited in the manual, however, involve denials of immigration benefits because of convictions for tax evasion and conspiracy to defraud the government.

“Previously the immigration system tried to reward people for participating in the tax system,” said Sarah Krieger, senior policy counsel at the National Immigration Law Center.

Finding applicants lack good moral character based on that one factor alone “would violate not just the statute and regulation, but their own recent policy,” she added.

Denial Details

The rejections by USCIS describe failure to fully pay tax obligations as an “unlawful act.” Several noted that the applicant hadn’t demonstrated extenuating circumstances for failing to pay all taxes on time.

Eric Welsh, a partner of Reeves Immigration Law Group, said each of the 12 attorneys at his firm has received a similar decision involving extensions and payment plans.

“Those do not per se indicate that a person lacks good moral character,” Welsh said. “That’s the problem with the good moral character standard, they’re so fuzzy.”

Kathleen Campbell Walker, immigration practice group chair at Dickinson Wright PLLC, said one client married to a US citizen was denied a naturalization request because of her spouse’s payment plans with the IRS — even though the policy memo states that such agreements shouldn’t be considered an adverse factor.

“There’s no doubt we have a different approach now to utilizing what’s lawful under the internal revenue code,” she said.

Scrutinizing Naturalization

Lora Ries, director of the Border Security and Immigration Center at the conservative Heritage Foundation, said good moral character was a “low hurdle to clear,” where officers looked for negative marks as opposed to the burden of proof being on the immigrant.

“This administration is saying, no, that’s the wrong approach,” Ries said. “You need to show evidence of good moral character. It’s not just, we don’t find anything negative.”

But USCIS officers don’t have the training or background in tax law to make those determinations, said Shev Dalal-Dheini, senior director of government relations at the American Immigration Lawyers Association. The tax scrutiny is another way for USCIS to stifle naturalizations, she said.

Sal Macias, an attorney in Phoenix, said immigrants are doing everything they can to meet a standard that’s constantly in flux.

He said one client, a green card holder of nearly 40 years, was approved for a naturalization oath ceremony. But documents reviewed by Bloomberg Law show the client was denied for being on a payment plan. The client has chosen to wait a few more years before trying again.

“I was actually happy that he decided to seek counsel instead of just doing it on his own,” Macias said. “It makes me feel inept at times to give advice that continues to shift on almost a weekly basis, especially when it comes to immigration proceedings that can take months, if not years, to have an outcome.”

text:
Harmeet Dhillon plans to step down from her role leading the Justice Department’s civil rights unit, marking the first senior DOJ official to resign following Democrats’ massive midterm wins.

Dhillon, who has vastly transformed the Civil Rights Division since her Senate confirmation in April 2025, has told allies that she would be leaving the department after the midterm elections, according to four people familiar. Her official announcement is expected as soon as Thursday, two of the individuals said.

Dhillon and DOJ spokespeople didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

The staunch Trump ally leaves behind a Civil Rights Division that’s shifted toward conservative causes, including religious liberties and the formation of a Second Amendment section. Following the mass exodus of career attorneys from the division, she’s recruited dozens of new attorneys with backgrounds steeped in conservative advocacy to work on litigation over state voter rolls, immigration, and alleged antisemitism on college campuses.

Former officials said the department is bracing for multiple other top political appointees to exit in the lame duck period before the New Year. Dhillon would be the second Senate-confirmed DOJ official to depart in recent weeks, following Patrick Davis’ resignation from the Office of Legislative Affairs last month.

Dhillon, a former Republican Party official and campaign lawyer for President Donald Trump, previously indicated in an August roundtable interview with Bloomberg reporters and editors that she planned to return to her California-based law firm, Dhillon Law Group, following her tenure at DOJ.

The firm, which has been managed by her brother Mandeep Singh Dhillon in her absence, is now much smaller than it once was, Dhillon said at the time.

“In terms of private practice, when the president is done with me, I loved being a lawyer in private practice,” Dhillon said, adding that she planned to take what she learned from her time at DOJ and “continue to help plaintiffs.”

Federal immigration authorities must take charge of removing an accused rapist from Guam before any plea deal can move forward, stalling resolution of the case.

Superior Court Judge Alberto Tolentino ordered all parties Thursday to return with revised terms the next day, Friday, making it clear sentencing would be delayed unless U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, ICE, oversees deportation.

Amit Das is facing four misdemeanor counts of fourth-degree sexual assault after allegedly assaulting a woman he knew in September 2025.

He was released on a $3,000 personal recognizance bond after his arrest.

Under the judge’s proposal, Das would plead guilty and receive a sentence, but the court would postpone executing it until ICE completes removal proceedings. Tolentino insisted federal authorities, not the local court, must supervise deportation and monitor any attempt by Das to reenter the country.

“Plead straight up. You have a guilty plea. All right, you have a guilty conviction. Hold off on execution of that sentence until he is removed by ICE. End of story,” Tolentino said.

The proposed sentence length remains in dispute.

A draft plea agreement previously called for 15 years. At Thursday’s hearing, prosecuting attorney John David Griffin said prosecutors sought a 25-year term, but defense attorney Joaquin “Jay” Arriola rejected it.

“I don’t want 25 years. I got 15 here,” defense attorney Joaquin “Jay” Arriola said, holding up the hard copy of the proposed agreement.

No plea agreement has been finalized or accepted.

Attorneys continued to negotiate whether Das would plead guilty to specified charges or enter an open plea, and how ICE would become involved. Griffin said prosecutors would notify ICE after a guilty plea.

Arriola said the defense needed clear terms from the court before drafting another agreement.

Tolentino ordered parties to prepare a revised document for Friday. If the plea is finalized, Das may change his plea at that hearing.

Visa expiring

The dispute follows an Oct. 28 hearing where the court questioned a plan requiring Das to leave Guam voluntarily while a bench warrant was put out for his arrest. Tolentino warned that such a warrant could leave the case unresolved indefinitely, especially if Das left the island and later returned.

“The court’s not in the business of deporting or facilitating deportation,” he said at the time.

Tolentino offered to instead have ICE initiate removal proceedings and assume responsibility for deportation. The court could then accept a guilty plea, impose a sentence, and delay its execution while federal authorities completed the process.

Tolentino said he did not want the local court left to monitor Das’s movements or determine whether he had violated a deportation order by returning to the United States.

Arriola said he understood the court’s concerns about ICE involvement and the bench warrant, and asked Tolentino to review the government’s draft and specify necessary changes. He said Das was prepared to leave Guam and had already bought a ticket to India. The defense told the court Das was instructed to leave by Nov. 10.

Arriola warned Das could be left waiting if ICE did not act.

“He’s going to sit out there Nov. 10 … he’s just going to be a sitting duck,” Arriola said.

Bonavita previously told the court that Das’s visa would expire on Oct. 31. At the Thursday hearing, Tolentino confirmed that Das’s visa had expired. Defense also previously told the court Das’s ticket was paid for the following day and that Das was to leave by Nov. 10.

Alleged 2025 sexual assault

Prosecutors allege a woman drinking with Das’s group in September 2025 became so intoxicated she could not walk without help. Others carried her to Das’s hotel room and left her alone with him, court documents state.

Prosecutors allege Das removed the woman’s shorts and sexually assaulted her. The woman told police she tried to resist, and that Das restrained her and continued touching her after she moved to a couch.

Previous hearings stated that the victim supported the proposed deportation arrangement. Arriola told the court she agreed to the deal, while Tolentino said the court must still consider the public interest and its responsibility to enforce Guam law.

text:
ICE arrested a foreign college student at a California airport as she prepared to jet off on vacation, according to reports.

​Paula Valentina Albornoz Hernandez, 23, is now being held at the California City Detention Facility after being arrested at San Francisco International Airport on Friday as she waited to board a flight to Portland.

​Albornoz Hernandez’s attorneys at Centro Legal de la Raza told KRON4 that the University of California Berkeley student is from Colombia and has lived in the U.S. since 2022.

​Speaking to Berkeleyside, the student’s boyfriend, Anthony, said that the couple had been waiting in the airport gate area when an ICE agent in plain clothes approached them and said that Albornoz Hernandez looked familiar. The agent went on to guess two names before eventually saying her name on the third attempt.

​Albornoz Hernandez was separated from her boyfriend once her name had been confirmed and told that she was being detained as her visa had expired.

​“She entered the country on September 6, 2022, with legal permission to stay until March 6, 2023,” a DHS spokesperson told KRON4. “In defiance of our nation’s laws, she did not depart. She will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.”

The spokesperson added: “This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.”

​A DHS spokesperson also denied to Berkeleyside that the officer did not identify himself and said that “work authorization or a pending application does NOT confer legal status in the United States.”

​Attorney Niko De Bremaeker told the outlet that Albornoz Hernandez had overstayed her visa because she experienced “severe gender-based violence” in Colombia and had applied for asylum in the U.S. Her application is still pending, but De Bremaeker says that she had a valid work permit to attend San Jose City College.

​Albornoz Hernandez later transferred to Berkeley, where she conducted research on artificial intelligence.

​Following her arrest, the student is now being held at the California City Detention Facility, located in the eastern California desert.

​“I’ve been to many of our detention centers in the country, and that one certainly stands out as a dark page in our nation’s history,” he told SFGATE. “The treatment that people are undergoing there is inhumane.

​“The medical treatment has been described as being wholly insufficient by independent auditors.”

​A report published by the American Civil Liberties Union argued that the medical site at the facility had “inadequate staffing, incomplete training, a lack of on-site management, and insufficient clinical oversight.”

​Anthony told The San Francisco Chronicle that Albornoz Hernandez was transported to an ICE facility in Stockton before being moved to Sacramento, back to Stockton and then over to California City.

​“She’s been moving around a lot,” he told the outlet. “She said she’s doing okay; she’s calm, a little more calm than we are.”

​A habeas corpus petition filed by Centro Legal de la Raza in the U.S. District Court on Monday alleges that the arrest of Albornoz Hernandez violates both the U.S. Constitution and federal law as the student was not presented with a warrant or found to be a flight risk.

​The document, which was reviewed by Berkeleyside, also demands Albornoz Hernandez’s release and says that the government should be prevented from detaining her again unless it proves that she is a danger to the community or is a flight risk in a court hearing.

​U.C. Berkeley Chancellor Richard Lyons told KRON4 that the university is working to support the student.

“This student is a valued member of our community, and campus leadership is doing everything within our power to support them so that they may return to their life at Berkeley to continue their studies with us,” he said.

Democrats are continuing to build on historic gains in U.S. midterm elections, as late returns show Tuesday’s blue wave could rival Democrats’ sweep of the 1974 elections that followed the Watergate scandal. When the 120th Congress convenes in January, Democrats will control both chambers of Congress for the first time in four years. And this time, they’ll have significantly larger majorities. In the House, Democrats have won at least 240 seats compared to 147 for Republicans, with four dozen races yet to be called. Democrats are projected to surpass 250 seats in the House. In the Senate, the Democratic caucus will grow to at least 54 senators, with two races — Alaska and Mississippi — too close to call.

In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola leads incumbent Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan by just 637 votes, with nearly a quarter of ballots yet to be counted. Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system means it could take days or weeks to determine the winner.

Mississippi’s Senate race remains dramatically close, with the latest numbers showing Democrat Scott Colom ahead of incumbent Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by just 1,100 votes. Colom is now favored to win, as only a few thousand provisional ballots and late-arriving mail ballots remain to be counted.

In a lengthy social media post, Vice President JD Vance blamed historic Republican election losses squarely on the war on Iran. Vance wrote, “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.”

On Wednesday, reporters asked President Trump about Vance’s comments.

Reporter: “Mr. President, Vice President Vance says the reason Republicans lost the war — lost last night was the war in Iran.”

President Donald Trump: “Well, I think it’s largely true, because it drove the gasoline up a little bit, short term. And probably that’s — probably it’s true. But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again, because, long term, it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”

President Trump held his post-election news conference outside the White House ballroom he’s building, signing one of the beams.

Iran’s leadership responded to the U.S. election with a warning that any renewed attacks would draw a far wider response. A written statement attributed to Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei argued Iran’s control of the Strait of Hormuz had shattered the “myth of America’s invincibility.”

An Israeli court has extended the detention of Abed Abu Shehadeh, a journalist, community leader and Palestinian citizen of Israel who was abducted from his home in Jaffa late Tuesday by police officers and members of Israel’s Shin Bet. More than a dozen officers raided his home around midnight while his two children were present. They confiscated his laptop and phone. Abu Shehadeh is an editor at the news site Arab48 and a contributor to +972 Magazine and other outlets. Rights groups have described his arrest as part of a “campaign to silence” Palestinian journalists and activists. This is Abed Abu Shehadeh speaking at an event hosted by Jewish Currents in New York just three weeks ago.

Abed Abu Shehadeh: “I understand that people like me die every day where I come from, that in the past decades, from Iraq to Libya to Gaza to Syria, people who look like me, who dress like me, who pray like me, we die all the time. And I understand that I am from the peasants of the world, and this is something I have to live with.”

Amnesty International is a global movement of more than 10 million people who take injustice personally.
text:
5 November 2026

Responding to reports that two Uyghur men recently moved to an Immigration Detention Centre in Thailand face imminent forcible deportation to China, Amnesty International’s Secretary General Agnès Callamard said:

“Thai authorities must immediately halt any plans to forcibly return these two Uyghur men to China, where they face a real risk of torture, arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance. Thailand must not repeat last year’s unlawful deportation of 40 Uyghurs, who were forced back to danger in China.

“Thai authorities must now allow them access to a lawyer of their choice and, together with the international community, urgently find a safe and voluntary third-country solution for them and the other Uyghurs still detained in Thailand.”

Amnesty International’s Secretary General Agnès Callamard

“These two men fled persecution only to spend more than a decade detained in Thailand. Amnesty International has documented crimes against humanity against Uyghurs and other predominantly Muslim ethnic groups in Xinjiang. Returning them would expose them to the abuses they sought to escape.

“Both men have previously made clear to their legal representatives that they fear for their lives if returned to China and do not consent to being sent back. Thai authorities must now allow them access to a lawyer of their choice and, together with the international community, urgently find a safe and voluntary third-country solution for them and the other Uyghurs still detained in Thailand.

“No amount of diplomatic assurance from China can override Thailand’s obligations not to return anyone to a real risk of torture or other serious human rights violations. After more than a decade in detention, these men must be released and given the chance to rebuild their lives in safety and freedom “

Background

The two men are among five Uyghurs remaining in Thailand from a group of over 300 who were apprehended without charge by the Thai authorities on 13 March 2014 after they had fled persecution and discrimination in China’s Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.

On 21 October 2026, two of the five men were released from prison under a royal pardon and transferred to the Immigration Detention Centre in Bangkok. Since then, Thai authorities have denied the two men access to their lawyers, as well as blocked access to the men by civil society organizations and the National Human Rights Commission of Thailand.

The two men have spent more than 12 years in Thai detention. In June 2015, Thailand allowed 173 women and children from the group to travel to Türkiye but unlawfully deported at least 109 people to China.

A document obtained by Amnesty International shows that, on 7 January 2025, the Chinese embassy in Thailand sent a letter to Thailand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs requesting the “repatriation” of 45 Uyghur men who remained in the country. In February 2025, Thailand forcibly deported 40 of them, in breach international law. Five remained in a Thai prison to serve sentences related to an attempt to escape the Immigration Detention Centre.

Following the deportations, Thai authorities made two visits to Xinjiang in February and March 2025 at China’s invitation, as part of its efforts to provide diplomatic assurances. NGOs monitoring the case reported that Thai authorities were able to meet fewer than 10 deportees and that no subsequent updates have established that all are alive and safe; their whereabouts and wellbeing remain unknown. Amnesty International previously called on both governments to disclose the whereabouts of all 40 men.

Amnesty International opposes any use of diplomatic assurances that a person transferred would not be subjected to torture or other ill-treatment as it undermines the universality of the prohibition of torture and cannot be considered reliable. Thailand is bound by the Convention against Torture, and the principle of non-refoulement under international law, which prohibits States from returning or transferring anyone to a place where they would be at real risk of persecution or other human rights violations. Article 13 of Thailand’s Prevention and Suppression of Torture and Enforced Disappearance Act, in force since 2023, prohibits deportation where there are substantial grounds to believe a person would face torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, or enforced disappearance.

Amnesty International issued a groundbreaking report in 2021 documenting crimes against humanity of imprisonment, torture and persecution against Uyghurs, Kazakhs and other predominantly Muslim ethnic groups in Xinjiang. Despite similar UN findings released in an assessment report in August 2022, China has taken no steps to implement recommendations, remedy documented violations or investigate and hold accountable perpetrators. Instead, the government continues to silence criticism from those within and beyond its borders, issue counternarratives denying abuse and maintains its discriminatory and assimilationist policies.

Amnesty International is a global movement of more than 10 million people who take injustice personally. We are campaigning for a world where human rights are enjoyed by all – and we can only do it with your support.

text:
The Trump Administration continues to claim U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents are targeting the "worst of the worst" offenders during ongoing immigration enforcement operations across the country.

During Operation Metro Surge in Minnesota earlier this year, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) — stated repeatedly that they were detaining rapists and murderers who were roaming the streets of Minnesota after being released from custody.

But those claims quickly fell apart last winter when state officials released detailed records proving many of the "worst of the worst" offenders were already in custody, had been transferred to ICE, or had no criminal records in Minnesota.

"Thin I.C.E.", a new docuseries from FOX 9 Documentaries, details one state official's efforts to expose what he called "propaganda" from the federal government.

‘This became a propaganda game’

What they're saying:

"Every name was checked. Every record was checked," said Paul Schnell, Commissioner of the Minnesota Department of Corrections.

Schnell, a long-time police chief, said he tried to explain to DHS officials that the information released on social media and at press conferences was inaccurate.

"Even when they were checked, they continued to push it," Schnell said in an interview. "You can only assume that this became a propaganda game."

Video of ICE transfers

Why you should care:

Schenell said his department coordinates the transfer of any inmate into federal custody if they have what’s known as an ICE detainer.

Yet, DHS repeatedly claimed several offenders were detained after being released from prison by Gov. Tim Walz.

Schnell eventually held a press conference in which he showed video of offenders being physically transferred to federal agents.

"I think showing the video became just a clear indication of what's happening and how what was being said by some in the federal government and what was being shared with Minnesotans, simply didn't match up to reality," Schnell said in the upcoming documentary.

Gov. Tim Walz said Schnell’s decision to release the video was a "big turning point" during the surge.

"It became very clear that this was about retribution," Walz said.

ICE detainers

The other side:

The Trump Administration also claimed that county jails were releasing violent offenders instead of holding them for ICE agents.

"The root cause of it was the refusal to cooperate with federal law enforcement in the first place," Rep. Walter Hudson (R-Albertville) said in an interview for the documentary.

ICE claims undercut by prison and jail records

Dig deeper:

However, records analyzed by the FOX 9 Investigators undercut DHS claims that ICE agents were picking up people recently cut loose by county jails.

Dozens of the "worst of the worst" offenders did not have criminal records or had not been incarcerated in Minnesota in years.

"They're giving us names that have, in some cases, have never even been arrested in our state," Schnell said.

Schnell and Walz said communication with the federal government improved once Border Czar Tom Homan took over immigration operations.

"I said, ‘you're asking, are we cooperating?’ You have just found out that we have always cooperated with you in our state prisons, and he acknowledged that," Walz said.

Watch Thin I.C.E. documentary series

What's next:

Thin I.C.E. is a three-part series by FOX 9 Documentaries detailing the Trump Administration's immigration operations in Chicago and Minneapolis that resulted in constitutional challenges, violent tactics and deadly shootings.

Thin I.C.E. Part I: "Worst of the Worst" premieres Wednesday, Nov. 4 at 10:35 p.m. on FOX 9 and streaming on FOX LOCAL and the FOX 9 YouTube channel.

title: Outcry after ICE violently detains US citizen walking to high school - The Guardian
description:
