text:
The midterm losses could delay, but not prevent, another Iran escalation

Trump’s policies toward the Middle East undoubtedly contributed to Republicans’ midterm defeats, and he appears to recognize that. Trump has already publicly acknowledged that his war with Iran contributed to his loss. Moreover, his surprising announcement early on Election Day that he would end US financial support to Israel’s military in two months suggests that he sees that issue as a pressing political problem on the right and left. In Israel, Trump’s statement was seized upon by Gadi Eisenkot who will likely get the first chance to form a new government in the wake of last week’s elections. The growing threat to the bilateral relationship will be a top priority for the next Israeli prime minister.

The Iranian regime will undoubtedly see the results as another example of their form of “regime change” in Washington. If they make this view public, they risk encouraging a Trump decision to escalate. Before the elections, Trump had already reviewed war plans and ordered additional military forces to the region. Thus far, encouragingly, statements from Iran about the US election results have generally been de-escalatory.

That respite may prove temporary. Iran has a relatively consistent track record of miscalculation and overplaying its hand, and while a Democratic Congress has the power to stymie Trump’s domestic legislative agenda, it doesn’t have much ability to stop a president from exercising his powers as commander in chief.

Trump may eventually surmise that a diplomatic agreement along the lines of the previous Memorandum of Understanding would only reinforce perceptions that his war was an unmitigated disaster that damaged US national security, the Republican Party’s electoral prospects, and his personal legacy. The only way out, Trump may therefore conclude, is to win the war. That could lead to a decision to restart major combat operations, if not immediately, then in the months to come.

Trump may double down on energy policy

With Democrats having gained control of Congress, Trump is likely to lean more heavily on his substantial executive and foreign policy authority. Despite mounting legislative headwinds, the president faces a narrowing window to translate his priorities into durable policy and investment decisions before the 2028 presidential race takes hold.

Affordability dominated the run-up to yesterday’s elections, with a Reuters/Ipsos poll finding that 48 percent of registered voters identified the cost of living as their top voting issue. Retail gasoline and diesel prices have also risen sharply this year, reinforcing the political pressure on the administration. But with the midterms behind him, Trump may increasingly weigh near-term consumer-price concerns against longer-term strategic objectives. The tension will be particularly apparent in energy policy, where foreign policy ambitions, domestic industrial priorities, and consumer affordability do not always align.

That starts with Iran, where Trump may place greater weight on his long-term objective of preventing a nuclear-armed Iran than on short-term electoral considerations. His behavior before the 2025 and 2026 strikes demonstrates that diplomatic rhetoric and military escalation can coexist. Sustained economic pressure remains a likely course, with renewed military escalation a viable alternative, even at the expense of regional stability and energy prices.

Presidential power has its limits, however. Trump may seek an energy-centered resolution to the war in Ukraine in negotiations with Moscow, but achieving one is another matter. Bipartisan congressional resistance to sanctions relief on this side of the Atlantic and Europe’s determination to eliminate its dependence on Russian gas—backed by a legally mandated phaseout through 2027—present formidable obstacles. And this doesn’t even account for the fact that restoring Russian energy flows to Europe would undercut US liquefied natural gas export interests and Trump’s broader energy dominance agenda.

Beyond foreign policy and diplomatic ambitions, the president has considerably more latitude to advance his domestic energy agenda without the cooperation of foreign governments or Congress. Expect a renewed push to expand conventional energy production, export capacity, and the infrastructure needed to power the United States’ artificial intelligence (AI) and manufacturing ambitions. These priorities may offer limited near-term consumer-price relief, but they present the administration with an opportunity to translate executive authority into long-term infrastructure investment and commercial commitments that will be harder for future administrations to unwind.

Markets are unsure what to make of the Democratic sweep

Two years ago, as Trump was reelected to the presidency, bond yields shot up—as markets expected higher tariffs and more deficit spending. They were right. Two years later, as Democrats swept Congress, bond markets initially reacted in the opposite direction—on the belief that AI-related infrastructure spending would have to slow down and gridlock would mean fewer spending deals. This time, the markets may be mistaken.

The Democrats are planning a hundred-hour legislative blitz in January on a range of their priorities, including rolling back tariffs—which, based on exit polls, were among the least popular policies of Trump’s second term—and restoring cuts from Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act. All of that would increase the deficit.

The markets assume Trump will veto the full package. But it’s not so simple.

The strength of the Democrats’ majorities in both the House and Senate means they will enter two major fiscal fights in a strong negotiating position. First up will be federal government appropriations, as current funding only runs through December 11. The lame-duck Congress may pass a continuing resolution, but in 2027 a budget fight will almost certainly take place. It could happen at the same time that the US hits the debt ceiling—the $41 trillion limit is projected to be breached sometime in the first half of the year. The Democrats will insist on their spending priorities as a condition of reaching an agreement. Don’t be surprised to see some deals in the coming year—ones where both sides get their spending priorities met and the debt continues to pile up.

Tariffs, meanwhile, are not likely to change. Voters delivered a clear message about how they felt about Trump’s trade policies and the impact they have on prices. But Trump will reject any attempt to limit the use of his favorite tool. The Democrats’ legislation will be important because it will show where the party wants to head on trade in 2028 and beyond. But for those countries looking for a break on tariff rates after the midterms, the wait will be at least a little longer.

The one exception may be China. Trump’s trade détente with Beijing was driven in part by the series of summits the two leaders had this year (with two more expected before year-end). Once those pass, Trump may refocus in his final two years on what has been the core animating economic idea since he first ran for president—China’s unfair trading practices. On that issue, he may find a rare area of bipartisan consensus.

The power of the purse will be the route to shaping US NATO policy

As long as Trump is in office, questions and concerns about US engagement in NATO will remain. It was not Congress, but rather the president, who created a transatlantic crisis by repeatedly threatening to annex Greenland, make Canada the fifty-first state, and withhold protection from NATO allies that do not spend enough on defense. It was also the administration, not Congress, that bypassed all efforts to build European support for (or even awareness of) its war with Iran. The administration took not only Europeans but also Congress by surprise when it canceled troop deployments to Europe earlier this year. Now that Democrats control the legislative branch, many on both sides of the Atlantic will be looking to see if the party can wrestle some degree of control away from the executive branch in foreign and security policy.

Democrats who favor a robust US presence in Europe and a strong commitment to NATO are starting from a solid foundation. Despite the administration’s unwieldy approach toward allies, support for NATO in Congress already crosses party lines—and to meaningful effect. In the fiscal year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), Republican majorities passed multiyear security assistance for Ukraine, as well as limits on the administration’s ability to enact troop cuts in Europe, and required the US military commander of European Command to retain the supreme allied commander Europe role in NATO.

Despite this already strong bipartisan support for NATO, Democratic control of Congress will still have a recalibrating effect on transatlantic security. Come January 2027, Democrats will chair every committee and subcommittee in the House and Senate, including the appropriations committees and those important for European security and foreign policy (the Senate Armed Services Committee, Senate Foreign Relations Committee, House Armed Services Committee, and House Foreign Affairs Committee). Democrats will decide which bills get hearings, control investigations, and oversee about two-thirds of committee staff and budgets. We will see the effects of this shift in the 2027 NDAA negotiations and hearings regarding US force posture in Europe. While Trump maintains broad executive privileges in the foreign policy arena, Democrats will start paving the way for a new approach to working with US allies.

Public trust is driving politics—and perhaps now policy—on AI

For the United States to compete effectively in the age of AI, the country must address the significant trust deficit the American public has toward the technology. This was a key finding of the Atlantic Council’s Commission on AI earlier this year, which brought together bipartisan members of Congress, industry leaders, and civil society experts.

The deep anxiety Americans feel about the technology and skepticism of the titans building it were on full display throughout the midterm elections and in the results. For example, an NBC News exit poll found 56 percent of voters said AI and associated infrastructure were a “crucial or major factor” in their vote for Congress. There is little reason to believe these concerns won’t remain on full display in the next Congress and at the state level in California, Texas, Ohio, and elsewhere.

Despite the significant Democratic gains in the election, AI skepticism transcended partisan lines, with many Republican candidates—from Michigan to Texas—advocating for slowing down the AI infrastructure buildout or increasing the regulation of the tech sector. Likewise, there are an increasing number of bipartisan policy proposals on AI safety in the current Congress—such as the FRONTIER ACT or the AI Kill Switch Act—which will likely reemerge in some form in the next Congress.

The bottom line is that, despite the increasing use and integration of AI in daily life around the country, polling as recent as last month shows that 75 percent of Americans view AI with fear or concern rather than excitement, especially when it comes to affordability, employment, education, the environment, safety and security, and many other issues. These concerns are especially prevalent among young people.

The election comes one week after one of the largest tech-driven sell-offs wiped out nearly one trillion dollars in market value due to subpar earnings reports across the AI industry. Much of that sell-off was driven by shaky confidence in whether the record borrowing and spending fueling the AI industry will translate into sustainable revenue, even as the infrastructure buildout takes time and has become a political flashpoint. Either way, the US economy is extremely dependent on whether the huge bets being placed on AI will pan out. Taken together, we’re likely in for continued market and policy adjustments related to AI.

AI is here to stay as a general-purpose technology, but it is also increasingly a determinant of geopolitical competition. As AI development outpaces institutions’ ability to manage it, we’re past due for a coherent national dialogue on AI’s impact and what US leadership in AI should look like. That debate will be on full display in the coming Congress.

US-China AI safety talks could be back on the agenda

Democratic control of Congress could strengthen political support for US-China coordination on AI safety, particularly around frontier-model risks, incident reporting, and crisis communications. The election comes at a consequential moment: During their September 2026 summit, Trump and Xi agreed to establish a bilateral AI dialogue and a communication channel for AI-related incidents, with follow-up talks scheduled for November.

Congressional Democrats have already articulated a more ambitious agenda for bilateral engagement: In September, representatives Gregory Meeks, Ami Bera, and Sara Jacobs, along with twenty-six of their colleagues, urged the administration to pursue shared AI safety standards, establish crisis communications mechanisms, address the proliferation of advanced capabilities, and facilitate exchanges between American and Chinese AI researchers. A separate initiative led by Senator Chris Van Hollen and sixteen Democratic colleagues went further, calling for a formal agreement on frontier AI testing, oversight, human control, and verification. The senators also proposed considering a mutual pause in frontier AI development, highlighting growing congressional interest in managing the risks of an accelerating technological competition.

With control of both chambers, Democrats could use committee hearings, appropriations, and legislation to press the administration to operationalize the new dialogue. Potential priorities could include defining which AI incidents trigger bilateral notifications, establishing protocols for information sharing, and supporting technical exchanges on model evaluations and catastrophic risks.

There is some bipartisan support for this approach. In September, members of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus also called for US-China coordination on AI testing and incident reporting. Growing public backlash against current AI policy—including data center buildouts, permissive AI self-regulation, and growing concerns about the impacts of AI on employment—could also add momentum to renewed engagement on AI.

However, significant constraints remain. The executive branch controls diplomatic negotiations, while disagreements over semiconductor restrictions, technology access, and verification complicate cooperation. Democratic lawmakers also differ significantly on how far bilateral commitments should extend, with more national-security-oriented Democrats expressing greater skepticism about such a process.

The election’s most immediate effect may be to make implementation of the existing AI safety dialogue a more prominent congressional priority. Whether this develops into formal agreements will depend on the administration’s willingness to negotiate and Beijing’s readiness to accept reciprocal safeguards—a tall order, considering that Beijing has previously rejected Washington’s efforts to frame AI safety talks around US-defined priorities.

Democrats could extract some concessions on Ukraine, but don’t expect a sea-change on Europe

Europe can expect the Democrats in the next Congress to signal a more constructive US reengagement in transatlantic relations, on Ukraine, and even on trade issues. But European decisionmakers are right to have tempered expectations about how much a Democratic Congress will translate into substantial US policy changes on what matters most to the continent: support for Ukraine, US commitments to European security, and greater stability in trade and tariff policies.

Even with a strong majority in both chambers of Congress, Democrats will struggle to impose meaningful limits on Trump’s conduct of foreign policy, given his constitutional powers and willingness to push the envelope. Democrats may put him and Republicans on the record with messaging bills on items such as the Russian diesel deal and waived Russia sanctions. They can put supplemental funding for Ukraine on the agenda and leverage must-pass legislation such as the NDAA to try to extract concessions on Ukraine support or US security and troop commitments in Europe related to the administration’s ongoing force posture review. The new majority will also try to claw back trade and tariff powers that Congress has ceded to the executive branch in Trump’s second term. But Trump has stated a willingness to use his veto, and hard limits on the president’s power are unlikely.

Much will also depend on where congressional Republicans go politically in response to the midterm rout. The remaining Reaganite hawks in the Senate may not continue to mute their opposition to the president’s dealings with Moscow and Beijing or his pressure on Kyiv and allied European capitals. Large Democratic majorities in both houses of Congress may make it easier to assemble the two-thirds majorities needed to override a presidential veto. Republican hawks will have more leverage to confront the White House, even if they will have to pick their battles.

Complicating matters, Europe will have to navigate two poles of power in Washington. Europe will, on the one hand, confront a Democratic Congress that wants to drive a reengagement agenda with European allies but will not be able to deliver significant policy changes on key areas of concern, at least not on its own. And on the other hand, Brussels and national capitals must be prepared to counter continued disruption from the president on trade and Ukraine, while avoiding antagonizing him with overly partisan approaches.

NATO and EU countries will continue to confront a mercurial US president who may double down on foreign policy as he is likely to come under significant pressure at home from congressional investigations, budget fights, and political gridlock under divided government. Unshackled from having to face voters at the ballot box again, Trump may shift into deal-making overdrive to cement his legacy. In doing so, he will lean into the instincts that have defined his foreign policy Weltanschauung—one of sphere-of-influence arrangements among supposedly great powers, personalized leader-to-leader dealings, and hard power realism. Trump’s deal-making mode carries both risks and opportunities for Europe and its adversaries.

Moscow and Beijing will now have to contend with a more boxed-in Trump administration. Trump’s instincts may still be to look for deals with Putin and Xi. So Europeans should assess which opportunities and deals they can shape, from Ukraine to European security and trade, even if these may turn out to be more tactical than strategic, as broader initiatives with this White House may remain elusive. But Europe simply cannot afford to fatalistically write off the next two years given the president’s powers and what is at stake for the continent in US foreign and defense policy.

Congress will double down on defense and intelligence oversight

Democratic leaders in the House and Senate will need to focus immediately on essential foreign policy issues such as Iran and Ukraine, but equally important will be the possibility of renewed oversight of core defense and intelligence issues. Expect Democrats to press on issues such as the Pentagon’s force posture plans around the globe and getting numbers on critical munitions stockpiles and associated defense production issues. Democrats are also likely to look into reports of inappropriate business practices within the department and seek out accountability on recent military actions against targets in the Caribbean and Iran. Trump’s programmatic priorities such as Golden Dome, and broader issues of personnel readiness, promotions, and recruitment, are also likely to be on the agenda.

On intelligence issues, we may see a revived bipartisan core of members who will want baseline information on how layoffs and retirements have affected US collection capacity, where AI offers expanded risks and opportunities, and how adversaries may be working together in new ways against US interests and those of the international community.

These fundamental issues won’t be easy to address. They will require urgent bipartisan attention and rapid coordination across several committees before the new Congress is even sworn in this January. Much more work lies ahead.

It’s time for bipartisan progress on immigration policy

Opinion polls have consistently made clear that the American people want an immigration system that is both just and fair, and they are prepared to vote against those who fail to deliver on that objective. Concerns about the US immigration system helped elect Trump president in 2016. Trump’s child-separation policy helped elect Joe Biden president in 2020. Chaos at the border helped elect Trump president in 2024. Cruelty in Trump’s immigration enforcement over the past two years helped create last night’s electoral triumph for Democrats.

Trump’s border adviser Tom Homan had it right two years ago: If Trump had focused on deporting only those unauthorized migrants with criminal records, he might have kept the support of the majority of Americans on this issue. Instead, Trump’s immigration policy appears to have lost the trust of the American people. As of early Wednesday morning, Democrats are expected to win in every single congressional district along the US-Mexico border, including in formerly deep-red (now looking purple) Texas.

With their new power, expect congressional Democrats to start investigations into the Trump administration’s immigration detention system.

The lesson Republicans and Democrats should learn is that only a bipartisan approach on border security and immigration will get the lasting support of the American people. The United States needs a solution along the lines of the 2023–2024 bipartisan Senate compromise or the bipartisan Dignity Act. The 120th Congress should update the 2024 compromise legislation, reallocate existing appropriations from Immigration and Customs Enforcement to other priorities, mandate a major shift in detention and asylum policy, and send it to the White House attached to whatever Trump considers must-pass legislation. Even if bipartisan immigration reform does not pass in 2027, it will help set the agenda for 2028.

Expect tougher scrutiny of Israel and Iran, and potentially more support for Ukraine

Last night’s resounding loss for the Republican Party will have some immediate impacts on foreign policy. First, the new Congress will be without a slew of experienced Republican national security voices, who either lost last night, retired, or passed away. Senators Susan Collins (ME), Thom Tillis (NC), John Cornyn (TX), Lindsey Graham (SC), and Mitch McConnell (KY), and representatives Mike Lawler (NY), Michael McCaul (TX), Ann Wagner (MO), Don Bacon (NE), and Brian Fitzpatrick (PA) have been advocates for American strength and strong alliances, including with Ukraine. That is a significant loss of expertise and experience for the Republican conferences in both chambers that will take years to rebuild.

Israel is also facing a brand-new world this morning—one with a Congress far less supportive of its causes and far more likely to cut military aid. The Israeli government and its supporters in the United States would be wise to begin immediate outreach to Democrats open to mending fences and attempt to rebuild support. Trump himself announced Tuesday that he would cut off four billion dollars in annual aid to Israel, but he will need Congress to agree, since it is actually responsible for appropriating that money. He now likely has a Congress that will.

On the war in Iran, which drove many voters to turn on Republicans, the next Congress is likely to prioritize legislation to halt, or at least significantly curtail, US military action. Still, it is unclear what that would look like beyond a resolution of disapproval, because Iran has been unwilling to have any reasonable discussions to end the conflict.

The new Congress also injects a measure of uncertainty into Ukraine policy. While Democrats have been generally solid in supporting Ukraine militarily and financially during the conflict, voters sent a resounding message in this election to focus on domestic policy and affordability. It’s unclear whether this new crop of Democrats will be interested in sending money and weapons overseas—regardless of the destination. In good news for Ukraine, the likely chairs of national security committees—particularly Representative Adam Smith (D-WA) at House Armed Services and Senator Chris Coons (D-DE) at Senate Foreign Relations—have a strong record of support. They will be powerful allies for Ukraine in the new Congress, as Kyiv fights for access to much-needed weapons.

Venezuela oil deals and military operations will come under scrutiny

Latin America policy wasn’t on the ballot yesterday, and Democrats are expected to focus on affordability and other pocketbook issues. But the Democratic-controlled House and Senate, especially with more seats flipped than expected, are likely to bring hearings, oversight, and investigations into some of Trump’s marquee policies in Latin America in at least four priority areas.

Top of that list will be Venezuela. There, investigations could stretch from looking at who benefits from oil agreements to how revenues are managed and the legal authority for those arrangements, as well as greater scrutiny of the extent to which a pathway to a democratic transition is taking shape. Senator Tim Kaine, a potential new chair of the Western Hemisphere Subcommittee in the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, may push the administration on the exact timing and plan for an election.

Expect possible involvement from the House Foreign Affairs and Oversight committees, and the Senate Foreign Relations, Banking, and Finance committees. Democrats have long been asking for more information on these issues, including in a September letter from Representative Gregory Meeks and Representative Robert Garcia to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Attorney General Todd Blanche requesting more information on the management of Venezuelan oil revenue and the September oil deal announced by Trump.

But it won’t only be about Venezuela. Representative Adam Smith, in line to chair the House Armed Services Committee, has stated that, with enough backing, he would push to investigate the boat strikes and the overall military campaigns that the United States has deployed across the region since the Trump administration took office. Hearings could include the legal basis for US actions, the costs, and the casualties. Global tariffs will also be on the congressional agenda, with the implications for countries like Mexico, Washington’s largest trading partner, likely to receive greater attention.

Hearings and investigations are not the only tools available to Congress. Ahead of elections in 2028, both parties will be pressed to show concrete results through legislation—and hopefully through bipartisan alignment—on the issues that will define the continued expansion of the US presence in the hemisphere.

text:
But Trump’s handling of immigration enforcement also remains at the forefront of that conversation. In the two years since he took office, the Trump administration’s increased crackdown on immigration has seen ICE agents shoot two American citizens dead in Minneapolis and leave hundreds of others involved in enforcement operations either injured, incarcerated or both.

Here in the Big Apple, 26 Federal Plaza’s immigration court became a powder keg in the summer of 2025, as journalists’ ability to enter the facility gave the public a rare glimpse into ICE arrests and subsequent family separations that saw children left in tears as they were torn from their parents’ arms.

Peter Melck Kuttel, detention coordinator for Father Fabian Arias’ Saint Peter’s Church, has worked with immigrants detained in the courthouse since the summer of 2025. In his mind, he does not doubt that the suffering in plain sight at 26 Federal Plaza and operations across the country had a major impact on how the country voted Tuesday.

“I think those images and the stories of those images played a huge role in Americans’ rejection of the administration’s spin on immigration and their enforcement on immigration. I don’t think it was just Iran,” Kuttel told amNewYork. “Many saw them as their neighbors, their friends, even employees.”

While Kuttel stated that a vote for Trump two years prior may have been to close the border, he says that is something different from voting for what he says is the cruelty of breaking apart families.

Over the course of his work, Kuttle noted that he has seen very few immigrants with serious criminal records, and did not see “the worst of the worst” that Trump Border Czar Tom Homan claimed to be targeted by ICE, as masked agents pulled families away in the halls of Federal Plaza and other courthouses across the country.

ICE agents’ actions in New York since 2025

In the end, he believes American voters also saw this and took action with their ballots.

“I think Americans, by and large, saw through that, and the images that they would see out of Minnesota, the images that they would see out of the courts, the images that they would see out of California or even Texas or even just in their own backyards. With the agents being masked up, being so unprofessional and so filled with hate, it didn’t even seem like an organized government operation. It just seemed like cruelty,” Kuttel added.

For almost one year, amNewYork gave the city a firsthand look at the drama unfolding in the halls of 26 Federal Plaza, from the arrest of then-Mayoral candidate Brad Lander to journalists being roughed up by masked ICE agents and children left in tears.

While enforcement in the courthouse continued, the scope of ICE operations eventually moved out into the streets of New York, including the apprehension of Canal Street vendors in Chinatown in October 2025.

In June, a hunger strike at New Jersey’s Delaney Hall also drew nationwide attention and weeks of protests that saw demonstrators doused in pepper spray, beaten with nightsticks, and thrown into oncoming traffic.

Then, in October of this year, ICE agents shot and wounded Oscar Belgal, a Dominican native, during a confrontation in Marble Hill. He was hospitalized, but ICE later took him into its custody; Belgal would be detained at the Metropolitan Detention Center with a bullet still lodged in his neck more than a week later. As of Oct. 23, he was still listed in ICE custody.

For Murad Awawdeh, President and CEO of the New York Immigration Coalition, the sights of ICE agents acting brutally inside Federal Plaza and beyond all contributed to what he called a rejection of Trump on Nov. 3.

“Voters across America and New York have resoundingly rejected Trump’s war on immigrants. The courthouse arrests at 26 Federal Plaza represent the extreme unlawfulness of this administration, as families have been systematically separated because they tried to follow our immigration procedures. New Yorkers want ICE out of our communities once and for all,” Awawdeh told amNewYork. “We call on the new Congress to conduct aggressive oversight hearings on ICE, including their unlawful abductions and detentions at 26 Federal Plaza, to take back enforcement slush funds and reinvest in programs that help all New Yorkers, and to provide a real pathway to citizenship.”

Meanwhile, religious leaders like Midtown pastor Father Fabian Arias, who has spent decades fighting for the rights of immigrants, says he hopes these vote results will allow for new discourse around immigration.

“I hope that new paths of dialogue and reconciliation will open, so that our immigrant families may live without fear of ICE raids, deportations, and family separation,” Arias said.

text:
NJ, 21 other states challenged restrictions on federal funding used for crime prevention, police equipment, mental health programs, and juvenile justice

A federal judge has blocked the Trump administration from requiring states to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement to receive public safety grants, protecting millions of dollars New Jersey uses for police equipment, investigations of gang activity, mental health programs, and other law enforcement initiatives.

Chief U.S. District Judge John McConnell Jr. of Rhode Island ruled Wednesday that the U.S. Department of Justice exceeded its authority by attaching immigration enforcement requirements to grants Congress established to support state and local criminal justice programs.

The ruling permanently prohibits the federal government from enforcing certain conditions on the states that brought the lawsuit. New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport helped lead the coalition, which included 21 other states and the District of Columbia.

Federal funding for programs including the Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant Program that supports police departments, prosecutors, crime prevention initiatives, and other criminal justice activities is at stake in the case.

Court documents show New Jersey was allocated about $4.2 million in Byrne grants for fiscal year 2025. Another $2.7 million was allocated through a related crisis intervention program supporting mental health services and violence prevention.

The Trump administration had required grant recipients to cooperate with federal immigration authorities by providing access to people in state custody suspected of violating immigration laws, notifying federal officials before their release, and complying with requirements concerning immigration-related information.

States argued that the restrictions improperly forced them to choose between federal public safety funding and their own policies governing cooperation with immigration authorities.

The lawsuit also challenged the administration’s authority to impose conditions unrelated to the purposes Congress established for the grants.

“Today’s victory in court makes clear that the federal government cannot unlawfully politicize law enforcement and public safety by threatening our access to critical funding,” Davenport said in a statement Wednesday.

She said the funding helps pay for protective equipment for officers, investigations into drug trafficking, the enforcement of Megan’s Law, and efforts to locate violent criminals.

“We will continue to fight the Administration’s brazenly unlawful actions that put politics over public safety,” Davenport said.

How New Jersey uses the money

The lawsuit provides a detailed accounting of how New Jersey has used federal criminal justice grants in recent years.

Between fiscal years 2019 and 2024, the state received more than $21 million through the Byrne Justice Assistance Grant Program, according to the coalition’s amended complaint.

The money supported anti-gang and narcotics task forces operated by all 21 county prosecutors’ offices, including purchases of protective equipment and funding for undercover drug investigations.

Grants also supported an anti-corruption initiative within the state Attorney General’s Office of Public Integrity and Accountability, additional staffing, law enforcement training, community policing programs, and the purchase of body cameras for municipal police departments.

Other funding helped maintain sex offender registries, enforce Megan’s Law, and support the State Police ballistics laboratory.

New Jersey also received more than $8.3 million in crisis intervention grants for fiscal years 2022 through 2024.

According to the lawsuit, the state planned to use that funding to expand its ARRIVE Together program, which pairs police officers with mental health professionals to respond to behavioral health emergencies.

The money was also intended to support training and public education about extreme risk protection orders, which allow courts to temporarily restrict firearm access for people considered a danger to themselves or others.

The lawsuit did not establish that New Jersey had already lost the funding. Instead, the states challenged conditions they would have been required to accept to access the grants.

A continuing fight over immigration enforcement

The dispute began in 2025, when the Trump administration imposed immigration-related requirements on more than $1.3 billion in federal funding distributed under the Victims of Crime Act.

A coalition of states challenged those restrictions, and the federal government subsequently removed them from that funding program.

The Justice Department later imposed similar conditions on other grants, including those supporting law enforcement, crisis intervention, and juvenile justice programs. New Jersey and the other states expanded their lawsuit to challenge those requirements.

In their amended complaint, filed Aug. 21, the states argued that Congress had established formulas and eligibility requirements for distributing the grants without authorizing the Justice Department to condition funding on cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. They also argued that the administration’s requirements violated constitutional protections against federal coercion of states and federal administrative law. The coalition maintained that states should be able to determine how best to use their own law enforcement resources, including whether local police should assist federal authorities with civil immigration matters.

The case is part of a broader series of legal disputes over the Trump administration’s attempts to use federal funding to encourage state and local governments to cooperate with immigration enforcement.

The fraud scandal touched Omar, with one of her ex-campaign staffers, Guhaad Hashi Said, among the defendants who pleaded guilty to laundering dollars from taxpayer programs meant to feed needy kids.

“I think the people of Minnesota have been lied to. They’ve had their money stolen. They want to see somebody that’s going to come in and fix things,” Nagel told Fox News following his primary win. “They’re tired of being told the same old things.”

While her re-election was a near-certainty, Omar has been battling accusations that she misrepresented facts about her family’s immigration history to obtain citizenship for herself — and for a man she married in 2009 suspected of being her brother.

Since 2016, the FBI and Department of Homeland Security have been looking into allegations that Omar legally wed one of her siblings to try to get him a marriage-based green card. The congresswoman has repeatedly denied the claim, calling it a racist conspiracy theory.

While married to her possible relative, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, Omar filed joint tax returns for 2014 and 2015 with a man, Ahmed Hirsi, with whom she entered an Islamic marriage in 2002, but later claimed to have separated from in 2011.

Other social media posts, marriage records and statements by Omar and Elmi have further complicated their relationship — including Instagram and Facebook photos first reported by the conservative blog Powerline a decade ago that apparently show the pair with their other siblings.

In a recent DC court filing, federal prosecutors referred to Omar as “Ilhan Nur Said Elmi,” which sources told The Post is the congresswoman’s “real” name.

“I’m ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar responded to the raid on X. “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.”

“I will not be silenced,” the congresswoman added.

Sources said that the investigation — led by the Minnesota US Attorney’s Office — is focused on allegations of green-card fraud as well as claims that either Omar’s father, Nur Omar Mohamed, or Omar herself lied about her birthdate to attain citizenship in 2000.

text:
A federal judge in Colorado ordered the Trump administration to immediately release a man who was arrested by immigration agents minutes after being freed from detention.

The judge accused the government of an "ongoing due process violation" and told officials they could face contempt proceedings if they detained him again without a hearing.

U.S. District Judge S. Kato Crews said Edgardo Garcia Vargas was released pursuant to an earlier court order. However, he was "immediately confronted and arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) before even leaving the detention facility grounds."

Read More on News

"Once again, the cruelty appears to be the point," Crews, a Biden appointee, wrote in the November 3 order.

Newsweek has contacted ICE and its parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, for comment and is awaiting responses.

The dispute comes amid mounting tensions between the Trump administration and federal judges over its immigration crackdown. Courts are repeatedly challenging the government’s detention practices and, in some cases, accusing immigration authorities of failing to comply with judicial orders.

The administration has been carrying out a widespread deportation operation as it seeks to increase arrests and removals. Immigration arrests in Colorado have climbed in recent months, according to federal data obtained through the Freedom of Information Act by the Deportation Data Project. Arrests nearly doubled from 259 in March to 499 in July 2026. The state recorded 549 arrests in July 2025.

Crews said the government argued that, because Garcia Vargas had technically been released, the habeas relief ordered by the court had been carried out and the case should be closed despite his subsequent re-detention.

The judge rejected that argument and said Garcia Vargas had effectively remained in custody continuously since his original arrest. Ruling otherwise, he wrote, would render any habeas relief "meaningless" and "reward Respondents’ apparent gamesmanship."

"No person would have felt free to leave under these circumstances," Crews wrote.

Garcia Vargas had argued in his application for a writ of habeas corpus that his original arrest violated his due process rights because he was never presented with a warrant, according to the order.

A habeas petition asks a court to determine whether someone is being lawfully detained.

Crews said the government did not respond to the petition, so the court accepted Garcia Vargas’ due process claim as conceded.

The judge said Garcia Vargas’ re-detention "mere minutes after his purported release was no release at all" and instead constituted an ongoing violation of his due process rights.

Crews ordered Garcia Vargas immediately released and directed the administration to file a status report within three days confirming his release.

The judge also barred authorities from detaining Garcia Vargas again unless they first prove at a bond hearing that he is a flight risk or danger to the community. The government would bear the burden of proof, and Garcia Vargas would be allowed to have a lawyer present.

Crews said that another arrest without such a hearing could lead to contempt proceedings.

"Should Petitioner again be instantly rearrested without receiving the foregoing due process," he wrote, "Respondents shall appear in this Court for consideration of whether contempt proceedings are warranted."

Court filings name Juan Baltazar, warden of the Aurora Contract Detention Facility, David Venturella, acting ICE director, and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in the case.

The ruling comes amid a separate legal battle over ICE's arrest practices in Colorado, where a federal judge has repeatedly found the agency violated court orders restricting warrantless arrests. In September, Judge R. Brooke Jackson said agents involved in two separate arrests should face sanctions, including one involving an 18-year-old who suffered a broken wrist and facial injuries. The government has appealed the underlying injunction, with oral arguments scheduled for November 16.

ICE has also been expanding its detention presence in Colorado. In September, Axios Denver reported that detention capacity in the state was poised to nearly double as the administration increased immigration enforcement.

title: My flabbers are gasted. - Doomsday Scenario
description:
“My flabbers are gasted,” she wrote.
The country elected its first female Native American governor, in New Mexico.
Kansas reelected Rep. Sharice Davids, one of the first two Native American women elected to congress and the first out LGBTQ+ person elected to Congress from Kansas.
(Photo by Paras Griffin/Getty Images) So much history was made last night — and so much was deeply colored and shaped by the 250 years of American history that came before.
The Democratic victories were broad and deep — Kansas elected its first Democratic senator in nearly 100 years.
text:
Welcome to Doomsday Scenario, my regular column on national security, geopolitics, history, and—unfortunately—the fight for democracy in the Trump era. I hope if you’re coming to this online, you’ll consider subscribing right here. It’s easy—and free:

Well, here’s a huge dose of hope and optimism to start your day!

I texted a Mississippi friend early this morning in seeing the news that a Democrat is currently leading by just the tiniest handful of votes in a US Senate race. “My flabbers are gasted,” she wrote. “Be on the lookout for pigs in the sky today!”

It will take much of the rest of the week for the full picture of the Democratic shellacking of Trump’s MAGA politics to come into view and the full list of superlatives to be assembled, but here’s a starting point:

Americans elected the nation’s first Black female governor, in Georgia.

The nation elected its first gay male senator, from New Hampshire.

Its first Muslim senator, from Michigan.

A new Black woman will serve in the US Senate from Illinois, just the sixth in the nation’s history.

The country elected its first female Native American governor, in New Mexico.

Minnesota elected the first Native American woman to the US Senate ever.

Texas elected its first Latina governor. Ohio, its first female governor.

California, its first Latino governor.

There are a million smaller personal superlatives too: In Georgia’s 13th district, the first Black woman with a STEM PhD won election to the US House. Robert Garcia, the first out gay immigrant elected to Congress, was reelected and is set to be the chair of the House oversight committee — his message to the Trump administration was blunt last night: “Lawyer up.” Nevada elected its first Black governor, my friend Aaron Ford, as did Wisconsin and Florida. A trans woman won Alabama House District 25, outside Huntsville. Colorado’s Melat Kiros will be the first Gen Z woman to serve in Congress; New Jersey elected its first Muslim to Congress, and New York its first Native American, Nebraska its first Hispanic.

Bentley Hudgins became the first out transgender and nonbinary state lawmaker in Georgia, winning election to the State Assembly. Kansas reelected Rep. Sharice Davids, one of the first two Native American women elected to congress and the first out LGBTQ+ person elected to Congress from Kansas. Similarly, Michigan elected its first out LGBTQ+ congressman in 11th district winner Jeremy Moss, who will take the seat vacated by Haley Stevens.

It appears that for the first time, more than 100 women will serve in the Democratic caucus in the US House simultaneously.

Newly-elected governor of Georgia Keisha Lance Bottoms onstage last night. (Photo by Paras Griffin/Getty Images)

So much history was made last night — and so much was deeply colored and shaped by the 250 years of American history that came before.

The lede of the Atlanta Journal-Constitution is worth quoting in full: “In 1860, an enslaved man named Sheppard Peek was listed among the possessions of William Peek, a white man in Crawfordville. His value was placed at $1,400. On another surviving document, Sheppard signed his name with an X. More than a century and a half later, Sheppard’s great-great-granddaughter, Keisha Lance Bottoms, was elected governor of Georgia.”

Coast to coast, after a period of white supremacy politics by the Trump administration unprecedented in modern politics, the country elected the most diverse set of leaders it has ever seen.

In Arizona, voters flipped a Republican House seat, electing JoAnna Mendoza, an openly LGBTQ+ former Marine drill instructor veteran who served during the military’s shameful and discriminatory “don’t ask, don’t tell” era.

The Democratic victories were broad and deep — Kansas elected its first Democratic senator in nearly 100 years. James Talarico wasn’t even born the last time Texas sent a Democrat to the senate. North Carolina. South Carolina, where a Everytown for Gun Safety volunteer — the first elected to the Senate — walked onstage for her victory speech to the music of Dolly Parton’s 9-to-5. Democrats came within a few percentage points of defeating Marsha Blackburn in Tennessee. At least Arizona, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Minnesota, and Michigan will start next year with new Democratic trifectas. North Carolina flipped both legislative chambers; Democrats won every statewide in both Georgia and Texas. The Texas Tribune’s lede was short: “Everything has changed.”

Virginia enshrined abortion in its constitution and, 124 years later, overturned its Jim Crow-era lifetime voting ban for felons.

The list goes on.

Political scientist Seth Masket wrote, “I'm not sure how to phrase this exactly but Dems are winning races they haven’t won since they were the white supremacist party.” This time, though, the party won it for being explicitly NOT the white supremacist party, winning in places where voters were angry and fired up and had had enough of the GOP’s voter suppression, gerrymandering, and the rollback of the Voting Rights Act.

The election results are all the more astounding because of how unfair the GOP had tried to ensure the electoral landscape would be. They last year gerrymandered four Florida House districts — only to lose them all last night. Rep. Shomari Figures held onto his gerrymandered seat in Alabama.

As one GOP consultant wrote in the middle of the evening, “I had a worst case scenario. A doomsday scenario. I never thought to have a zombie apocalypse meets thermonuclear apocalypse with zombie invasion from the sun scenario.”

Talarico in Austin last night. (Photo by Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

Punchbowl’s headline this morning described the election results as an “extinction-level event for Hill GOP.”

WIRED’s headline was blunt too: “Democrats sweep Republicans in nearly every race that matters.”

As my favorite pollster G. Elliot Morris wrote: “This is shaping up to be the biggest House popular vote victory for any party since 1974. This is a Watergate-level repudiation of the party in power.”

But beyond the diversity of Democratic victories, there was a more fundamental point too.

Authoritarianism lost, bigly.

One Austinite posted video of the downtown, filling with cheering and honking horns, commenting, “Austin, Texas sounds like an Eastern European city that just overthrew a dictator.”

And in a way, we did.

Hispanic voters, who just two years ago Republicans believed had been key to a historic electoral realignment, turned out not to appreciate themselves and their families being racially profiled, assaulted, and rounded up in mass arrests.

Donald Trump, with the complete assent of the GOP-led Congress, tried to speedrun an unwinding and descent into authoritarianism last year — and failed. They failed not because of the strength of institutions — many of which actually capitulated, twisted themselves, and kowtowed to accommodate Donald Trump — but because of the strength of individuals, many of whom stood up to the terroristic attacks of Border Patrol on ICE on America’s streets at great personal risk.

“I Voted” stickers were left in Minneapolis on the memorials to Alex Pretti and Renee Good, and in Texas more than 1,000 “I Voted” stickers blanketed a memorial to Lorenzo Salgado Araujo.

Jon Ossoff won handily in Georgia on a platform that boiled down to basically: “I don’t like Nazis.”

The “No Kings” protests mattered — and were real.

So much for the Thousand-Year Trump Reich.

While the top line is a clear rejection of authoritarianism, to me there’s a clear and relatively simple recipe for Trump’s collapse: Corruption mattered. Up, down, and across the country, the nation rejected kleptocracy, oligarchy, and Silicon Valley’s new era of techno-fascism. Data centers lost coast to coast.

History will record that Trump’s speedrun to authoritarianism failed in specific places at specific times. ABC’s forced retreat from taking Jimmy Kimmel off the air last September after Kimmel criticized Charlie Kirk broke the fever of institutional collapse and “chilled speech” that had settled over the country in the first half of 2025; ICE’s failed invasion of Minneapolis, and to a lesser degree Chicago, ended what was supposed to be the Trump administration’s signature domestic agenda item and its ticket to steal future elections; the Iran war ended its vision of remaking the world order in Trump’s image. At home, the controversy and cover-up of the Epstein Files collapsed the support of Trump’s base, and the combination of the Iran War and Trump’s capricious and illegal tariffs allowed inflation and the cost of living to spiral out of control.

In the end, one of the most shocking aspects of yesterday’s election was how normal it was. There were no ICE checkpoints on the way to polling places. No attempts by FBI agents to seize ballot boxes. The Justice Department sent a 1000 polling monitors out across the country, to all 50 states for the first time, targeting minority districts, and … nothing happened. Lawyers were ready — and never got called.

Also, in the breadth of victories yesterday, the 2028 election got a lot harder to steal.

Ohio and Georgia both flipped their secretaries of state to Democrat.

Other states, potentially like North Carolina and Texas, might be able to undo their GOP gerrymandering. It’s possible — possible — that Democrats now control enough state houses that they could secure the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact and do away legislatively with the electoral college. (Huzzah!)

It is an incredible statement of where we are that we need to think like this — and it should be a warning about the next stage of where we go as a country. Barack Obama called overnight for “a politics that brings people together rather than divides them.” Hakeem Jeffries demonstrated how out of touch he is with the country’s mood this morning by saying, “The American people don't want us to get even; they want us to get things done on their behalf.” I disagree. America needs to ensure that MAGA never rises from the electoral grave it was buried in last night. Impeachment, prosecutions, investigations, subpoenas — Democrats need to spend these years ahead focused on ensuring justice.

That doesn’t mean NOT focusing on making Americans’ lives better, but a key part of making Americans’ lives better is ensuring that our country can be more just, more equal, and more free. And that involves burying MAGA for good.

This wasn’t about a few bad candidates — a la Ken Paxton or Vivek Ramaswamy. This wasn’t “just” about the cost of eggs or diesel. As Brian Buetler wrote this morning, “No one wins a historic realignment election because inflation is slightly above trend. The public wants an end to the scourges of tyranny. Deliver it.”

There is a better path ahead. And Democrats should embrace this as a broad mandate to deliver a better future, more just, more equal, and more free. Already today the DC media and punditocracy will try to pretend that this is not as huge a mandate as it is.

The sheer terror of ICE and Stephen Miller has opened a window and pathway for a pro-immigration politics. Greg Sargent saw this coming last month, in the strength of James Talarico and Abdul El-Sayed. America — contrary to the rhetoric of Fox News and worse — likes immigrants. In Sargent’s interview with El-Sayed, the Michigan candidate said, “People like [JD] Vance think America is too small for some of us. I think America is big enough. America has been big enough include people whose families came, were here before anybody else showed up, or who were brought here despite themselves. His view of America is small -- small like him.”

I’ve spent this last year working on this new book about the story of progress and retrenchment in American history, about how progress is never linear nor guaranteed. My thesis is that the great beauty of the American experiment, despite the fact that we’ve never achieved our Founding creed, is that each generation takes up the challenge and works the hard work of making our country better, of making our imperfect nation a more perfect union.

In the introduction, I quote historian Joseph Ellis saying, “What Martin Luther King, Jr., called ‘the arc of the moral universe’ is really an undulating up-down syndrome.” And I write about how “the success of the forces of progress often provoke backlash, retrenchment, and sometimes even bloodshed. There were a hundred years in between the promises of Reconstruction and the moment that pieces of that vision became reality with the Civil Rights Movement. Heather McGhee, in her book on America’s history of structural racism The Sum of Us, recalls that her parents ‘were the first generation of Black Americans to live full adult lives with explicitly racist barriers lowered enough for them to even glimpse the American Dream.’”

That same generation that McGhee writes about had watched their rights steadily eroded over the last decade across the South — and then last night fought back, vigorously and in places where Democrats themselves were surprised. Democrats came, it appears, within about a point of winning the Louisiana senate seat!

We timed the book to come out right after the midterms because we hoped that it would inspire Americans to pick up the mantle of progress and recommit themselves to the hard work of making America better.

This is that moment.

This is that hope and optimism.

As historian Nicole Hemmer wrote this morning, “2026 sets the stage. It puts Democrats within striking distance of a world where, with a Democratic president, they could set to work on the fundamental reconstruction of democracy in the U.S. That's the work of the next two years: building both the vision and the blueprint for that reconstruction.”

I don’t pretend to know what the next two years bring. American politics continues to surprise me.

But I do know this: Thanks to last night the unfinished project of America has a better chance.

Reconstruction — with a capital “R” — is possible. “Reconstruction” — the first — is Chapter 3 of my book, our third national revolution. We can hope that the years ahead will enshrine a “Second Reconstruction” as America’s 26th revolution.

GMG

Dear Colleague:

America is back!

Congratulations on your election to the 120th Congress. I write to humbly request your support in connection with my candidacy to serve as the next Speaker of the House of Representatives.

Almost two years ago, Donald Trump was sworn into office in the same Capitol where he incited a violent mob to try and overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election. The days, weeks and months that followed were deeply challenging. MAGA extremists tried to break America. A flood-the-zone strategy was unleashed throughout the land. But our country is a resilient one.

In the face of great turmoil and uncertainty, House Democrats did not back down. Together, we stood in the breach, aggressively pushed back against the Trump Administration’s extremism and overwhelmingly turned the tide.

In the 119th Congress, House Democrats forcefully stood up for the American people and charted a path for dramatic change. We remained unified and as a Caucus repeatedly delivered. House Democrats:

1. Exposed the harm done by the One Big Ugly Bill, relentlessly denouncing the largest cut to Medicaid in American history while Republicans provided massive tax breaks to their billionaire donors.

2. Established a first-of-its-kind litigation task force to oppose the Trump Administration in court, helping win critical cases to uphold birthright citizenship, protect the right to vote by mail and stop the President from unilaterally deploying the National Guard to intimidate the American people.

3. Led the fight for transparency and accountability in connection with the Epstein Files, partnering with the courageous and patriotic survivors while exposing the ongoing cover-up by the Department of Justice.

4. Decisively won the healthcare battle in connection with the 43-day government shutdown, setting the stage for the House to pass a three-year extension of the Affordable Care Act tax credits over the objection of Republican leadership.

5. Refused to provide taxpayer dollars to Donald Trump’s violent mass deportation machine because we believe that immigration enforcement should be fair, just and humane.

6. Repeatedly forced successful votes through historic use of the discharge petition, passing legislation to restore TPS for Haitian migrants, enforce the right to a swift negotiation of union contracts and repeal the Trump Administration’s Executive Order banning collective bargaining for over a million federal workers.

7. Aggressively opposed the reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed gas prices while undermining our national security.

8. Kept the pressure on corrupt and incompetent cabinet officials, forcing Kristi Noem and Pam Bondi to resign in disgrace.

9. Obliterated the Republican gerrymandering scheme that MAGA extremists claimed would net 16 seats and thereby made sure there was a free and fair election.

10. Delivered the most meaningful housing affordability bill in 40 years, reinforcing our commitment to drive down the high cost of living for everyday Americans.

Against all odds, House Democrats were consistently successful in the minority. We must now deliver the dramatic change the American people are demanding in the majority.

In the new Congress, we will aggressively fight for an affordable America. Life is way too expensive, and millions of hardworking taxpayers are drowning in this failed economy. As part of our effort to turn things around, every single member of our majority will play a meaningful role. My goal is to empower you to act decisively in three key areas: (1) Affordability (2) Accountability and (3) American Values.

Affordability

Donald Trump and House Republicans promised to lower costs on Day One. They failed. Instead, toxic GOP policies like the Trump tariffs and war in Iran have done the exact opposite. People are suffering. Everyday Americans can’t thrive and can barely survive.

House Democrats must do everything in our power to meaningfully lower the high cost of living. In doing so, we will try to find bipartisan common ground whenever and wherever possible. Earlier this year, our Caucus established five working groups to address the affordability crisis: (1) housing; (2) healthcare; (3) groceries and goods; (4) gas and utilities and (5) caregiving. In partnership with our Chairs, the committees of jurisdiction and the entire Caucus, it’s imperative that we get to work immediately. Accordingly, we must decisively address these affordability issues in the new Congress. Here in America, when you work hard and play by the rules, you should be able to live an affordable life, a comfortable life and a good life. That’s the American dream, and House Democrats are determined to revive it.

In addition to the forward progress that we must make in the next two years, there is a lot of damage done by the MAGA extremists that needs to be repaired. During the first 100 days, House Democrats must act to reverse the Medicaid cuts, restore SNAP funding, extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits, eradicate the Trump tariffs and stop the reckless war of choice in Iran. The era of MAGA extremism is coming to a crashing end.

Accountability

The days of the House functioning like a wholly owned subsidiary of the Trump Administration are over. Congress will assume its place as a check and balance on an out-of-control executive branch.

We must root out corrupt price gouging, clean up the mess at the Supreme Court and ban Members of Congress from trading stocks. Accountability begins at home.

The massive corruption the country has experienced from the Trump Cartel explains why very little is getting done to help everyday Americans. That changes immediately. Anyone who is stealing from the American people, ripping off the American people or screwing over the American people can no longer hide. We are going to hold the crooks accountable.

American Values

Finally, we must restore classic American values like liberty and justice for all, equal protection under the law, the unfettered right to vote in a representative democracy and our heritage as a nation of immigrants. To that end, I look forward to drawing upon the insights and perspectives of every single part of the Caucus in the days and weeks ahead. House Democrats must deliver dramatic change.

MAGA extremists failed to break our country. The American people have now broken the fever of MAGA extremism once and for all. Our hard-fought success gives us the opportunity to restore the promise of an affordable America in every community. The next chapter in our country’s 250-year journey begins today.

Thank you for your consideration of my candidacy to serve as the 57th Speaker of the United States House of Representatives.

Sincerely,

Hakeem Jeffries

Democratic Leader

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has demanded that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) immediately stop unauthorized and illegal use of New York City-owned property to stage immigration enforcement operations and warned that the city will take legal action if ICE doesn’t stop.

According to Mamdani’s office, ICE agents are reported to have parked vehicles and held meetings in several unstaffed city-owned parking lots, including a lot at Van Cortlandt Park in the Bronx and lots along 111th Street on the west side of Flushing Meadows Corona Park in Queens. The lots in Queens are next to a city-run preschool and several cultural institutions that welcome hundreds of children and families every day.

In a letter to Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Acting ICE Director David J. Venturella, and ICE New York Field Office Director Kenneth Genalo, Mamdani called on ICE to issue guidance explicitly prohibiting agents from using city-owned lots to stage or conduct its operations.

“ICE has no right to use our property as a base for tearing families apart,” Mamdani said. “That goes for every park and every lot this city owns. This unauthorized use of City property must end now.”

Gov. Kathy Hochul backed up Mamdani saying, “I am deeply disturbed by reports that ICE is using public property to carry out aggressive immigration enforcement operations. I stand with Mayor Mamdani in demanding an end to the unauthorized use of city property for these operations.”

The city’s top lawyer, Corporation Counsel Steven Banks said, “Now that the Department of Homeland Security is clearly on notice regarding its unauthorized use of city lots, there is no excuse for continuing to commandeer city property and we are prepared to go to court if it does not stop.”
