text:
On November 3, the Democratic Party won a resounding majority in both the Senate and House of Representatives, giving it control of the 120th Congress that will convene on January 3, 2027. While Donald Trump remains the U.S. president for two more years, the dramatic shift in the balance of power gives Democrats in Congress an opportunity to conduct robust oversight of the Trump administration and shape the direction of U.S. policy, particularly by setting funding priorities, confirming nominees, and legislating.

Now is the time to curb the excesses of the past two years, while restricting and rolling back policies that have harmed communities at home and abroad and have worked to dismantle the rules-based international order that past U.S. governments spent decades helping to build.

While WOLA will issue more comprehensive analyses and proposals in the months ahead, here are four key areas that the new Congress should prioritize regarding Latin America and the Caribbean.

Conduct rigorous oversight

The Trump administration has embarked on a long list of actions and policies that range from blatantly unlawful, to potentially corrupt, to harmful to human rights, to militarily overreaching. Its pursuit of oil and minerals, its desire to stop all migration, and its wrongheaded “kinetic” approach to the very real problem of organized crime deserve far more scrutiny and public access to information, which is the first step toward real accountability and reform.

Areas of high priority for congressional oversight in the Americas include, but are not limited to:

Ordering the U.S. military to extrajudicially execute at least 243 civilians in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific, based on unproven claims of “narcoterrorism.”

Using the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 to transfer, without due process, 280 people, including 252 Venezuelan migrants, to El Salvador’s CECOT megaprison where they were subject to torture and other forms of ill-treatment, for which the administration paid the Salvadoran government $4.76 million in State Department Narcotics and Law Enforcement funds.

Failing to disclose information about billions of dollars held in the Treasury account from the sale of Venezuelan oil and a questionable legal deal to give control of several oilfields to the private company NABEP.

Violating congressional war powers by involving U.S. personnel in hostilities—through the boat strikes, the Venezuela intervention, and possibly elsewhere under a new “joint operations” framework—without constitutionally required congressional authorization.

Deciding that the best approach to organized crime—a threat that, unlike insurgencies, thrives on its corrupt ties to governments and licit businesses—is to relabel criminal groups as “terrorists” and pursue them militarily, even though that approach has never done more than fragment criminal groups and pave the way for successors.

Members of Congress, mainly from the minority, have sent dozens of letters to administration officials voicing opposition and requesting information about policies and actions, usually to no avail. Now, Democrats will have more power to demand the release of information and to halt unlawful behavior. They should use their majority for high-profile scrutiny, holding hearings with administration officials, the private sector, former officials, civil society organizations, and others to get a clearer view of the impact and excesses of the past two years’ policies. Refusal to comply with information requests or requirements to testify must trigger stiff consequences.

Start rethinking foreign aid

The fiscal year 2026 budget demonstrated that a Republican-led Congress was willing to assert at least some of its authority over foreign aid. However, the harm from the previous year’s abrupt slashing of foreign assistance and dismantling of USAID persists, as do administration and House Republican efforts to pursue further cuts. Likewise, even as funding has gone to accounts the administration sought to eliminate, like the Democracy Fund, media reports have indicated that most of this support has moved away from the traditional backing of human rights defenders and journalists. Funding to civil society has also been restricted for any group that subscribes to “gender ideology,” around $500 million is being spent to resettle White South Africans as refugees, and programs supporting women and girls have been reduced or cut.

As WOLA has noted, although the law requires transparency, current aid spending is opaque. Since 2025, the State Department has not provided Congress or the public with “the dollar value of all foreign assistance and grantees by category and by country” as spent in the previous year, or planned funding for the current and coming year, as the law requires. Congress should demand transparency over the aid budget to have a clear view not only of the impact of the 2025 and 2026 spending cuts, but also where funds are actually being used and for what. This transparency is especially urgent regarding security assistance, including that flowing through Defense budget channels, which appears to be growing rapidly.

Congress also has the opportunity to rethink, restore, and condition foreign aid for 2028 (and perhaps 2027, depending on what happens with budget negotiations in the coming months). This does not mean reconstructing the aid apparatus that existed before 2025: the Trump administration’s dismantling of the majority of the foreign aid infrastructure opens up the opportunity to build something more nimble, more capable of ensuring that most assistance reaches targeted communities, and more in line with long-term U.S. interests, including lasting security, accountability, and the rule of law. The new Congress can begin designing effective channels for providing robust support for civil society organizations defending universal human rights, restoring and/or increasing support for regional and international agencies, and increasing humanitarian assistance, particularly given the potentially dire consequences of the “Super El Niño” on Latin America and the Caribbean. It also means restoring human rights conditions on U.S. security assistance, including for Colombia, Mexico, and Central America, and ensuring compliance with the Leahy Law (no funding for security units that violate human rights with impunity).

Congress should ensure that the State Department’s International Narcotics Control and Law Enforcement funding focuses on strengthening criminal justice institutions, protecting citizens, and combating organized crime-tied corruption, rather than an outdated “drugs and thugs” approach that focuses too heavily on militaries, lethal operations, or deportations. Grants to governments like that in El Salvador, where INL funds were used to imprison expelled migrants, deserve very heavy scrutiny and conditioning. No funding should be provided, through any budget category, for additional boat strikes.

Faced with an executive branch that has ignored congressional appropriation directives, Congress should carefully craft appropriations legislation to safeguard against deliberate circumvention of congressional intent. This means vigorously applying the Impoundment Control Act through the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) and even censuring or impeaching officials who violate Congress’s constitutional power of the purse. It also means a revival of committee chairperson authority to place “holds” on aid when Congress’s intent is not respected. These “holds” are only enforceable when there is a likelihood that ignoring them will have consequences for the administration’s priorities in the next years’ appropriations legislation; committee chairs will have to demonstrate a willingness to go this route when necessary.

Hold DHS accountable

This congressional majority was elected on a wave of outrage at the many excesses and abuses committed by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) since 2025: blatant and too frequently fatal use of force violations, racial profiling, cruel and inhumane conditions in detention centers including the in-custody deaths of at least 60 people, family separations, and dangerous deportations—all, at least so far, committed with impunity. The new Congress has a mandate and a moral duty to hold DHS accountable, even if it lacks the executive-branch control and veto-proof majority needed to fundamentally remake a Department whose hasty post-September 11, 2001, creation installed deep flaws that enable today’s politicization and unprofessionalism.

One challenge is that the 119th Congress, using a special legislative rule called “reconciliation,” passed two bills granting Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) about a quarter of a trillion dollars, a massive amount of money that is guaranteed through 2029 with less oversight than in the past. While the new Congress probably lacks the two-thirds majority needed to overcome a presidential veto, it must try—repeatedly if necessary—to rescind or claw back as much of this funding as possible.

It should be possible to use the appropriations process to condition future DHS funding on adherence to professional use-of-force standards; use of body-worn cameras; cooperation with local prosecutors when rights are violated; bolstering the credibility of internal investigations and the now-eviscerated agencies charged with carrying them out; ending racial profiling; vastly improving detention standards; upholding standards for pregnant and lactating women; closing family detention facilities; ending cruel third-country deportations; restoring asylum access at the border; halting expedited deportations of unaccompanied children; rescinding ICE’s arrest quotas and detention mandate; and ceasing agents’ non-return of belongings and identification documents. Conditions could also seek to rescind at least some of the most harmful border wall construction, in areas of great environmental sensitivity, Indigenous lands, and lands in private hands. The list of potential budget conditions is long because DHS’s abuses have been so severe.

Whistleblowers and witnesses will also play a crucial role in curbing abuse, ending corruption and waste, especially with DHS contractors, and beginning the larger process of reform. The new Congress must ensure that they are protected from professional, judicial, or political retaliation and must follow up on well-founded complaints.

Defend civic space and support human rights defenders, journalists, and others at risk

Civil society organizations in many Latin American countries face governments aligned with the Trump administration that are advancing military-led and punitive security strategies, restricting civic space, reducing checks over executive power, and advancing an anti-rights agenda. In Latin America, laws restricting and regulating civil society organizations exist in Cuba, Nicaragua, Guatemala, Paraguay, Venezuela, Peru, El Salvador, and Ecuador; in the latter five, they were enacted since 2024, while the Milei government in Argentina is also proposing a transparency and lobbying law that could restrict civil society organizations. There are political prisoners in Cuba, Nicaragua, and Venezuela, as well as in El Salvador, a government, under Nayib Bukele, that the Trump administration considers a close ally.

Members of Congress have frequently served as a counterbalance to the executive branch, regardless of the party in office, speaking out in favor of human rights defenders and journalists at risk, demanding the release of political prisoners, calling out human rights violations by militaries even if they are U.S. allies, and defending democracy and the role of the international community in advancing common goals. Now, with a new Congress in January, WOLA calls on members to continue to uphold the principle that the promotion and protection of democracy, human rights, and fundamental freedoms are “fundamental components” of U.S. foreign policy, as enshrined in U.S. law.

The administration’s actions will likely continue to put human rights and democracy at risk at home and abroad. That makes it more important that members use their platforms and increased power to speak out against injustices and uplift the work of courageous human rights defenders, journalists, and others working to expose government wrongdoing, and to strengthen democracy and the rule of law in Latin America and across the world.

text:
When the 120th Congress begins, Congress must prioritize an agenda that curbs the most dangerous forms of corruption and starts rebuilding the trust of the American people, according to a letter submitted by CREW, Common Cause and 23 other good government organizations, including National Association of Social Workers, End Citizens United and People For the American Way.

Corruption is an existential threat to democracy. According to polling, corruption was the number one issue in the midterms, surpassing concerns about things like housing, the cost of food and groceries and immigration and border security. In addition, Americans see both political parties as corrupt and view corruption as infecting all three branches of government with significant majorities viewing Congress, the president, the Cabinet and the Supreme Court all as corrupt.

When the public no longer trusts the government, it creates a downward spiral of cynicism and apathy that makes people susceptible to authoritarian strongmen. Corruption also costs people directly—extractive tariffs, reckless abuse of public funds, mergers that drive up prices are all deepening the affordability crisis. Meanwhile, corruption creates national security vulnerabilities that make American diplomatic, trade and aid decisions susceptible to foreign adversaries. Given what is at stake, it is imperative for Congress to pursue an agenda that confronts corruption in government, specifically prioritizing the following six steps:

Conduct robust oversight

Congressional oversight of the Trump-Vance administration has been largely lacking. From companies backed by Trump’s sons receiving over $6 billion in defense contracts to corporations donating hundreds of millions of dollars to Trump’s ballroom project to curry favor with the government, corruption in the executive branch has been staggering. Congress must use all of the tools at its disposal to prioritize oversight of corruption and build the case for more muscular anti-corruption guardrails. And if necessary, Congress should use its investigative powers to compel information, not only from the executive branch, but from the corporations who have enabled this corruption by bankrolling his various vanity projects. The American public has a vested interest in understanding how corporations have enabled corruption under the Trump administration, and what those corporations may have gotten in exchange. Congress must not only expose corruption but also offer bold solutions to fix it so that the American public does not become even more disenchanted.

Ban congressional stock trading and prediction market betting

Congress must get its own house in order by passing a stock trading ban and prohibiting members and high-ranking staff from using their positions of public trust to make money by betting on prediction markets. Bipartisan majorities including 87% of Republicans, 88% of Democrats and 81% of independents support a congressional stock trading ban, such as the bipartisan Restore Trust in Congress Act. A similar approach needs to be taken with prediction markets. The House needs to follow the Senate’s lead and ban members and their staff who could have access to non-public information from placing prediction market bets.This harm is not theoretical—NPR reported that campaign staffers have made thousands by using tips about soon to be released polls to place bets on their own candidates. Additionally, the markets themselves must be prohibited from holding event contracts for war, terrorism or elections in the first place. Promptly passing these common sense reforms will show the American public that Congress is taking its concerns about corruption seriously.

Reverse the Supreme Court’s corruption jurisprudence

In a series of cases decided over the past 39 years, the Supreme Court has systematically gutted the country’s public corruption laws. The Court’s rulings have helped foster a culture of corruption and impunity among public office holders across the ideological spectrum. Congress must prioritize reversing this trend by passing legislation that rebuilds public trust and reverses the Court’s decisions in a series of cases including McDonnell v. United States, Snyder v. United States, United States v. Sun Diamond and Skillings v. United States. Luckily, legislative solutions have already been introduced in both houses of Congress to undo these disastrous decisions. Passing these legislative fixes is a necessary first step to ensuring we have meaningful anti-corruption laws on the books.

Ban presidential profiteering

President Trump has used the White House to get rich, reportedly earning over $2 billion in 2025 alone. But no president, regardless of political party, should be able to leverage the power of their office to get rich. Congress needs to respond by banning any current or future president from earning outside income while they are in office. Executive branch political appointees are already banned from earning outside income. Extending this prohibition to the president is both legal and necessary.

Anti-corruption enforcement

The Trump administration has systematically dismantled the anti-corruption investigative and prosecutorial apparatus at the federal level. That needs to be reversed. Congress should establish a dedicated anti-corruption agency, or agencies, for all three branches of government and should use its appropriations powers to ensure that these efforts are funded through non-discretionary sources and should, where appropriate, create causes of action that also allow for state attorney general enforcement.

End slush funds and personal payouts

The Trump administration has bypassed Congress and created slush funds throughout the government—from the Commerce Department to the Justice Department—to channel money however it chooses. These funds not only undermine Congress’s appropriations powers, but create unguarded pools of money that can be used for payouts to allies and cronies. Although the Trump administration’s attempt to create a $1.776 billion payout to January 6th insurrectionists was enjoined by the courts, the pattern continues, with Trump recently asserting direct personal control over a $25 million dollar “antifraud” fund. Congress must immediately pass guardrails to curb the use of slush funds and also make significant reforms to the federal government’s Judgment Fund that curb the ability to make unwarranted payouts including prohibiting payouts to the president, vice president, and their immediate family members while they are in office.

Corruption is a serious problem in the United States—but we have also seen globally how robust anti-corruption movements can help reinvigorate democracy. The 120th Congress must understand that addressing corruption is essential to preserving our democracy and should accordingly pursue effective anti-corruption measures with all due urgency.

text:
By Gisela Salomon / Associated Press

MIAMI — A federal judge in New York temporarily blocked the Trump administration’s plans to deport Afghans detained in the United States to Afghanistan or Pakistan on Tuesday, after advocates and dozens of members of Congress warned that their lives would be at risk.

The government told the court Tuesday that Immigration and Customs Enforcement had no chartered or commercial flights for deporting Afghan nationals to Afghanistan or to Pakistan at least to the end of the week. Judge Valerie Caproni’s order, which expires Saturday, asks all officials to adhere to that. ICE books the flights weeks in advance.

A letter led by California Democratic Rep. Scott Peters and signed by 65 other members of the House and Senate said they were “extremely concerned that sending vulnerable people” would expose them to “persecution, torture, or even death.” The letter was sent Monday to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

Immigrant rights organizations have also warned that those deported could face retaliation from the Taliban.

Thousands of Afghans fled persecution and feared for their lives after helping the U.S. military and aid groups in Afghanistan.

READ MORE: He fled Afghanistan fearing the Taliban. Now a judge has temporarily halted his deportation

According to court documents obtained by the Associated Press, the U.S. planned to deport Afghan immigrants on Monday on flights from Louisiana, where ICE has immigrant detention and processing facilities, to Pakistan.

President Donald Trump’s administration has deported thousands of immigrants to countries other than their own. In some cases, it has resorted to third-country deportations when removal to their countries of origin was not possible, like when formal diplomatic relations were absent, as is the case with Afghanistan’s Taliban government. In other instances, third-country deportations have been used as a deterrent.

SEE ALSO: A year in ICE detention: Cuban man’s case tests Supreme Court detention ruling

Advocates and attorneys said that more than 80 detained Afghans had contacted them after ICE notified them that they could be deported this week via Pakistan. Among them are women, a police officer, members of religious minorities, and people whose family members served in the U.S. military.

Most fled Afghanistan because of persecution and do not have legal representation, according to Human Rights First and AfghanEvac, a nonprofit organization that advocates for immigrants.

Afghanistan expressed ‘serious concern’ for the deportations

Before the judge signed her order, Zia Ahmad Takal, deputy spokesman of foreign ministry, said “the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan expresses its serious concern” about the reports that U.S. plans to transfer Afghans to Pakistan.

Takal called the U.S. to make sure that decisions or actions are based on rights and “legitimate demands” of those involved, and said “third-party countries should not engage in dealings concerning the fate of another nation’s citizens.”

Immigrant advocates cautiously welcomed the judge’s order

“Today is a good day,” Shawn VanDiver, president at AfghanEvac, said at a news conference Tuesday. “But I want to be honest with you, this is a reprieve, not a resolution. We haven’t stopped this fight forever. This is just a pause.”

FROM THE ARCHIVES: 298 days: Iranian asylum seeker released after judge rules ICE violated his rights

Savitri Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights for Human Rights First, said individuals returned to Afghanistan “face grave, systematic dangers,” including arbitrary detentions, executions, public flogging and retaliatory violence.

“The stakes were very, very high,” she said, and noted that women and girls faced severe restrictions in Afghanistan, like systematic denials of education, employment and public speech.

Advocates expressed their concern about the role of the Pakistani government in facilitating the returns to Afghanistan and the fact that there is no information about the arrangements that the U.S. has made with Pakistan.

“We celebrate today, but we’re getting right back to work tomorrow, continuing to make sure through our flight tracking that none of these flights are taking off,” Arvey said.

Abdul Qahar Afghan contributed from Jalalabad, Afghanistan.

text:
A federal judge in Colorado ordered the Trump administration to immediately release a man who was arrested by immigration agents minutes after being freed from detention.

The judge accused the government of an "ongoing due process violation" and told officials they could face contempt proceedings if they detained him again without a hearing.

U.S. District Judge S. Kato Crews said Edgardo Garcia Vargas was released pursuant to an earlier court order. However, he was "immediately confronted and arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) before even leaving the detention facility grounds."

"Once again, the cruelty appears to be the point," Crews, a Biden appointee, wrote in the November 3 order.

Newsweek has contacted ICE and its parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, for comment and is awaiting responses.

The dispute comes amid mounting tensions between the Trump administration and federal judges over its immigration crackdown. Courts are repeatedly challenging the government's detention practices and, in some cases, accusing immigration authorities of failing to comply with judicial orders.

The administration has been carrying out a widespread deportation operation as it seeks to increase arrests and removals. Immigration arrests in Colorado have climbed in recent months, according to federal data obtained through the Freedom of Information Act by the Deportation Data Project. Arrests nearly doubled from 259 in March to 499 in July 2026. The state recorded 549 arrests in July 2025.

Crews said the government argued that, because Garcia Vargas had technically been released, the habeas relief ordered by the court had been carried out and the case should be closed despite his subsequent re-detention.

The judge rejected that argument and said Garcia Vargas had effectively remained in custody continuously since his original arrest. Ruling otherwise, he wrote, would render any habeas relief "meaningless" and "reward Respondents' apparent gamesmanship."

"No person would have felt free to leave under these circumstances," Crews wrote.

Garcia Vargas had argued in his application for a writ of habeas corpus that his original arrest violated his due process rights because he was never presented with a warrant, according to the order.

A habeas petition asks a court to determine whether someone is being lawfully detained.

Crews said the government did not respond to the petition, so the court accepted Garcia Vargas' due process claim as conceded.

The judge said Garcia Vargas' re-detention "mere minutes after his purported release was no release at all" and instead constituted an ongoing violation of his due process rights.

Crews ordered Garcia Vargas immediately released and directed the administration to file a status report within three days confirming his release.

The judge also barred authorities from detaining Garcia Vargas again unless they first prove at a bond hearing that he is a flight risk or danger to the community. The government would bear the burden of proof, and Garcia Vargas would be allowed to have a lawyer present.

Crews said that another arrest without such a hearing could lead to contempt proceedings.

"Should Petitioner again be instantly rearrested without receiving the foregoing due process," he wrote, "Respondents shall appear in this Court for consideration of whether contempt proceedings are warranted."

Court filings name Juan Baltazar, warden of the Aurora Contract Detention Facility, David Venturella, acting ICE director, and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in the case.

The ruling comes amid a separate legal battle over ICE's arrest practices in Colorado, where a federal judge has repeatedly found the agency violated court orders restricting warrantless arrests. In September, Judge R. Brooke Jackson said agents involved in two separate arrests should face sanctions, including one involving an 18-year-old who suffered a broken wrist and facial injuries. The government has appealed the underlying injunction, with oral arguments scheduled for November 16.

ICE has also been expanding its detention presence in Colorado. In September, Axios Denver reported that detention capacity in the state was poised to nearly double as the administration increased immigration enforcement.

title: Advocating for public health in ICE detention | American Friends Service Committee
description:
A public health emergency behind the walls In June, health officials confirmed an active case of tuberculosis inside GEO.
Colorado law requires public health officials to investigate cases like this and mandates access to facilities and records.
They include Dr. Maureen Daly, a retired public health physician, and Holly Cheng, a public health nurse.
His office pointed us to the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (CDPHE), which had the power to issue a public health order.
Using a previous state health order as a template, we created the People’s Public Health Order.
text:
As a coordinator with AFSC’s Colorado Immigrant Rights Program, much of my work is accompaniment. I walk alongside people facing detention and deportation, and their families. I help people find lawyers, follow their cases, push for medical care, and keep their loved ones informed.

Many of the people I support are held at the immigration detention center in Aurora. It’s run by GEO Group, one of the largest for-profit prison companies in the country, under a contract with ICE. GEO profits from locking people up, and the people inside pay the price.

Through Not1More Deportation (Ni1Mas), an immigrant-led project of AFSC, I kept hearing stories of medical neglect inside GEO and of critically ill people being deported. One of our member leader’s loved ones died soon after being deported, and their death was never counted as a death in ICE custody.

In another example, ICE deported a man I was helping after he spent nearly five months in detention at GEO. For weeks afterwards, no one could reach him. He had become so sick in detention that, when he finally arrived in Guatemala, he basically crawled to an emergency room.

At the same time, our partners at Casa de Paz noticed a growing trend of ICE “patient dumping,” releasing critically ill people on the edge of collapse into hospitals. Together, N1Mas and Casa de Paz began pushing back, centering the experiences of people detained and released, and the knowledge of medical professionals.

Detention makes people sick. People inside face medical neglect. That’s why we’re doing everything we can to support individual releases, get people the care they need now, and end detention for good.

A public health emergency behind the walls

In June, health officials confirmed an active case of tuberculosis inside GEO. TB spreads through the air, is very difficult to treat and can kill if it isn’t treated.

Colorado law requires public health officials to investigate cases like this and mandates access to facilities and records. But when local and state health agencies showed up, GEO and ICE refused to let them in. Meanwhile, people inside and their families told us they were being denied TB testing. Some said sick people were kept in the same spaces as everyone else. Others described being isolated in a wing with the air conditioning turned off.

A 78-year-old priest had TB symptoms for months and received little more than cough medicine. Another man has kidney failure and needs dialysis every few days. If he stays inside, and contracts TB, he could die.

TB doesn’t just stay behind GEO’s walls, either. Staff go home to their families every night, making this a public health emergency for all of us.

Healthcare professionals step up

N1Mas and Casa de Paz brought together a cohort of doctors and nurses who volunteer their time. They include Dr. Maureen Daly, a retired public health physician, and Holly Cheng, a public health nurse. More medical professionals joined as word spread about the group.

Their expertise made all the difference. Because they knew what proper TB care looks like under CDC guidelines, we could cite exactly what GEO was failing to do and move fast. They also review medical records of people in detention and write letters urging medical release, including for the man who needs dialysis.

Their voices have helped policymakers and the public understand the injustice, and they’ve been a key support for immigrants and their loved ones. At the height of the crisis, we organized a public action almost every week.

Pressing the state to act

Dozens of health and immigrant rights groups signed our letter asking Attorney General Phil Weiser to step in. His office pointed us to the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (CDPHE), which had the power to issue a public health order. That is a legal demand requiring GEO to share information and cooperate with an investigation.

We met with the governor’s office and CDPHE leaders, joined by Casa de Paz and a state senator who outlined the protections in Colorado law. Our medical experts pressed state officials on why they hadn’t used their power.

Weeks went by with no order - so we wrote one ourselves! Using a previous state health order as a template, we created the People’s Public Health Order. Close to 300 people signed online, and dozens more signed on the steps of the State Capitol during one public action. Our street theater portrayed the inaction of CDPHE and Gov. Polis. The action drew press and social media attention, raising the pressure.

We invited the governor and CDPHE to the action. The director of CDPHE, Jill Hunsaker Ryan, came and expressed her support. We welcomed her, but words alone couldn't be enough. People inside GEO needed action.

During the event, I said what I believe with my whole heart. “There’s a part of your humanity that dies when you don’t help a person asking for help, and those detained are asking.”

Days later, the Colorado Department of Health and Environment issued its public health order. When GEO refused to comply, Colorado’s attorney general sued. The lawsuit doesn’t address medical neglect itself, but it is an important step toward accountability and a declaration that GEO cannot exist outside the law.

Bearing witness

We’ve also worked to make sure the public can see what’s happening inside. Through open records requests, our Shut Down GEO campaign obtained recordings of 911 calls from inside GEO. These recordings revealed the same patterns of medical neglect and GEO’s dangerous lack of emergency training for non-medical staff.

N1Mas and Casa de Paz built a publicly available website that hosts the 911 recordings alongside voices of immigrants in our community.

In September, N1Mas, Shut Down GEO, and Casa de Paz, organized a pop-up audio-visual installation outside GEO. We hung QR codes from the trees so people could walk from tree to tree and listen on their phones. Dr. Daly also spoke, offering to connect GEO workers with legal help if they’re asked to do anything unethical or illegal. To people trapped inside, she said, “We believe you, and we haven’t forgotten you.”

I believe that if any one of us has to bear witness to this horror, everyone should, because we aren’t supposed to be the same after we witness it. What’s happening at GEO is a small window into every detention center.

The TB threat isn’t over. Since 2024, our Shut Down GEO Aurora campaign has documented hundreds of cases of medical neglect. Our healthcare cohort is planning its next campaign, and a state senator has offered to help us write health legislation for the next session. Organizers who accompany people in detention now meet regularly to track patterns, support one another, and bring ideas for action back to people inside, so those most affected guide our work.

At AFSC, we believe every person has worth and that healthcare is a human right. No one’s health is safe in a cage. That’s why we’re committed to ending immigration detention for good.

title: 'If you vote illegally, we will find you' | ICE shares Election Day warning - WCIV
authors: JESSICA A. BOTELHO | The National News Desk, JESSICA A. BOTELHO, The National News Desk
description:
"If you vote illegally, we will find you," ICE wrote on X.
Federal law generally bars noncitizens from voting in federal elections, though some local jurisdictions allow noncitizens to vote in local contests.
"American elections are for American citizens.
"Only American citizens should be deciding American elections."
Federal authorities may investigate violations of federal election law.
text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Tuesday warned that anyone who votes in America illegally will be held responsible.

"If you vote illegally, we will find you," ICE wrote on X. "We will track you down, arrest you, and prosecute you. There will be no escape."

The Election Day message drew attention to the Trump administration's focus on investigating alleged voting by people who are living the U.S illegally. Federal law generally bars noncitizens from voting in federal elections, though some local jurisdictions allow noncitizens to vote in local contests.

ICE said multiple "unlawful voting" arrests were recently made in multiple states, including New Jersey and Pennsylvania.

"American elections are for American citizens. Anyone who unlawfully votes will be found and brought to justice," ICE noted in a separate post.

Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin also issued a warning, saying the department will pursue people who vote despite being ineligible.

If you vote illegally in this country, and you are NOT eligible to vote, @DHSgov will find you, hunt you down, and you will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law," Mullin wrote on X. "Only American citizens should be deciding American elections."

The social media posts came amid expanded federal efforts to investigate suspected election offenses. The administration has announced arrests and prosecutions involving alleged illegal voting, with voting-rights groups challenging some administration election efforts in court, arguing they risk voter intimidation and rely on unreliable data.

ICE's posts did not say that the agency would be present at polling places, but election administration is primarily handled by state and local officials. Federal authorities may investigate violations of federal election law.

The FBI separately urged voters to report suspected election crimes.

text:
November 9 marks a tragic milestone: 100 days since the Trump administration cut off competent legal support for tens of thousands of children who are going through the immigration courts alone, abandoning them to the whims of ‘deportation judges hired to carry out Stephen Miller’s mass deportation agenda.’

The immigration court data already show the effects of these policies. Acacia’s October 15 fact sheet, The Data Behind a Due Process Crisis, found that 69 percent of unaccompanied children’s cases completed in the first eight months of 2026 ended in a removal order, up from an average of 28 percent from 2021 through 2024. Voluntary departures for children also climbed, reaching 1,831 in those eight months, compared to 527 in all of 2024. The immigration courts haven’t just become a deportation machine for adults in the system, they’re a deportation machine for kids, too.

To ensure that these children are not forgotten and to push for practical solutions that protect them, I am hosting a virtual conversation this Monday, November 9 at 1:00 PM Eastern, with three of the most recognized subject matter experts: Dr. Marsha Griffin, President and CEO of Community for Children; Katie Fleming, Director of Public Education and Engagement at Acacia Center for Justice; and Neha Desai, Managing Director of Children’s Human Rights and Dignity at the National Center for Youth Law.

Together, they will help us understand what has gone wrong for children in court in the past 100 days. While more Americans are aware of the shocking fact that kids are going to court alone, few people truly understand what that means and just how consequential this is for these children.

Dr. Marsha Griffin, Katie Fleming, and Neha Desai will share new findings and firsthand stories from courtroom observation that reveal how dangerous courts have become for children. The government is offering unrepresented children $3,000 to accept voluntary departure, even when it is not in their best interest and before they have a chance to have their case heard. Hearings are being shuffled around and added to virtual videoconferencing dockets that make it even harder for children to know what’s going on. So far, the multi-million dollar contract has gone to a firm with ties to the Trump administration, then to an organization called Our Rescue founded by a former ICE agent. And HHS is now attempting to send its own attorneys to represent children, a move that six senators called a “clear conflict of interest.”

We will also discuss real solutions, especially putting pressure on states to do their part to ensure that children have basic access to legal counsel. California is one example. Its 2026-27 state budget renewed the Children’s Holistic Immigration Representation Project, which pairs unaccompanied children with legal and social service teams, for more than 1,000 children, and created a new Immigration Counsel Access Pilot Program. In August, New York committed $7.25 million in new state funding for legal services for about 1,400 unaccompanied children in removal proceedings.

Moreover, with the stunning results of the midterms now in, this 100-day retrospective on the loss of competent legal services for children in court is also a forward-looking appeal to the incoming representatives of the 120th Congress to prioritize real fixes to the Trump administration’s sabotage of due process for children.

Join us at 1:00 PM Eastern on November 9, 2026. Registration is open to the public, including reporters, Hill staffers, researchers, NGOs, and concerned members of the public. Registration is free but required. Register at the link below.

REGISTER NOW

No recording, transcription, republication, or AI notetakers are permitted without advanced approval. Registrations that appear to be automated will be notified and removed before the event.

About the speakers

Dr. Marsha Griffin

Marsha Griffin, MD, is a co-founder, President and CEO of Community for Children, Inc., a non-profit formed by three pediatricians and an educator to fill critical gaps in care for immigrant children and families, and she serves on the Board of Trustees for the Acacia Center for Justice. A retired Clinical Professor of Pediatrics at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley School of Medicine, she was a founding member of the Executive Committee of the American Academy of Pediatrics Council on Immigrant Child and Family Health, co-authored the AAP Policy Statement “Detention of Immigrant Children,” and chaired the AAP Border Strategy Team. From 2014 to 2020 she was Medical Director of the Humanitarian Care Respite Clinic in McAllen, Texas, organizing volunteer medical teams from around the country to care for immigrant families passing through the border region. Her current research and advocacy centers on health inequities suffered by asylum-seeking pregnant mothers and children with serious medical conditions.

Katie Fleming

Katie Fleming is the Director of Public Education and Engagement at the Acacia Center for Justice, where she leads national training and advocacy initiatives that equip community members, legal professionals, and partner organizations with the knowledge and tools to support immigrant communities and strengthen the immigration field. Katie also oversees Acacia’s Witness for Justice initiative, which creates opportunities for community members to engage directly with the immigration court system through court observation, public education, storytelling, and advocacy. Katie is an attorney with nearly 15 years of experience in immigration law, including direct representation of individuals navigating the complex immigration court system.

Neha Desai

Neha Desai is the Managing Director of Children’s Human Rights & Dignity at the National Center for Youth Law, where she leads the organization’s work on behalf of immigrant children. Neha’s team works to ensure that immigrant children are able to live in communities rather than in government custody and have access to the resources and opportunities they need to heal and thrive. For nearly 20 years, Neha has been a children’s rights attorney working with youth in government custody. She began her legal career at the Juvenile Law Center on the team that litigated Pennsylvania’s “Kids for Cash” scandal, in which two judges took kickbacks from private detention centers for sending thousands of children to them, many without a lawyer. While at NCYL, Neha has served as counsel on multiple federal class action cases representing children detained in federal immigration custody. Neha received her law degree from Berkeley School of Law and her undergraduate degree from the University of Chicago.

text:
Roxbury, a Morris County Republican stronghold where Donald Trump won by nearly 19 points two years ago, voted Democratic in Tuesday’s congressional election after a bitter controversy over the Trump administration’s decision to locate an immigration detention center in the township.

Rep.-elect Rebecca Bennett (D-Bridgewater) defeated Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (R-Westfield) by 338 votes, 4,898 to 4,560, a remarkable turnaround in a municipality where Kean had posted landslide victories in his previous two congressional campaigns.

Bennett received 51.1% of the vote to Kean’s 47.5%, a 3.5-point victory that represents a swing of more than 21 percentage points since 2024.

In 2022, Kean carried Roxbury by more than 19 percentage points against then-Rep. Tom Malinowski (D-Ringoes); he won Roxbury by 5,611 votes – more than half of his 9,309-vote margin. He took a thousand-vote haircut in four years. (His margin against Sue Altman in 2024 was more than 18 points).

The township’s Republican credentials were hardly in doubt. Trump carried Roxbury by 18.5 points in 2024, and Republican Jack Ciattarelli defeated Democrat Mikie Sherrill by nearly 11 points in last year’s gubernatorial election.

But the Trump administration’s decision to purchase a warehouse on Route 46 for an Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facility scrambled local politics, putting Republican elected officials at odds with a Republican president and, for a time, their own Republican congressman.

Roxbury’s all-Republican Township Council unanimously opposed the facility and joined the Sherrill administration in a federal lawsuit seeking to block the project.

Mayor Shawn Potillo and the council publicly criticized Kean, saying he had not provided the level of advocacy they expected on behalf of township residents.

Kean defended his involvement, saying he had contacted senior Department of Homeland Security officials and was working toward a solution. In February, he introduced legislation that would reimburse municipalities for costs associated with federal immigration detention facilities, including lost property tax revenue and infrastructure improvements.

But Kean stopped short of formally opposing the detention center until September 27, when he announced his opposition during his only debate with Bennett, sponsored by the New Jersey Globe and Rider University.

Bennett had opposed the project for months, siding with local Republican officials who maintained that the township lacked the infrastructure to accommodate a facility that could house as many as 1,500 detainees.

Instead of debating federal immigration policy, the issue was entirely local. Township officials raised concerns about water and sewer capacity, traffic, environmental damage, and the loss of local property tax revenue.

In May, federal officials agreed not to proceed with converting the warehouse into a detention facility until an environmental assessment was completed, following the lawsuit filed by Roxbury and the Sherrill administration.

Roxbury didn’t just vote against Kean.

Democratic U.S. Sen. Cory Booker carried Roxbury by 226 votes, defeating Republican Justin Murphy, 4,745 to 4,519, or 49.7% to 47.3%. Independent candidates received another 210 votes.

In the Morris County commissioner race, Democrat Christopher Russo defeated Republican incumbent Tayfun Selen by 141 votes, 4,712 to 4,571, or 50.7% to 49.2% of the votes cast for commissioner candidates.

The results were striking in a municipality that has traditionally given Republicans substantial margins in countywide, statewide, and congressional elections.

Bennett ran 153 votes ahead of Booker, while Kean received 41 more votes than Murphy. Russo received 33 fewer votes than Booker, while Selen received 11 more votes than Kean.

Bennett’s margin of victory was also larger than Booker’s or Russo’s, suggesting the Democratic nominee attracted support beyond voters who backed the rest of the Democratic ticket.

The election drew 9,738 voters from Roxbury’s 18,682 registered voters, a turnout of 52.12%. Of those ballots, 6,487 were cast on Election Day, 1,896 during early in-person voting and 1,355 by mail.

The results don’t prove how many voters have changed their minds because of the detention center controversy, particularly in an election that produced substantial Democratic gains across New Jersey.

But the magnitude of Kean’s drop in Roxbury, where he had previously enjoyed margins exceeding 18 points, shows how suddenly the township’s political landscape changed in a one election cycle.

For Republicans, the loss of Roxbury was particularly significant because the township had been a reliable source of votes in Kean’s two successful congressional campaigns.

And for Bennett, who defeated Kean districtwide by 16 percentage points, Roxbury was one of the clearest examples of how far Democrats penetrated traditionally Republican territory in 2026.

title: ACLU of Texas Border Poll Highlights Voter Rejection of ICE, Anti-Immigrant Policies
description:
The ACLU of Texas commissioned the survey to better understand how border residents across the political spectrum feel about the surge in immigration enforcement.
Key findings include: 53% of border residents think state and local immigration enforcement presence makes life harder without making their communities safer.
63% of border residents, including people who have a family member employed by a federal immigration enforcement agency, believe ICE tactics have gone too far.
64% of border residents want local and state law enforcement to prioritize preventing and solving crime rather than immigration enforcement.
The ACLU of Texas recommends several policies to prioritize public safety, improve conditions for residents, and represent the interests and prevailing views of border residents.
text:
AUSTIN, Texas – The American Civil Liberties Union of Texas conducted polling prior to the midterm election that revealed widespread concern among border residents about federal, state, and local immigration enforcement. Those findings bore out on Election Day as voters — especially Latino/e voters — overwhelmingly swept pro-ICE, anti-immigration candidates out of office.

“Voters along the border and throughout the state sent a resounding message to Texas leaders: We have had enough, get ICE out of our communities,” said Osvaldo Grimaldo (he/him), policy strategist on border and immigrants’ rights at the ACLU of Texas. “We’re not surprised by these election night results after our poll of El Paso and Rio Grande Valley showed residents felt that anti-immigration policies had gone too far. Latino voters have been impacted by this state’s harmful immigration policies and hope for the day that Texas creates a welcoming environment for our immigrant communities — now more than ever, that day is near.”

The report, entitled “Gone Too Far: Border Residents in Texas Are Concerned About Immigration Enforcement” and released in early October, shared results from a poll conducted by Change Research of 1,031 adults in El Paso County and four Rio Grande Valley counties (Cameron, Hidalgo, Starr, and Willacy) between August 25 and September 2.

The ACLU of Texas commissioned the survey to better understand how border residents across the political spectrum feel about the surge in immigration enforcement. Key findings include:

53% of border residents think state and local immigration enforcement presence makes life harder without making their communities safer. Only 34% say it makes their communities safer.

63% of border residents, including people who have a family member employed by a federal immigration enforcement agency, believe ICE tactics have gone too far.

64% of border residents want local and state law enforcement to prioritize preventing and solving crime rather than immigration enforcement.

“ICE isn’t helping by deporting our hardworking immigrants regardless of their status. This whole region and country has been built on the backs of immigrants,” said one respondent who lives in the RGV and voted for Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election.

Across the surveyed regions, Trump had an approval rating of 34% and disapproval rating of 60% — with 57% disapproval in the RGV and 65% disapproval in El Paso. The president won the four surveyed Rio Grande Valley counties during the 2024 election but lost El Paso County.

The federal government continues to expand immigration enforcement presence along the Texas-Mexico border despite the disruption it causes for residents of all political backgrounds who live there. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, who lost his re-election bid on Tuesday night, and the state legislature have also mandated local cooperation between law enforcement and ICE.

The ACLU of Texas recommends several policies to prioritize public safety, improve conditions for residents, and represent the interests and prevailing views of border residents. Those recommendations — which are explained in greater detail in the full report — are:

Halt 287(g) agreements and end existing local law enforcement collaboration with ICE.

End state police involvement in federal immigration enforcement.

Support victims of crime.

Tailor local law enforcement priorities to avoid targeting sensitive locations such as schools, places of worship, and hospitals.

A copy of the report with crosstabs is available here: https://www.aclutx.org/publications/gone-too-far-border-residents-in-texas-are-concerned-about-immigration-enforcement/

title: Federal courts in New Mexico, New York temporarily block ICE deportations of Afghans
authors: Julia Gentin, Gabriela Campos, New Mexican file photo
description: A federal court in New Mexico on Monday blocked the deportation of an Afghan national who had been held at the Torrance County Detention Facility.
text:
The winner of the sheriff race will replace retiring Sheriff…

Twenty new cases have been identified in the state since Wed…



A view of the Torrance County Detention Facility in September 2025

A federal court in New York on Tuesday blocked the Trump administration’s plans to deport Afghans to their Taliban-controlled country of origin through Pakistan in a temporary order that expires Saturday.

The decision came the day after a federal judge in New Mexico prohibited the removal of Sardar Akbari, 31, an Afghan national who had been held at the Torrance County Detention Facility in Estancia. That order also was temporary, pausing the deportation for 14 days, “until the Court is satisfied that the government has put in place adequate safeguards to protect Akbari against the risk of suicide,” according to a statement from the American Civil Liberties Union of New Mexico.

After learning of the federal government’s plans to send him to Pakistan, Akbari suffered an “acute mental health crisis,” the ACLU of New Mexico said in the statement.

Deportation flights for Afghans were set to go through Pakistan because the U.S. has no diplomatic relations with the Taliban government to arrange flights to Afghanistan. The State Department also places Afghanistan under a “Level 4 — Do not travel” advisor y “due to civil unrest, crime, terrorism, risk of wrongful detention, kidnapping, natural disasters, and limited health facilities.”

New York Judge Valerie Caproni’s order on Tuesday does not put an end to deportations through Pakistan. But it prevents the flights from taking off until Sunday.

Akbari is represented by the Clinical Law Program of the University of New Mexico Law School and the ACLU in his habeas proceedings, in which he is challenging the legality of his detention.

He has been in the custody of the federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement since late 2024 and was transported from the Torrance County facility to El Paso’s Camp East Montana — the nation’s largest immigrant detention center — Oct. 27. The move was to prepare him for deportation, according to court documents.

“Mr. Akbari’s case is a window into the abject horrors of our immigration system, and the government’s ‘third country removals’ in particular,” said Shaw Drake, assistant professor of Law at the UNM School of Law, in a statement. “If ICE is able to deport vulnerable immigrants like Mr. Akbari to a country other than his own without any notice or opportunity to claim fear, the fundamental due process safeguards to which we are all entitled are rendered virtually meaningless.”

Camp East Montana is plagued with controversies, including allegations of life-threatening medical neglect, coercive removals, inhumane confinement, three detainee deaths and an alleged riot, according to a July report from the ACLU.

The El Paso City Council voted unanimously Oct. 27 to draft a resolution calling for the detention center’s closure, though the decision ultimately falls to the federal government.

Julia Gentin is a reporter for The Las Cruces New Mexican, The Santa Fe New Mexican and Searchlight New Mexico through a partnership with Report for America, a national service program that places journalists into local newsrooms. She covers the Southern New Mexico region. Learn more about Report for America at reportforamerica.org .





Keep up with the stories impacting Southern New Mexico, delivered every Friday.

name: Policy
title: What a Democratic Congress Means for Latin America
description:
Presidents facing opposition on Capitol Hill often turn toward foreign policy, where they retain considerable authority.
New Congressional leadership on Latin America Representative Gregory Meeks (D-NY), expected to chair the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has already delivered that message.
We anticipate even greater turbulence in U.S. policy toward Latin America over the next two years than in the last two.
Latin America watchers also should remain alert to issues that may appear to have receded.
Tags: Trump and Latin America, U.S. midterms, U.S. Policy
text:
Reading Time: 4 minutes

In a historic vote, Democrats pulled off a blue wave in the U.S. midterms that was stronger than many, including us, had anticipated in the months and weeks leading up to the elections. The party won both chambers handily, paving the way to restoring a congressional check on President Donald Trump’s approach to a broad range of issues, with Latin America high on the list.

Just as important as the new Congress will be the impact of opposition control on a president staring down his last two years in office. Presidents facing opposition on Capitol Hill often turn toward foreign policy, where they retain considerable authority.

Latin American governments and business leaders should now prepare for two main developments: a U.S. Congress ready to reclaim its authority and a president likely to respond to domestic constraints by becoming more aggressive abroad, particularly in the Western Hemisphere.

Some in the region will need to recalibrate their relationships with Washington. A case in point: Endorsements of Representative Maria Elvira Salazar (R-FL) by Colombia’s Abelardo De La Espriella, Argentina’s Javier Milei and Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado reflected a shortsighted approach. Although Salazar appears most likely to win narrowly, those endorsements were unwise: They tied foreign leaders and national causes to one side of an American election, inserted themselves into our democratic elections, and complicated relationships with Democrats.

Effective diplomacy requires playing the long game, and those who neglected Democrats should now seek to repair relationships.

New Congressional leadership on Latin America

Representative Gregory Meeks (D-NY), expected to chair the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has already delivered that message. In October, he warned that De La Espriella’s electoral intervention jeopardized bipartisan U.S. support for Colombia: “Congress will be watching,” he said. Looking ahead, Meeks’ longstanding commitment to Colombia across administrations makes his leadership especially important for that country and the wider Americas region.

Representative Joaquin Castro (D-TX), expected to lead the House Western Hemisphere Subcommittee, has previewed his agenda through actions while in the House minority. In September, he sought subpoenas for records concerning the administration’s oil agreement in Venezuela involving the controversial Barbados-based company North American Blue Energy Partners. Republicans blocked the motion. But now, with a majority, Castro can pursue that investigation.

In the Senate, Tim Kaine (D-VA), likely to lead the Western Hemisphere Subcommittee, brings a deep knowledge of the Americas to his position. Meanwhile, Senator Chris Coons (D-DE), the likely next Chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, has already challenged the administration’s Venezuela policy in hearings and through war powers votes. Earlier this year, Coons publicly pressed Secretary of State Marco Rubio over the failure to consult Congress before Maduro’s removal and backed efforts to restrict further military operations.

With new congressional leadership on Latin America in both chambers, those involved in deals in Venezuela (and elsewhere in the Americas) should expect scrutiny of beneficiaries and possible corruption. Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY), likely the next Speaker of the House, has identified countering corruption as the Democrats’ guiding principle for oversight next year.

Meanwhile, confirmations in the Senate will likely slow dramatically, particularly for controversial non-career nominees. Career diplomats with bipartisan credibility should expect to fare much better. Regional governments should anticipate vacancies and a reliance on acting officials.

Congressional Democrats’ agenda

As we previewed in May, immigration enforcement will also be central to oversight. Democrats will investigate ICE’s conduct, detention practices, and spending. But scrutiny does not mean ending funding: Republican reconciliation laws provided substantial enforcement resources to ICE through 2029.

The Trump administration’s use of El Salvador’s CECOT prison under its arrangement with Nayib Bukele will also face renewed scrutiny, including of the legal authorities for transferring detainees, their treatment, and Washington’s financing commitments. Other arrangements to send migrants to unsafe third countries—or those where integration will prove difficult—will raise similar questions.

Congress’s greatest leverage is its power of the purse, placing the House and Senate Appropriations Committees at the center of the coming policy debates. Democrats will seek to reclaim spending authority as they confront the administration’s dismantling of foreign assistance and withholding of approved funds. Expect debates over conditions, disclosure, and compliance with spending laws. Funding agreements will require negotiations with Republicans and the White House, and further shutdowns remain possible.

Democrats in Congress will be wise to look beyond oversight and put forward an affirmative regional agenda, showing the American public that they can deliver results, while—through the oversight agenda—restoring a congressional check on the executive. Investigating illegal and ineffective lethal boat strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific will be essential.

At the same time, Americans devastated by overdose deaths and Latin Americans confronting organized crime also deserve effective policy responses. Democrats should put forth credible legislative alternatives, particularly on the security front. In the economic realm, Democrats plan to quickly consider legislation to end Trump’s global tariffs and restore congressional control over trade policy.

Trump may take an even harder line

The midterms may begin the end of the Trump political era. But they do not end the president’s desire to seek to transform the Americas. We anticipate even greater turbulence in U.S. policy toward Latin America over the next two years than in the last two.

Cuba is the clearest place to watch. Constrained domestically, Trump will find a confrontation with the Caribbean island especially attractive. Confrontation could take the form of an even more aggressive drive toward negotiations that attempts to force economic and political change in the nation, or it could take the form of military force. The latter seems less likely in the short term than it did several months ago, principally due to resumed hostilities in Iran, but Trump’s willingness to use force and ambitions toward Cuba—especially if Havana refuses to negotiate—must be taken seriously.

Assuming Trump will inevitably retreat—or that a Democratic Congress would serve as a check on his power vis-à-vis Cuba—is dangerous.

Latin America watchers also should remain alert to issues that may appear to have receded. U.S. strikes against criminal groups in Mexico remain a possibility, with potentially profound consequences for bilateral cooperation and ongoing USMCA negotiations. The Panama Canal could also return to Trump’s agenda, even though it has slipped from the headlines. Governments and businesses should resist the temptation to treat a quieter period as evidence that these risks have passed. With Trump, an issue can quickly return to the center of the relationship without warning.

The Democratic wave gives Congress a renewed mandate to constrain presidential overreach and offer an alternate vision for the Americas. Governments and businesses should engage Congress early and substantively, while also preparing for a U.S. president determined to assert his power abroad as his options narrow at home.

Tags: Trump and Latin America, U.S. midterms, U.S. Policy

text:
Chuck Jenkins, the notoriously anti-immigrant Maryland sheriff who boasts of having helped deport 2,000 people, was wiped out in Tuesday’s blue wave.

Voters in Frederick County, a fast-growing and increasingly liberal area north of Washington, D.C., denied his bid for a sixth term. They opted for his opponent, Democrat Karl Bickel, by a margin of 56 to 44 percent.

César Díaz, president of the city council in Frederick, which is the county’s largest city, called Jenkins’s defeat “a repudiation of evil.”

“He is the face here of cruel, inhumane federal policy,” Díaz told Bolts late Tuesday. “Everybody knows somebody, or knows somebody who knows somebody, who’s been directly affected (by ICE). He’s proud of being the face of that, and people have had enough.”

Jenkins, 70, gained national fame for his staunch support of ICE, often appearing on Fox News and visiting with Donald Trump at both the White House and Mar-a-Lago. He joined ICE’s 287(g) program, which deputizes local officials to act on the agency’s behalf, in 2008, long before the program exploded in popularity among conservative sheriffs. He was an early backer of President Donald Trump, and vowed, during Trump’s first run for office, “As long as I am sheriff of Frederick County, we are going to work with ICE.”

Bickel, who is 76 and worked in the sheriff’s office in the 1990s, and who had run and lost against Jenkins in each of the previous three cycles, has vowed not to collaborate with ICE and says he plans to dispatch his deputies to monitor ICE activity in the county. “A lot of what ICE is doing, if a deputy did it they’d be fired or arrested,” Bickel told Bolts in August. “The use of force, the utilization of chemical agents, things like that. It’s just not right.”

In a brief text exchange Wednesday morning, Bickel said, “Now the real work begins.” Jenkins did not respond to a request for comment.

Ahead of the election, Bolts spoke with many immigrants in the county who said Jenkins has, since his first election in 2006, created a culture of fear in Frederick County, which is home to a large Latino population.

Some immigrants told Bolts they’ve been living in hiding lately, frequently unable to work and sometimes unable to obtain food and other basic needs as a result. Many have kept their children out of school and seen family members deported.

“We’re excited. We’re really excited,” one immigrant from El Salvador said of the election result. His stepfather was deported under Jenkins’ 287(g) program, and Bolts is not identifying him by name because he, too, is vulnerable to deportation.

“With him out of his position, Frederick will change for the better,” the man added. “What happened with my stepdad—it was because of policies like his. With him out of office, I hope it will change.”

Jenkins’ defeat speaks both to Frederick County’s changing demographics and to a huge amount of organizing in recent years by immigrant rights activists in the county and throughout Maryland. This coalition successfully lobbied the state legislature to ban 287(g) partnerships earlier this year and to install other immigrant protections—changes Jenkins and 16 other Maryland sheriffs vigorously opposed and sued to prevent.

Of these 17 sheriffs, most were running for reelection unopposed on Tuesday. That lack of competition is quite common across the country, as sheriffs frequently face no challengers, even in some places that are otherwise quite politically competitive.

This year’s blue wave did take out at least one other sheriff famous for harsh policing of immigrants: Republican Terry Johnson, of Alamance County, North Carolina, who faced a federal investigation for his profiling of Latinos, was denied a seventh term in office, losing narrowly to Democratic pastor Shannon Long.

Díaz, the Frederick council president, cautioned that defeating people like Jenkins and Johnson does not alone assuage the fears of immigrants who are still living under the threat of ICE.

“The community is under attack from more than just Chuck Jenkins,” he said. “But that fear did go down a tick after 287(g) was banned. Now Jenkins is gone, and the fear goes down another tick.”

title: U.S. judge temporarily blocks deportation of detained Afghans to Afghanistan or Pakistan
description:
A federal judge in New York temporarily blocked the Trump administration’s plans to deport Afghans detained in the United States to Afghanistan or Pakistan on Tuesday (November 3, 2026), after advocates and dozens of members of Congress warned that their lives would be at risk.
