text:
A UC Berkeley student was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents at San Francisco International Airport, according to the university and a Bay Area immigrants' rights attorney.

What we know:

The 23-year-old student, an asylum seeker from Colombia with no criminal record, was at the airport departing for an out-of-town trip on Friday when she was taken into custody.

"She was arrested for a visa overstay, but the arrest was unlawful and unconstitutional," according to managing attorney with Alameda County Immigration Legal and Education Partnership, Nikolas De Bremaeker.

In an email correspondence with KTVU, De Bremaeker confirmed that the student, Paula Albornoz Hernandez, was being held at ICE's California City Detention Center in Kern County.

De Bremaeker said the arrest came despite the fact that the college student had been adhering to every legal requirement of her asylum process.

"She filed her asylum application well before her filing deadline," the attorney said. "She has attended her biometrics appointments, which she cleared, and subsequently received her work permit."

De Bremaeker said ACILEP has filed a habeas petition in federal court and is concurrently seeking immediate emergency intervention.

KTVU reached out to SFO officials seeking information about the ICE activity at the airport.

"We have no information on this one; we don’t assist in immigration enforcement and were not notified of this," SFO Public Information Officer Doug Yakel told KTVU in an email.

UC Berkeley response

On Monday, UC Berkeley Chancellor Richard Lyons addressed the incident in a campus-wide message.

"This student is a valued member of our community, and campus leadership is doing everything within our power to support them so that they may return to their life at Berkeley to continue their studies with us," Lyons wrote.

He said while he could not provide specifics about the case, the university is taking action and said that efforts are underway on and off campus to support the student.

"We understand the urgency of this moment. While student privacy laws and university policy limit what we can share publicly, I want our community to know that we’ve mobilized legal support and are working to ensure our student has access to advice and representation," the chancellor wrote.

Lyons also said university officials are in close contact with the student’s family.

Student resources

The chancellor acknowledged the uncertainty and fear an incident like this can stoke, and he reminded students of the resources in place through UC Berkeley'sUndocumented Student Program.

"The university’s commitment to supporting every member of this community remains as strong as ever," Lyons said, as he encouraged students to stay informed amid a surge in ICE activity.

SEE ALSO: Federal immigration agents seen near Milpitas and San Jose jails, sheriff's office confirms

"Given the increase in immigration enforcement actions, we urge the community to review Know Your Rights Information," the chancellor said in his message.

Berkeley mayor's response

Berkeley Mayor Adena Ishii also issued a statement on the incident and had a message for ICE.

"Detaining a student under these circumstances does nothing to make our community safer. It creates fear among immigrant families and students who call Berkeley home," the mayor said.

Ishii urged federal immigration authorities to release Albornoz Hernandez.

"I'm calling on ICE to release her so she can return to her studies while her case moves forward," the mayor said, stressing the city's support for its immigrant communities.

"Berkeley is a sanctuary city, and we will continue to stand with our immigrant neighbors and students," Ishii said.

Person ‘government should celebrate’

Dig deeper:

De Bremaeker described Albornoz Hernandez as "an exceptional student" who previously graduated with honors at San Jose City College, where she received several awards.

"She was then admitted into one of the country's most competitive undergraduate business administration programs at UC Berkeley," the attorney noted.

He also highlighted her contributions to the community.

"She serves our community by volunteering with her church and other community groups. This is a person our government should celebrate," said De Bremaeker, "rather than detain under inhumane conditions at the California City Detention Center."

KTVU reached out to the ICE Office of Public Affairs as well as the Department of Homeland Security but had not received a response from either federal entities by the time of this story’s publication.

title: Massive expansion of immigration detention under new EU return rules - Statewatch
description:
It is part of a two-part series on the new EU Return Regulation.
The Return Regulation has been presented as a means to make returns more effective and “to simplify and speed up procedures” across the EU.
PICUM dubbed the Return Regulation the “Deportation Regulation,” given the deeply punitive and coercive nature of the legislation.
More reasons to detain The ‘Deportation Regulation’ significantly expands the grounds for immigration detention (Article 29) compared to the 2008 Return Directive.
Harsher detention conditions Detention conditions will become harsher under Article 32 of the regulation.
text:
A version of this article was originally published on the Border Criminologies blog at the University of Oxford. It is part of a two-part series on the new EU Return Regulation.

The European Commission launched its proposal in March 2025 for a new EU ‘Return Regulation’, as part of a series of reforms pushed through the European Parliament at “break-neck speed” over the last year. The rules were adopted on 1 October, and have been met with widespread criticism from civil society organisations, human rights bodies and members of academia.

The Return Regulation has been presented as a means to make returns more effective and “to simplify and speed up procedures” across the EU. To do this, the new rules aim to expand the grounds and prolong the use of immigration detention – including for children – while ramping up deportations for people without a valid residence permit in the EU. This includes using questionable US-style externalisation practices. Meanwhile, it introduces a range of surveillance-based measures framed as “alternatives to detention” (ATDs), which effectively risk replicating detention outside its formal facilities.

Read alongside the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum, which became applicable from June 2026, as well as proposals to digitise the EU’s deportation system and give Frontex a new role in returns, the Return Regulation embodies a broader EU migration-management culture increasingly reliant on control, detention, and removal.

Brussels-based organisation, The Platform for International Cooperation for Undocumented Migrants (PICUM), has highlighted the potential human rights violations caused by this regulation. PICUM dubbed the Return Regulation the “Deportation Regulation,” given the deeply punitive and coercive nature of the legislation. This stance informs this two-part series, which focuses on how the new regulation paves the way for the expansion of detention and surveillance.

More reasons to detain

The ‘Deportation Regulation’ significantly expands the grounds for immigration detention (Article 29) compared to the 2008 Return Directive. The earlier directive limited detention primarily to cases involving a risk of absconding, based on a shorter list of circumstances, and/or the obstruction of return procedures.

The regulation adds grounds for immigration detention, including:

being considered a security risk;

to verify identity and nationality;

non-compliance with the obligation to cooperate set out in article 18 in the agreed text;

“other relevant grounds related to return provided for in national law”.

It is not specified how any of these grounds and risks (e.g. absconding, hampering return and security risk) are to be assessed, which raises concerns about the potential for arbitrary detention at the national level. By adding grounds for detention that are vaguely defined (e.g. “other relevant grounds related to return provided for in national law”), the regulation risks leading to broad interpretations and inconsistent application across EU member states. It also weakens some existing safeguards under the 2008 directive, for instance by no longer explicitly requiring the immediate release of a person where detention is found to be unlawful.

The regulation also introduces an expanded list of criteria based on which third-country nationals may be presumed to present a risk of absconding (Article 19), which is itself a ground for detention. People may be considered at risk of absconding – and therefore be detained – where there is an absence of “social anchoring”, such as a lack of stable housing, family connections or financial resources. This approach risks effectively criminalising poverty and social exclusion.

Similarly controversial is paragraph 2(c), which broadly provides that detention can be justified when “departure is imminent and there are reasons to believe that the third-country national intends to violate the obligation to cooperate”, without clearly specifying how these reasons are to be assessed. This leaves considerable room for interpretation at national level.

The ‘Deportation Regulation’ – alongside the EU Pact on Asylum and Migration – has consolidated a tendency in EU legislation whereby punitive and restrictive migration measures are justified through appeals to “security” or “public order”. PICUM has emphasised that this has concrete consequences for people navigating migration and asylum procedures, since it reinforces associations between migration and criminality or security threats, increases legal uncertainty and discrimination, while reducing prospects for regularisation and integration in society.

A person is considered to pose a security risk if there are “clear indications” that they intend to commit an offence (under Article 13), yet such determinations rely on weak and speculative assessments. The new detention grounds are part of this wider shift: they give EU member states more scope to use deprivation of liberty in response to perceived and loosely described risks.

Longer detention periods

The EU co-legislators also agreed to increase the maximum period of detention from 18 months under the 2008 Directive to 24 months (under Article 30). In some circumstances – including when there is a perceived risk of absconding and “a reasonable prospect of removal” – detention can be applied for a further six months, making the total duration up to 30 months. This is not simply a technical extension: it means that people could spend two and a half years (or more under certain circumstances) in immigration detention.

Paragraph 3 also provides that if a situation arises where the undocumented person goes to another EU member state after a period of detention, a new period of detention can be applied. This is particularly concerning as it can result in a cumulative effect, thereby prolonging the overall duration of detention even further.

Indefinite detention for people posing a security risk

The most serious concern arises for people considered to pose a security risk: the regulation provides no maximum period of detention in these cases. Instead, detention may be extended beyond the general time limit through successive judicially authorised extensions, subject to periodic judicial review. In practice, this creates a risk of open-ended, potentially indefinite detention for people presumed to pose a security risk.

Harsher detention conditions

Detention conditions will become harsher under Article 32 of the regulation. This weakens several key safeguards put in place by the 2008 directive, by both diluting the language and removing important protections. For instance:

it creates a new provision restricting access to open spaces for a limited period of time in order “to ensure a well-functioning detention facility”;

it allows member states to restrict external actors (including family members, legal representatives, consular authorities, representatives of NGOs) from accessing detention facilities if it is “objectively necessary” due to “security, public order or administrative” reasons;

it allows the placement of people deemed to pose a security risk under “enhanced security arrangements” and “stricter separation measures” within the detention facilities. Taken together with the new measures allowing for indefinite detention of people posing a security risk, there is a real possibility that some people may be left in isolation, and without a clear end.

These new provisions risk exacerbating the harsh conditions already documented by PICUM and its member organisations under the current legal framework. These include inadequate access to information and interpretation, insufficient medical and psychosocial care, isolation, and the detention of people whose vulnerabilities are aggravated by detention, including people with mental health conditions, disabilities or past experiences of trauma.

Spanish and Belgian civil society organisations have reported cases where people with mental health issues were placed in solitary confinement, further deteriorating their conditions. PICUM and its members have also documented practical barriers to accessing legal assistance and information in detention, as well as restrictions on communication with the outside world. In Belgium, for example, detainees must pay for phone calls themselves, which can make maintaining contact with family, lawyers and support organisations difficult.

These existing shortcomings are particularly concerning in light of the new regulation’s weaker safeguards. Those who are already struggling to access healthcare, communicate with lawyers or maintain contact with support networks could be particularly vulnerable to further restrictions on outdoor access, external contact and separation under enhanced security arrangements.

Considered collectively, the new provisions signify a systematic and disproportionate extension of detention and worsening of its conditions compared to existing measures under the 2008 directive.

text:
People’s Party MP Sasinan Thamnithinan has warned that returning two Uyghur detainees to China would violate Thailand’s anti-torture law.

The opposition lawmaker on Tuesday urged the government and the National Security Council to halt any possible deportation of the two detainees, warning that they could face torture or enforced disappearance.

Ms Sasinan, a Bangkok MP and lawyer, called on authorities to suspend any repatriation pending independent assessments of the risks the two men face.

Both were recently granted royal pardons and transferred to the Immigration Detention Centre at Suan Phlu on Oct 21. One was a minor when first detained in 2014.

Ms Sasinan said both had submitted written statements refusing to be repatriated to China. However, lawyers, the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) and the UN refugee agency have been unable to meet them since their transfer.

She cited Section 13 of the Prevention and Suppression of Torture and Enforced Disappearance Act, which prohibits returning people to countries where they face a risk of torture or enforced disappearance.

She also questioned Clause 8 of the Prime Minister’s Office’s 2026 deportation regulation, arguing that its provision for automatic repatriation after a specified period undermines legal protections.

Ms Sasinan called for access to legal assistance, disclosure of the men’s legal status, independent risk assessments, arrangements for resettlement in a safe third country and amendments to Clause 8.

Thailand deported 109 Uyghurs to China in 2015 and another 40 in February last year. The NHRC subsequently found that the latter deportation violated human rights and the principle of non-refoulement, and that assurances from China were insufficient.

The Uyghur Human Rights Project (UHRP) issued a similar appeal on Friday, urging Thailand to halt deportations and calling on other governments to offer resettlement to the Uyghurs remaining in detention.

UHRP executive director Omer Kanat warned against repeating past deportations, saying the whereabouts and wellbeing of the 40 men returned in February last year remained independently unverified.

Ms Sasinan said Thailand’s economic and security cooperation with China should not override its human rights obligations.

title: Thailand: Halt imminent forcible return of two Uyghur men to China - Amnesty International
description:
Responding to reports that two Uyghur men recently moved to an Immigration Detention Centre in Thailand face imminent forcible deportation to China, Amnesty International’s Secretary General Agnès Callamard said: “Thai authorities must immediately halt any plans to forcibly return these two Uyghur men to China, where they face a real risk of torture, arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance.
Amnesty International has documented crimes against humanity against Uyghurs and other predominantly Muslim ethnic groups in Xinjiang.
The two men have spent more than 12 years in Thai detention.
Following the deportations, Thai authorities made two visits to Xinjiang in February and March 2025 at China’s invitation, as part of its efforts to provide diplomatic assurances.
Amnesty International previously called on both governments to disclose the whereabouts of all 40 men.
text:
Responding to reports that two Uyghur men recently moved to an Immigration Detention Centre in Thailand face imminent forcible deportation to China, Amnesty International’s Secretary General Agnès Callamard said:

“Thai authorities must immediately halt any plans to forcibly return these two Uyghur men to China, where they face a real risk of torture, arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance. Thailand must not repeat last year’s unlawful deportation of 40 Uyghurs, who were forced back to danger in China.

“These two men fled persecution only to spend more than a decade detained in Thailand. Amnesty International has documented crimes against humanity against Uyghurs and other predominantly Muslim ethnic groups in Xinjiang. Returning them would expose them to the abuses they sought to escape.

“Both men have previously made clear to their legal representatives that they fear for their lives if returned to China and do not consent to being sent back. Thai authorities must now allow them access to a lawyer of their choice and, together with the international community, urgently find a safe and voluntary third-country solution for them and the other Uyghurs still detained in Thailand.

“No amount of diplomatic assurance from China can override Thailand’s obligations not to return anyone to a real risk of torture or other serious human rights violations. After more than a decade in detention, these men must be released and given the chance to rebuild their lives in safety and freedom “

Background

The two men are among five Uyghurs remaining in Thailand from a group of over 300 who were apprehended without charge by the Thai authorities on 13 March 2014 after they had fled persecution and discrimination in China’s Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.

On 21 October 2026, two of the five men were released from prison under a royal pardon and transferred to the Immigration Detention Centre in Bangkok. Since then, Thai authorities have denied the two men access to their lawyers, as well as blocked access to the men by civil society organizations and the National Human Rights Commission of Thailand.

The two men have spent more than 12 years in Thai detention. In June 2015, Thailand allowed 173 women and children from the group to travel to Türkiye but unlawfully deported at least 109 people to China.

A document obtained by Amnesty International shows that, on 7 January 2025, the Chinese embassy in Thailand sent a letter to Thailand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs requesting the “repatriation” of 45 Uyghur men who remained in the country. In February 2025, Thailand forcibly deported 40 of them, in breach international law. Five remained in a Thai prison to serve sentences related to an attempt to escape the Immigration Detention Centre.

Following the deportations, Thai authorities made two visits to Xinjiang in February and March 2025 at China’s invitation, as part of its efforts to provide diplomatic assurances. NGOs monitoring the case reported that Thai authorities were able to meet fewer than 10 deportees and that no subsequent updates have established that all are alive and safe; their whereabouts and wellbeing remain unknown. Amnesty International previously called on both governments to disclose the whereabouts of all 40 men.

Amnesty International opposes any use of diplomatic assurances that a person transferred would not be subjected to torture or other ill-treatment as it undermines the universality of the prohibition of torture and cannot be considered reliable. Thailand is bound by the Convention against Torture, and the principle of non-refoulement under international law, which prohibits States from returning or transferring anyone to a place where they would be at real risk of persecution or other human rights violations. Article 13 of Thailand’s Prevention and Suppression of Torture and Enforced Disappearance Act, in force since 2023, prohibits deportation where there are substantial grounds to believe a person would face torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, or enforced disappearance.

title: High Court finds ARAP reviews a suitable remedy despite 3500 case backlog
description:
The High Court has refused to allow an Afghan former security guard at the British Embassy in Kabul to challenge his relocation refusal in court before completing the scheme’s own review process.
It did so despite the government’s evidence that complex reviews are taking between 18 and 24 months and that more than 3,500 reviews remain outstanding.
In R (on the application of COR) v Secretary of State for Defence [2026] EWHC 2655 (Admin), Mr Justice Bourne held that the review process under the Afghan Relocations and Assistance Policy, known as ARAP, was a suitable alternative remedy and had to be pursued first.
Although the case turned on procedural grounds rather than the merits of the claimant’s relocation application, the judgment does shed light on delays within the ARAP process.

title: Loophole in an Illinois contract lets ICE access immigrant data, privacy advocates warn
description:
Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul signed the current contract with Appriss in May 2021, initially committing about $6.07 million.
Privacy advocates warn this creates a pathway for information collected by Illinois jails to enter commercial databases used by ICE to identify and locate people for immigration enforcement.
In 2022, The Guardian reported that ICE paid about $4.8 million to access Appriss data.
Commissioners approved an ordinance restricting how county employees and contractors share residents’ information with ICE and data brokers.
Laura Rivera, an attorney with Just Futures Law said the ordinance doesn’t solve the problem of data sharing elsewhere in Illinois.
text:
A multimillion-dollar contract with Appriss Insights LLC, which runs the state’s crime victim notification system, contains a provision that allows the company to share jail data with third parties, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement, immigrant advocates say.

The state’s victim notification system known as VINE alerts crime victims when someone is released from jail, transferred or experiences a change in custody status. Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul signed the current contract with Appriss in May 2021, initially committing about $6.07 million. The contract runs through June 2028.

A clause in that contract allows Appriss to share jail records with third parties. Privacy advocates warn this creates a pathway for information collected by Illinois jails to enter commercial databases used by ICE to identify and locate people for immigration enforcement.

Illinois’ sanctuary laws limit state and local law enforcement from cooperating with federal immigration authorities— including sharing information about anyone held at a local jail or prison — unless that person has a federal criminal warrant. But advocates say even though the state isn’t sharing this information directly, the loophole in the state’s contract offers a back door around the sanctuary laws.

“This is why we’ve been raising alarms for years,” Jacinta González, a former policy director at Mijente who is now head of programs at MediaJustice, told the Sun-Times in June. “When these loopholes are allowed to exist, they’re going to lead to concrete harm. They’re going to lead to people being detained and people being deported.

How ICE uses jail records

Federal procurement records show that in 2021, ICE sought access to Appriss records that contained information about bookings and incarcerations from more than 2,800 jails and correctional facilities nationwide. In 2022, The Guardian reported that ICE paid about $4.8 million to access Appriss data.

As of November 2024, 88 county jails, 96 court systems and 31 Illinois Department of Corrections-affiliated facilities participate in the statewide victim-notification system, according to a report from the attorney general’s office.

Privacy advocates have argued for years that data provided to Appriss could move beyond state and county systems and into commercial databases like LexisNexis that are accessible to agencies like ICE. They allege ICE is able to access information that includes names, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, custody status dates, release information, court hearing details and other sensitive personal data. Advocates say ICE’s contract with LexisNexis includes an add-on for a database called Justice Intelligence, a product offered by Appriss that collects release data from U.S. jails and prisons and makes it easily searchable.

“Basically, this is a loophole paragraph,” said Steven J. Kochevar, an attorney and law fellow at the University of Chicago, who has reviewed the state’s contract. Kochevar said the language in the contract leaves unclear exactly how Appriss may use the data it collects.

Without effective restrictions, companies can combine government records with information from other sources into commercial databases sold to customers, including government agencies, he explained.

“They package it and they sell it through these systems like LexisNexis,” he said.

Such databases can combine booking records with addresses and other personal information, creating profiles of people regardless of immigration status, including those arrested but never convicted.

“It’s not like one straight pipeline,” Kochevar said. “They [ICE] get a bunch of data in a lot of different ways.”

In a statement, a spokesperson for the attorney general’s office said they were committed to protecting residents’ information from improper use, including for immigration enforcement.

“We are engaged in ongoing conversations with Appriss Insights LLC,” the spokesperson said.

The attorney general’s office did not say whether information from the statewide system had reached ICE, and they did not identify any specific restrictions preventing access to the data. The office would not answer questions about whether the attorney general plans to change or retain the contract’s data-sharing provision.

Appriss also did not respond to questions about its contract with the state.

Cook County as a model

Last month, Cook County moved to strengthen protections against this type of data sharing with ICE. Commissioners approved an ordinance restricting how county employees and contractors share residents’ information with ICE and data brokers.

For Fred Tsao, senior policy counsel at the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights, the county ordinance addresses a basic concern: information residents provide to government offices being used to target them.

“We wanted to make sure that that information that we are providing to the county — at the very least, to county offices — does not get weaponized against us for immigration enforcement purposes,” he said.

Tsao said Cook County’s ordinance could provide a model for restrictions elsewhere in Illinois.

Laura Rivera, an attorney with Just Futures Law said the ordinance doesn’t solve the problem of data sharing elsewhere in Illinois.

“The fact remains that this company is still obtaining the personal information of people across other parts of Illinois, and that information is being shared with ICE through this contract,” Rivera said. “So there’s a lot of work to do.”

text:
A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer accused of deliberately running over a fleeing Mexican construction worker in Houston appeared in court Monday, November 2, 2026, after a Texas grand jury indicted him on a felony assault charge.

Mario Alberto Morales surrendered to authorities three days after being indicted on a second-degree felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Harris County District Judge Matthew Peneguy set his bond at $30,000, below the $75,000 prosecutors requested. Morales was released following the hearing.

The charge stems from an October 10 immigration enforcement operation in northwest Houston, where prosecutors say Morales drove his unmarked SUV into Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, as he fled through a parking lot. Parra Hernandez suffered multiple fractures to his right leg and ankle that required surgery. He remains in federal immigration custody while recovering.

Surveillance footage from a nearby business shows two men leaving a white pickup truck and running in different directions as immigration officers approach. Morales pursued Parra Hernandez in a black Jeep Grand Cherokee, crossing a median before turning toward the fleeing man and striking him. His body camera captured the collision and Parra Hernandez crying out as the officer approached him on the ground.

In a recorded 911 call, Morales told a dispatcher he had attempted to drive around Parra Hernandez before the man struck his vehicle. Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare disputes that account, saying the recordings show Morales steering toward him.

Two handcuffed immigrants were reportedly inside Morales' SUV without seat belts during the pursuit, according to accounts of the incident. The circumstances of their detention and presence in the vehicle have also drawn scrutiny as investigators examine the operation.

ICE agents had been attempting to locate Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, whom the agency identified as a man with an outstanding deportation order. His daughter subsequently said her father died in 2017, raising questions about the information federal authorities relied on when conducting the operation.

Teare said Parra Hernandez had lived in Harris County for more than 30 years and had no known criminal record or existing deportation order. His family said he was traveling to a construction job when officers began pursuing the pickup truck.

ICE has maintained that the collision occurred while officers were carrying out their duties and described the indictment as politically motivated. Morales' attorney, David Lindenmuth, characterized the incident as an accident and disputed the criminal allegations. Former Harris County District Attorney Kim Ogg has joined the officer's defense team.

Following Monday's hearing, defense attorney Michael Wynne said the legal team expects to seek transfer of the prosecution to federal court, potentially raising a constitutional immunity defense.

Under the Constitution's Supremacy Clause, federal officers may be protected from state criminal prosecution for actions authorized by federal law and necessary to carrying out their official duties. Transferring the proceedings to federal court would allow Morales to seek that protection, although the change in venue would not automatically dismiss the charge.

Teare maintains that the evidence supports prosecuting Morales under Texas law. A conviction for second-degree aggravated assault with a deadly weapon carries a potential prison sentence of two to 20 years.

text:
MIAMI — A federal judge on Tuesday temporarily blocked the Trump administration’s plans to deport Afghans detained in the United States to Afghanistan or Pakistan, after advocates and dozens of members of Congress warned that their lives would be at risk.

The government told the court that Immigration and Customs Enforcement had no chartered or commercial flights for deporting Afghan nationals to Afghanistan or Pakistan at least before the end of the week. Judge Valerie Caproni’s order, which expires Saturday, asks all officials to adhere to that. ICE books the flights weeks in advance.

A letter led by California Democratic Rep. Scott Peters and signed by 65 other members of the House and Senate said they were “extremely concerned that sending vulnerable people” would expose them to “persecution, torture, or even death.” The letter was sent Monday to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

Immigrant rights organizations have also warned that those deported could face retaliation from the Taliban.

Thousands of Afghans fled persecution and feared for their lives after helping the U.S. military and aid groups in Afghanistan.

According to court documents obtained by The Associated Press, the U.S. planned to deport Afghan immigrants on Monday on flights from Louisiana, where ICE has immigrant detention and processing facilities, to Pakistan.

President Donald Trump’s administration has deported thousands of immigrants to countries other than their own. In some cases, it has resorted to third-country deportations when removal to their countries of origin was not possible, like when formal diplomatic relations were absent, as is the case with Afghanistan’s Taliban government. In other instances, third-country deportations have been used as a deterrent.

Advocates and attorneys said that more than 80 detained Afghans had contacted them after ICE notified them that they could be deported this week via Pakistan. Among them are women, a police officer, members of religious minorities and people whose family members served in the U.S. military. Most fled Afghanistan because of persecution and do not have legal representation, according to Human Rights First and AfghanEvac, a nonprofit organization that advocates for immigrants.

Before the judge signed her order, Zia Ahmad Takal, deputy spokesperson for the Afghan foreign ministry, said “the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan expresses its serious concern” about the reports that the U.S. plans to transfer Afghans to Pakistan.

Takal called on the U.S. to make sure that decisions or actions are based on rights and “legitimate demands” of those involved, and said “third-party countries should not engage in dealings concerning the fate of another nation’s citizens.”

“Today is a good day,” Shawn VanDiver, president at AfghanEvac, said at a news conference. “But I want to be honest with you, this is a reprieve, not a resolution. We haven’t stopped this fight forever. This is just a pause.”

Savitri Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights for Human Rights First, said individuals returned to Afghanistan “face grave, systematic dangers,” including arbitrary detentions, executions, public flogging and retaliatory violence.

“The stakes were very, very high,” she said, noting that women and girls face severe restrictions in Afghanistan, including systematic denials of education, employment and public speech.

Advocates expressed their concern about the role of the Pakistani government in facilitating the returns to Afghanistan and the fact that there is no information about the arrangements that the U.S. has made with Pakistan.

“We celebrate today, but we’re getting right back to work tomorrow, continuing to make sure through our flight tracking that none of these flights are taking off,” Arvey said.

By Texas Border Business

HOUSTON, Texas — U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer Mario Alberto Morales voluntarily surrendered in a Harris County courtroom Monday, November 2, 2026, following his indictment on a second-degree felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.

Morales appeared before District Judge Matthew Peneguy, who set bond at $30,000. Morales surrendered directly in the courtroom under a non-arrest bond procedure and was not booked into jail.

Prosecutors requested a $75,000 bond, while defense attorneys sought $25,000.

The charge stems from an October 10 incident near Clay Road and Highway 6 in northwest Houston, where ICE officers pursued a white pickup truck carrying two men.

Both men fled the vehicle. During the pursuit, Morales’ SUV struck Miguel Parra Hernandez, a construction worker who suffered serious leg injuries requiring medical treatment.

On Friday, October 30, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare and Sheriff Ed Gonzalez held a press conference announcing the grand jury indictment.

During the presentation, officials showed surveillance footage, Morales’ body-camera recording and portions of a 911 call. Prosecutors said the recordings supported their allegations concerning the officer’s actions during the pursuit.

Gonzalez discussed the Sheriff’s Office investigation and the responsibility of law enforcement agencies to investigate potential criminal conduct involving officers.

The defense maintains Morales swerved to avoid a collision with another vehicle and describes the incident as an accident.

Following Monday’s court appearance, Teare rejected allegations that the prosecution was politically motivated.

“I don’t know what side is on the other side of people getting run over,” Teare told reporters. “But this is not a political prosecution.”

Teare said prosecutors presented the evidence to a Harris County grand jury, which returned the indictment.

Michael Wynne, Morales’ lead defense attorney, addressed reporters after the hearing, with Morales standing behind him.

Wynne questioned whether a local district attorney should prosecute a federal officer for actions undertaken during immigration enforcement operations.

“We feel that is unfair and improper to make Mr. Morales the recipient of partisan politics,” Wynne said.

The attorney said the defense intends to pursue the case in federal court.

“We’ll press this case and litigate it the way the framers designed it, that is, in a federal forum,” Wynne said.

Morales’ defense team also includes attorney David Lindenmuth and former Harris County District Attorney Kim Ogg.

In a statement reported by Houston news organizations, ICE characterized the indictment as a political stunt and disputed allegations that Morales intentionally struck Hernandez.

Morales is scheduled to return to court December 2. A conviction on the second-degree felony charge could carry a prison sentence of two to 20 years.

The allegations remain unproven, and Morales is presumed innocent unless convicted.

MILPITAS, Calif. (KGO) -- Community members gathered outside the Elmwood Correctional Facility in Milpitas on Monday night, voicing concerns about what they say is an increase in federal immigration enforcement activity at the jail.

Some attendees wore masks, saying they feared being identified while helping people released from custody.

"We are protecting our identities because unfortunately even folks who like I said are documented can be targets of ICE," one volunteer said.

Advocates said they have been monitoring the facility for several days after learning that Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents were conducting operations near release points.

"We've been here for about four or five nights now ever since we found out that ICE was conducting raids as people were being released," another volunteer said.

MORE:

Santa Clara County Executive James Williams confirmed an increase in ICE activity at the county's two jails.

"In the last week or so, we've seen a significant increase," Williams said.

Williams said county officials were not notified ahead of time.

"Were you guys made aware that there was going to be an increase in ICE activity? No, no, not at all," he said.

While the county cannot prevent federal immigration enforcement actions, Williams emphasized that county resources are not being used to assist ICE.

"We are firm in our noncooperation policies," Williams said.

"That's really for everyone's safety and security," he said.

She said volunteers are trying to help people leave the facility safely before encountering federal agents.

text:
SALINAS, Calif. — On Oct. 27, six ICE agents arrived at the Monterey County Jail in Salinas requesting custody transfer of three suspected criminal illegal aliens. What should have been a simple, routine operation quickly went sideways.

The agents were there to recover Eduardo Castro-Lopez, also known as Jordan Eduardo Yac; Jose Luis Quinones, also known as Jose Manuel Garcia; and Angelina Ramirez-Sepulveda. The suspects have prior arrests for multiple offenses including DUI, drug offenses and providing false identification.

The officers waited outside the jail and cordoned off the area with yellow tape to facilitate the targeted operation. A crowd of protesters began to form, and Monterey County Sheriff Tina M. Nieto opted to place the facility on lockdown.

The lockdown lasted approximately three hours. During that period, new bookings and inmate releases were suspended, and public visitor doors were closed, though the jail continued regular operations and published an online custody log.

“None of the suspects were turned over to ICE during the lockdown,” said ICE Assistant Director of Public Affairs Micah Bock. “A local county supervisor told the ICE officers that the sheriff would not release the inmates to them. It’s borderline obscene that a facility that’s there to protect the public would go on lockdown to protect criminal illegal aliens from the consequences of violating federal immigration law.”

By the next day, the online custody log showed that Castro-Lopez had been released from custody and Quinones was no longer shown as being in custody. Ramirez-Sepulveda remained in custody.

“Two of the individuals ICE sought were reportedly released from custody. This is where we are: Criminals are being protected in sanctuary cities and states, and a law enforcement facility is siding with CRIMINALS instead of cooperating with federal law enforcement," ICE posted on social media.

Under President Trump, ICE is focused on its core mission: enforcing immigration law and protecting the American people.

text:
A 23-year-old UC Berkeley student who fled gender-based violence in Colombia is being held in ICE detention after agents arrested her at SFO Friday.

Paula Albornoz Hernandez was on her way to Portland with her boyfriend Friday when she was taken into ICE custody while waiting to board a flight at San Francisco International Airport, as the Chronicle reports. Agents reportedly told the 23-year-old UC Berkeley student she was being detained for overstaying her visa.

Albornoz Hernandez's boyfriend, Anthony, who contacted the Alameda County Rapid Response Network for assistance, said he wasn't able to speak with her until midday Saturday, after she had already been transferred to a detention facility in Stockton. ICE reportedly moved Albornoz Hernandez between facilities in Stockton and Sacramento over the next several days before transferring her to California City, in Kern County.

Her attorney Nikolas De Bremaeker, a managing attorney at Centro Legal de la Raza in Oakland, filed a habeas corpus petition late Monday challenging the detention and arguing that she is being held unlawfully.

De Bremaeker told the Chronicle that Albornoz Hernandez, who is seeking asylum from gender-based violence in Colombia, had complied with immigration requirements and had previously interacted with federal officials without being detained.

"She had all these points of contact with the government and the government didn’t detain her (before)," he said, speaking to the Chronicle. "She’s an important member of the community and her future should be protected."

Back in Berkeley, university officials and Hernandez's friends and family began working to secure her release. The Daily Californian reports that UC Berkeley Chancellor Rich Lyons sent a campuswide email Monday confirming that the university was coordinating with her family and providing legal support to help her obtain advice and representation.

"This student is a valued member of our community," Lyons wrote, adding that campus leadership was doing everything possible to help her return to Berkeley and continue her studies.

De Bremaeker said Lyons also wrote a letter of support expressing that he was "deeply concerned" about Hernandez's detention and the possibility that it could "unnecessarily interfere" with her education. The attorney told the Daily Cal that Albornoz Hernandez was struggling with the conditions of her confinement and was extremely distressed.

Her arrest reportedly coincides with the Trump administration's 45-day immigration enforcement operation, dubbed Operation Safe California.

As SFist has reported previously, several immigrants have been arrested and detained at SFO during the past year, including over two dozen who were unlawfully held at the airport for more than 72 hours.

The Bay Area has also been experiencing a surge in ICE arrests and sightings at people's homes and workplaces in recent weeks, possibly to meet a reported nationwide quota of 3,000 arrests per day.

The Trump administration has also been carrying out "Operation Protect the Vote," targeting green card holders and other immigrants who have illegally cast ballots in recent elections, including 28 individuals in California.

As the Chronicle reported in June, De Bremaeker, who’s a Belgian national, was himself detained for 45 minutes at SFO while waiting to go through security. He was reportedly told he was on a watch list, possibly because of his involvement in a high-profile lawsuit resulting in a first-in-the-nation federal court ruling that barred ICE from re-arresting immigrants at their immigration court hearings without legal justification.

Per the Chronicle, attorney Andrew Fels, who filed a Freedom of Information Act request on De Bremaeker's behalf seeking information about the alleged watch list, said the incident appeared to be part of a large-scale effort to target immigration attorneys, pointing to a March 2025 executive order from President Donald Trump.

text:
Democrat Rep. LaMonica McIver cruised to a second full term representing New Jersey’s 10th Congressional District Tuesday, despite facing federal criminal charges over a confrontation with immigration officers last year — and giving birth to her second child just weeks before Election Day.

The Newark Democrat defeated Republican challenger Carmen Bucco in a rematch of their 2024 contest in the heavily Democratic district.

McIver garnered about 86% of the vote to Bucco’s 13% with about a third of the ballots counted as of 8:30 pm EST.

McIver, 40, has been fighting to avoid trial over an encounter with federal officers at the Delaney Hall Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facility in May 2025.

The congresswoman and two other Democratic lawmakers were visiting the facility for an oversight inspection when a protest erupted outside. Prosecutors accused McIver of assaulting, resisting, impeding and interfering with federal officers.

McIver has denied wrongdoing and argued that her prosecution violates constitutional protections for lawmakers performing their official duties.

A federal appeals court in August allowed two counts against her to proceed while sending a third back to a lower court for further review. She subsequently asked the full appeals court to reconsider the ruling.

The legal battle continued as McIver welcomed her second child, a baby girl, on Oct. 1.

McIver entered Congress in 2024 following the death of Rep. Donald Payne Jr. (D-NJ). She previously spent six year’s on Newark’s Municipal Council, the last two as its president.

Bucco, a small-business owner from Kenilworth, has sat on the Belleville Board of Education in addition to making two runs for Congress. The Republican, who grew up in foster care, has highlighted support for law enforcement, public safety and eliminating government corruption.

McIver’s victory adds another chapter to the history of federal lawmakers who have faced criminal charges while serving in Congress.

Former Sen. Bob Menendez (D-NJ), the onetime chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, was convicted in July 2024 of all 16 counts in a federal corruption case involving bribery, fraud and acting as a foreign agent.

Prosecutors said Menendez accepted cash, gold bars and other valuables in exchange for political favors. He was sentenced to 11 years in prison in January 2025.

text:
The family of a popular D.C.-area baseball coach said they are “deeply disappointed” by an immigration judge’s decision to deny a bond request for the man known as “Coach A” to his middle and high school players.

Amaury Monsalve, who also drove for Uber, was arrested last month while driving a group of passengers in the early morning hours of Oct. 18.

Related stories

Youth baseball coach detained by ICE in Louisiana after DC traffic stop, family says

Federal judge temporarily blocks Trump plan to deport detained Afghans to Afghanistan

ICE officer accused of hitting immigrant in Houston with an SUV turns himself in

During the arrest, police found open alcohol containers, a gun and drugs in the vehicle.

Monsalve’s attorney Ava Benach told Judge David Gardey that the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia did not pursue the charges against Monsalve, and that the items found in the car were “the result of passengers he picked up.”

WTOP contacted the U.S. Attorney’s Office about the case and was told in an email that “Monsalve and his passengers were no papered,” using the term for when prosecutors opt not to move forward with a case.

But following that arrest, Monsalve, who is originally from Venezuela, was detained by ICE and an immigration judge ordered him deported. He’s being held an ICE facility in Louisiana.

In denying bond, Gardey told the court that while the case related to the Oct. 18 traffic stop was not being pursued, it was up to Monsalve and his attorney Ava Benach to provide evidence that Monsalve was not a danger to the community, and they had not done that. Gardey continued, “given these circumstances and the lack of any evidence; the court cannot find that he’s not a danger to the community.”

Gardey also asserted that Monsalve, who’s been in the United States since 2003, was a flight risk due to the fact that he has a removal order pending. Gardey also said that Monsalve “made false statements” in the course of obtaining a green card. Gardey referred to Monsalve’s failure to disclose he had children.

Benach had argued that Monsalve was not a danger to the community, is married with two children, has no criminal history, and that Monsalve “goes through background checks in order to work as a coach at Alice Deal Middle School and Jackson Reed and in the McLean Little League.”

Benach also pointed out that “there are testimonials in the bond package from dozens of parents who talk about the positive impact that Mr. Monsalve has had on their children.”

Benach also told the judge that “community support has been overwhelming” and that as of Tuesday morning, more than $90,000 had been raised to support the Monsalve’s family in his absence.

After the hearing, a statement was issued on behalf of the Monsalve family.

“For more than 25 years, Amaury has mentored young baseball players, teaching lessons that extend beyond the field; integrity, teamwork and respect,” the statement said. “The family is consulting with Amaury’s attorneys regarding the bond decision and any available next steps.”

The family added that they’re grateful “for the compassion and encouragement shown to our family. Our hope remains that Amaury will have a fair process and an opportunity to return home.”

text:
A federal judge in Oregon wants more ICE agents on the witness stand after finding that an officer lied in an official arrest record, saying live testimony helped expose it.

U.S. District Judge Mustafa T. Kasubhai, a Biden appointee, said the case showed why courts should hear directly from government officers when their accounts are disputed, rather than rely solely on written statements.

"Evaluating live testimony is a time-tested method for truth finding," Kasubhai wrote in court filings reviewed by Newsweek. "Written declarations are convenient, but insufficient on their own when witnesses are willing to lie."

Read More on News

"Live testimony is necessary. Examination and cross-examination are necessary," the judge continued.

The unusually blunt comments came in an order enforcing an earlier injunction against the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) over warrantless immigration arrests in Oregon. The case challenged ICE arrests made without judicial or administrative warrants. Kasubhai's earlier injunction required officers making warrantless civil immigration arrests to first determine, based on individualized circumstances, that a person was likely to escape before a warrant could be obtained.

The Trump administration has repeatedly clashed with federal courts over the president's mass deportation agenda, accusing judges who block its policies of being "activist judges." At the same time, judges have imposed additional guardrails on ICE as the agency faces lawsuits and accusations of racial profiling, aggressive arrests and other constitutional violations while carrying out the administration's immigration crackdown.

Newsweek has contacted DHS and ICE for comment via email outside office hours.

ICE Officer Lies on Official Record

After subsequent evidentiary hearings that included testimony from immigration officers, Kasubhai said federal authorities had failed to comply with aspects of his order, and that ICE's reporting of warrantless arrests could not be relied upon.

An arrest report prepared by an ICE deportation officer identified as J.G. was a key part of the judge's decision.

The form said officers had identified H-D-G-H- before approaching his vehicle, and that a supervisor had issued a warrant for his arrest.

But J.G. testified under oath that he did not know H-D-G-H- existed when officers first stopped the vehicle and had no warrant for him at the time, according to the court's order.

J.G. said he had copied much of the account from a report of the driver's arrest and failed to correct it. Kasubhai rejected his explanation that the discrepancies were a mistake.

"He lied in an official record to facilitate the impression he was conducting a lawful warrant-based arrest," the judge wrote, characterizing what occurred as "intentional, coordinated falsification."

The judge said the discrepancy might not have been discovered had the officer not been required to appear and answer questions under oath.

"This case underscores what happens if people were not called to testify under oath in a courtroom, if as a society we do not demand that government agents explain their actions, and if the public fails to shine a spotlight on what is happening under cover," Kasubhai wrote, "people with authority know they will not be held to account."

Judge No Longer Presumes ICE Acted Properly

Kasubhai also said he would no longer give the defendants the "presumption of regularity," which generally allows courts to assume government officials have properly carried out their duties unless evidence shows otherwise.

"This presumption no longer holds for Defendants. The evidence in this case proves as much," the judge wrote, adding, "One must earn credibility by acting with integrity."

Kasubhai pointed to similar concerns in courtrooms across the nation. In September, a federal judge in Massachusetts said that after "repeated misrepresentations by ICE officers," the court would no longer give ICE the presumption of regularity.

Judge Questions ICE’s Arrest Records

Kasubhai also found problems with ICE's arrest records and reporting. ICE reported 13 warrantless arrests over six months, but Kasubhai concluded there had been "significantly more than thirteen." The agency made 574 arrests in Oregon between February 5 and July 31, including 504 that it classified as noncustodial, according to court filings.

Kasubhai said he also found errors, repeated language and false information in ICE's I-213 arrest records. He said the problems made the records unreliable for determining whether warrantless arrests were valid. The misconduct, Kasubhai wrote, "calls into question the veracity of all I-213 forms completed by ICE officers in Oregon."

The judge did not find every disputed encounter unlawful. In one case, he ruled officers had reasonable suspicion to temporarily detain a man they initially mistook for the person they were seeking.

text:
A federal judge in Oregon says he can no longer assume ICE agents are telling the truth in their arrest paperwork, declaring Monday that live testimony is now "necessary" after finding that warrantless arrests are still being made and facts are being "fabricated in official records" by immigration officers.

In a 50-page opinion, U.S. District Judge Mustafa Kasubhai ruled that ICE repeatedly violated an existing court order governing warrantless immigration arrests in the Beaver State, with inaccurate reports, missing records and accounts that did not match what actually happened.

The judge's loss of confidence in the agency was so pronounced that he withdrew the usual presumption that government officials have properly performed their duties.

"This presumption no longer holds for defendants," Kasubhai wrote. "Defendants are held to the same expectation as any other litigant before this court. One must earn credibility by acting with integrity."

Love true crime? Sign up for our newsletter, The Law&Crime Docket, to get the latest real-life crime stories delivered right to your inbox.

According to Kasubhai, an ICE officer "fabricated facts in official records to justify an arrest." The judge, appointed by President Joe Biden, said the court knows this because at an evidentiary hearing on a motion to enforce a preliminary injunction barring warrantless arrests, the ICE officer "testified under oath" that what he wrote in the official records of the arrest "was incorrect."

On the witness stand, the officer tried to minimize the error "as mere oversight," according to Kasubhai.

"This court found he lied after evaluating his live testimony and the documentary evidence," the judge said in Monday's order. "Evaluating live testimony is a time-tested method for truth finding. Written declarations are convenient, but insufficient on their own when witnesses are willing to lie."

The ruling means ICE must now provide plaintiffs challenging its arrest practices with a much broader collection of records, including administrative arrest warrants, supporting evidence, documents given to detainees and body-camera footage from civil immigration arrests conducted since Sept. 1. The agency must also turn over previously disclosed material without redactions and repeat the court's instructions to relevant employees every 30 days.

The incident that helped convince Kasubhai that written arrest records could not be trusted without live testimony involved the ICE officer preparing a report claiming agents had recognized a passenger in a vehicle before stopping it and already had an arrest warrant for him. The officer admitted during a September evidentiary hearing that he had copied much of the narrative from a separate report about the driver and simply failed to change the details.

In reality, the officer said that he had not known the passenger was in the vehicle and did not even know who the man was when agents first stopped the car. He also acknowledged there was no warrant for the passenger at that point.

"[The ICE officer] was a sworn police officer for several years before becoming an ICE agent," Kasubhai explained. "On the stand he recounted the details necessary for obtaining search warrants and arrest warrants as well as the information needed for affidavits in criminal complaints. … This Court finds that he did not make a mistake … He lied in an official record to facilitate the impression he was conducting a lawful warrant-based arrest."

The incident demonstrates "intentional, coordinated falsification that would in all likelihood never have been uncovered but for this evidentiary hearing," according to Kasubhai. "Evidentiary hearings are essential tools to ensure that a rigorous record of something closer to the truth is preserved, and to hold liars to account," Kasubhai said.

The incident was not the only documentation problem the judge identified, according to his order.

In another report, ICE recorded an arrest as taking place near an address in Napa, California, when it actually happened in Hood River, Oregon. The agency also described a man's vehicle as a Toyota Camry when he was driving a Toyota Corolla — apparently confusing it with his brother's car, according to Kasubhai and the plaintiffs suing the government over the warrantless arrests, who are represented by the nonprofit firm Innovation Law Lab.

The government reported 13 warrantless arrests in Oregon over a six-month period, according to court records. After reviewing testimony and other evidence, Kasubhai concluded that the actual number was "significantly more than 13," per his order.

Kasubhai also found that agents had sometimes relied on immigration status itself to justify believing someone might flee, despite the court's requirement for an individualized assessment.

The court battle over the arrests began with an injunction issued Feb. 4, prohibiting ICE from making warrantless civil immigration arrests in Oregon without first determining that the person was likely to escape before officers could obtain a warrant. Kasubhai found that the agency continued making arrests without the required advance assessment and failed to provide the detailed records necessary to demonstrate compliance.

The Monday order makes clear that ICE's own classification of an arrest as warrant-based will no longer be enough to keep it outside the disclosure requirements.

"Defendants, through their own conduct, have lost trust," Kasubhai determined.

More from Law&Crime: 'Trump's a loser!': Former cop hauled off to jail for dissing the president and chanting about 'treasonous' Jan. 6 rioters during solo protest, lawsuit says

The judge emphasized that the consequences of misleading arrest records extend beyond litigation and paperwork. "Real people's lives and liberties are at stake and they should remember that," Kasubhai said, admonishing government lawyers involved in defending another challenged arrest.

The court's hearings are necessary, according to Kasubhai, because declarations and official reports cannot substitute for questioning the people who carried out the arrests — particularly when those accounts may be false, the judge said.

"The presumption of regularity directs the courts to assume, unless clear evidence indicates differently, that government officials have properly discharged their duties, acted in good faith and followed required procedures," Kasubhai concluded.

“Prior to the UN Human Rights Council’s review of Thailand’s human rights record on November 9, governments should press Thailand to immediately end its abusive treatment of Uyghurs,” Pearson said.

text:
(Bangkok) – Thai authorities should not forcibly return two Uyghur men to China, where they face grave risks of torture and other serious abuses, Human Rights Watch said today. The two men, whose names are not public for security reasons, were transferred from prison to immigration detention in Bangkok after receiving a royal pardon, apparently in preparation for deportation.

“Previous Thai governments have kept Uyghurs in inhumane detention for years and then complied with Beijing’s demands to send them to China, where they were forcibly disappeared,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul should end forced returns to China and allow the two Uyghur men to travel to a safe third country.”

The two Uyghur men have been detained by Thai authorities since 2014, when one of them was only 14 years old. They were serving a prison sentence for offenses related to an escape attempt from immigration detention in January 2020. On October 21, 2026, the authorities transferred them from Bangkok Central Prison to the Bangkok Immigration Detention Center Suan Phlu after they had served most of their seven-year sentence. Thai Foreign Ministry officials told a parliamentary committee that in August the Chinese embassy in Bangkok demanded their return to China.

Under Thai immigration law and regulations, the two Uyghur men will be deported to China unless they object to the deportation and are resettled to a third country. Lawyers representing them told Human Rights Watch that they have already informed Thai authorities that the two do not consent to be sent to China. Thai immigration authorities have repeatedly refused to allow the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR) access to the men to determine their refugee status.

The Thai government is obligated to respect the international law principle of nonrefoulement, barring anyone’s forcible return to a place where they would face a genuine risk of persecution, torture or other ill-treatment, or a threat to their life or other comparable serious human rights violations. Refoulement is prohibited by the UN Convention Against Torture, to which Thailand is a party, as well as customary international law. Thailand’s Prevention and Suppression of Torture and Enforced Disappearance Act prohibits deportation when there is a substantial risk of torture or ill-treatment.

In March 2014, Thai police in Songkhla province, near the Malaysia border, arrested about 220 Uyghur men, women, and children, charged them with immigration violations, and soon after transferred them to an immigration detention facility in Bangkok. In several separate incidents around the same period, the authorities arrested dozens of other Uyghurs and placed them in immigration detention facilities around the country. In July 2015, about 170 of the Uyghur women and children detained in Songkhla were released to Turkey. A week later, however, the Thai authorities forcibly transferred over 100 Uyghur men to Chinese authorities, who flew them to China.

On February 27, 2025, Thai authorities took 40 Uyghur men from immigration detention and forcibly returned them to China. Upon the men’s return, the Thai authorities participated in a Chinese government-organized propaganda trip to show some of these men with their families. Despite promises by the Thai and Chinese authorities, there has been no credible monitoring of those Uyghurs since their return.

UN human rights experts issued a statement on the one-year anniversary of the deportation and said the families of returnees “have received no communication, no confirmation of the place of detention or whereabouts, and no indication as to whether their loved ones are even alive.”

Following the deportation, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk said in February 2025 that it was “a clear violation of international human rights laws and standards,” and urged Thai authorities to “ensure there are no further deportations and the remaining members of the group, including potential refugees and asylum-seekers, being held in Thailand are fully protected in accordance with their obligations under international law.”

Uyghurs are Turkic-speaking Muslims, most of whom live in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region in China’s northwest. Over the past 10 years, China’s repression of Uyghurs has increased significantly as the authorities have intensified a widespread and systematic campaign of human rights abuses against them, several amounting to crimes against humanity.

The authorities have subjected the population to arbitrary detention, unjust imprisonment, mass surveillance, forced labor, cultural and religious persecution, and severe movement restrictions. Uyghurs considered to have left China illegally are, if forcibly returned, viewed with intense suspicion and subject to arbitrary detention, interrogation, torture, and other cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment.

“Prior to the UN Human Rights Council’s review of Thailand’s human rights record on November 9, governments should press Thailand to immediately end its abusive treatment of Uyghurs,” Pearson said. “The Thai authorities should be protecting Uyghurs fleeing persecution, not jailing them, and certainly not returning them to harm’s way.”

text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

EVERETT — Federal immigration enforcement agents are continuing to access data about Washingtonians through the state Department of Licensing and are using the records to assist in hundreds of arrests, according to a recently released University of Washington report.

Researchers have said the practice continues to occur in Snohomish County, as well as across the state, and local community organizers said that the recent rise in immigration enforcement activities has had a chilling effect on immigrant communities.

“People are living in fear,” said Arun Sharma, the head of Utsav, a Bothell-based nonprofit that provides services to the south Asian community. “I’ve been in this county since 1992. I’ve never seen a situation like this.”

Immigration enforcement officers are able to access the data through a system called Nlets, a network that allows law enforcement officers to query databases, including criminal records or state department of motor vehicles records, and get information about a vehicle and its owner in real time. According to the report, released by the University of Washington Center for Human Rights on Oct. 13, immigration officers have submitted queries in Nlets for information about drivers in Washington, then will often cross-reference with their own internal databases to determine a vehicle owner’s immigration status and make arrests.

In an interview Monday, Angelina Godoy, the director of the UW Center for Human Rights and the principal author of the report, said that the center’s research had found 389 instances of a direct connection between an Nlets search and a confirmed arrest in Washington. The database is sorted by cities of arrest, not counties, but Godoy said that Snohomish County cities like Everett and Lynnwood are “amply represented among our data set” in terms of immigration arrests tied to Nlets searches.

Godoy said in an Oct. 13 press conference that Washington state has been a leader in immigration-related policy, through both allowing non-citizens to obtain driver’s licenses since the 1990s and through the passage of the Keep Washington Working Act in 2019, which prohibits state and local agencies from assisting in civil immigration enforcement. But Godoy said that “repeated scandals” of immigration agents accessing driver’s license data — uncovered in 2018 by the Seattle Times, in 2025 by KING 5 and earlier in 2026 by the Center for Human Rights — mean that the state can no longer be considered a leader in that regard, she said.

“If that information that the state holds is now being weaponized against those very communities, the state needs to be accountable to its own promises,” Godoy said in an interview Monday.

One woman, who has lived in south Everett for three years under asylum status and spoke with The Daily Herald on the condition of anonymity due to fear of retribution, said her husband had been arrested after immigration agents searched his vehicle registration data through Nlets. Records obtained by The Herald show that Customs and Border Patrol agents in Washington used Nlets to search the registration information of an owner of a car — a pickup matching the description of her husband’s vehicle — shortly before his arrest in July.

The woman said her husband, who was living in the United States without legal status, was later deported to Mexico. The woman and her two children are still living in Everett, and she is weighing a difficult decision whether to reunite their family in Mexico or stay in the United States and build a better future for her children, she said.

Another woman, Gabriella, who only gave her first name in a phone interview, had been living and working with her husband in Washington for about 17 years when immigration agents arrested her husband in June, she said. Neither had permits to be in the country, and her husband had previously been deported, she said. After his arrest, Gabriella sought legal help but was scammed out of $8,000 of savings by somebody impersonating an attorney, she said. Her husband was then deported to Mexico; she went with him.

Previous research by the Center for Human Rights found that immigration arrests in Snohomish County had increased significantly between 2024 and 2025, and were at the highest levels since 2011. Joomi Kim, who leads a nonprofit in south Snohomish County that serves immigrant communities, said she’s been able to see the impact as fewer people seek services and more are living in fear.

“Their daily routine of their lives are really affected, and many of them are becoming increasingly fearful of going to public places or attending religious services or even seeking resources and information,” she said.

Sharma, whose organization also serves south Snohomish County, said that communities of color are more afraid to ask for help, go to community centers or go to religious places, and it’s like “they are living underground,” he said.

“Every day, they are going to our community centers, religious places, and they are tracking those things,” Sharma said.

Kim said that the ability for immigration enforcement officers to have access to Washingtonians’ drivers licence data represents “an erosion of trust in public institutions.”

“The possibility that information is being used for immigration enforcement undermines confidence in government assurances of privacy,” Kim said. “And we want the Governor to really close that loophole.”

In a statement, Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson wrote that the state is a “national leader on protecting the private information of our residents,” and that the state has taken actions to try and curtail immigration enforcement officers’ access to drivers’ data. He wrote that the state shut off ICE’s access to driver license and vehicle data and limited access for Customs and Border Patrol officers, but added that it maintained some access “necessary to protect public safety, such as human trafficking investigations that require real-time access to data.”

“Shutting off the federal government’s access to our state’s DOL data across the board is not an option because there are many legitimate public safety reasons why we need to share data with some federal law enforcement agencies — such as preventing violent crime, child abductions, and human trafficking,” Ferguson wrote. “No states have fully shut off federal access to Nlets.”

Ferguson wrote that between November 2025 and mid-October 2026, Washington State Patrol has blocked over 174,000 attempts from federal agencies to use Nlets for civil immigration enforcement.

But the UW Center for Human Rights report said that the action that Gov. Ferguson has taken to this point has been “insufficient.” The state has blocked certain access to certain Originating Agency Identifiers, or ORIs — essentially usernames used by law enforcement to access the Nlets system — associated with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Homeland Security, and Customs and Border Patrol. Evidence obtained by the Center for Human Rights suggested that after certain ORIs were blocked, federal agents have switched to using different ORIs and are still able to perform searches on vehicles.

The report states that between January 2025 and May 2026, agencies affiliated with the Department of Homeland Security searched the driver’s license database for driver and vehicle information nearly 3.7 million times.

“This game of whack-a-mole is not providing meaningful protection for Washingtonians’ data,” the report read.

Godoy said she understands that Customs and Border Patrol has legitimate law enforcement functions, but agencies should be required to pursue and obtain a warrant before they are able to access this information, she said.

“If ICE, or the police, for that matter, want to enter my home, they have to show a judicial warrant. If they want to search my property, they have to show a judicial warrant. So why would Washington not require the same if they want to access my data, which is stored in a state repository?” Godoy said during an Oct. 13 press conference.

In Ferguson’s statement, he wrote that, as far as he knows, no state requires judicial warrants for all federal inquiries involving driver data, but his team is “reviewing what other states have done, and what is lawful, to require judicial warrants for civil immigration-related requests,” he wrote.

“My team has worked to limit Customs and Border Protection access for immigration enforcement, while maintaining access necessary to protect public safety, such as human trafficking investigations that require real-time access to data to protect vulnerable Washingtonians,” Ferguson wrote. “Looking ahead to the next two years, this will be an ongoing process for us to adapt to what federal government does next to work around what we do to protect our data.

The report also explores other ways immigration agents could access data from the Department of Licensing, including through third-party data brokers, although the Center for Human Rights had no specific information linking data brokers to individual immigration arrests in Washington. But in the short term, Godoy said the existence of multiple ways for immigration agents to access state driver data shouldn’t inhibit the Governor from taking more immediate action to address the primary pathway the state is aware of, Nlets.

“We’re really talking about core principles of the Constitution, which is that you should not be subjected to unlawful search and seizure, you should not be subjected to violence upon your arrest — much less for a civil infraction — you should not be subjected to racial profiling and be pulled over on the side of the road because you’re driving while broad, and that’s exactly what we see happening in our communities,” Godoy said. “And worse yet, that our own state is abetting it, is outrageous.”
