text:
SALT LAKE CITY — The Trump administration cut naturalization sharply over the past year, leading to accusations that it's holding back hundreds of thousands of people who might have voted in the midterms.

It's hard to say how those people might have voted had they become U.S. citizens. Naturalized citizens voted Democratic for president by a wide margin in 2020, but in a shift, almost half voted for President Donald Trump in 2024, according to a Pew Research Center analysis last year. However, recent elections in immigrant areas in Florida and New Jersey show a return to traditional Democratic voting patterns as anger mounts over mass arrests and deportations of non-criminal immigrants.

The most recent quarterly report from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services shows the agency approved about 55,000 requests for citizenship between April and June, compared with more than 230,000 for the same period last year.

Naturalizations began dropping late last year as USCIS started a new, longer process for applicants, including screening social media accounts for "anti-American activities," and requirements for more English language and civics knowledge, USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler told Stateline in a statement.

The potential impact: Almost 380,000 immigrants might have become citizens — and therefore voters — over the past year had the approval rate stayed the same. Almost all would have been potential midterm voters since only adults can complete the naturalization process recorded in statistics — children can get naturalized citizenship in other ways based on their parents' status.

The processing delays come amid broader attacks by the Trump administration related to voting and citizenship, with officials attempting to block some ballots from being counted and threatening election officials with prosecution. This week, a coalition of civil rights groups accused the administration of targeting naturalized citizens, saying legitimate voters might be disenfranchised.

Had USCIS processed naturalization applications this past year at the rate it has in the past, significantly more new U.S. citizens could be voting on Election Day.

The potential difference of 380,000 voters is calculated by the lag between about 871,000 new citizens approved between mid-2024 and mid-2025 — including during parts of the Biden and second Trump administrations — and the latest year, with about 481,000 approvals.

Kahler, the USCIS spokesperson, defended the slowdown.

"Naturalization is a privilege, not a right," Kahler wrote in the statement to Stateline. "U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services is reinforcing robust screening and vetting and has implemented reforms to ensure U.S. citizenship is reserved for those who qualify."

Changes he mentioned include reestablishment of a civics test, reinforcing English language proficiency requirements, screening applicants' social media and "ensuring applicants demonstrate good moral character and attachment to the Constitution," he wrote, adding that "USCIS will not take shortcuts in the naturalization process."

An immigrant advocacy group, the National Partnership for New Americans, said the result is fewer immigrants gaining voting privileges and other rights with citizenship.

"The administration is deliberately extending wait times across the naturalization process — including significant delays between interview approval and the Oath of Allegiance — in an apparent effort to deny otherwise eligible people their civil and voting rights," the organization wrote in October.

Nicole Melaku, the partnership's executive director, told Stateline that "we see a very clear attempt to curb legal pathways, including who gets to the finish line on naturalization. The stark decline (in new approvals) shows that reality."

About 10% of eligible voters, 25 million, are naturalized immigrants as of 2024, according to an Oct. 27 Pew Research Center report, up steadily since 2000, when it was 6.2%.

The share of voters is especially prevalent in California (22%), New Jersey (20%), New York (19%), Florida (17%) and Hawaii (16%), according to the Pew report.

In the latest U.S. Census Bureau estimates released Oct. 29, there were large shifts in the way respondents reported naturalized status between mid-2024 and mid-2025 in the opening months of the new Trump administration.

About 1.2 million fewer immigrants said they were noncitizens and about 1.3 million more said they were naturalized citizens. The change was especially lopsided in Texas, where 155,000 fewer people said they were noncitizens but an additional 244,000 said they were naturalized citizens.

The monthly survey reached about 1.7 million households last year, fewer than the usual 2 million partly because of government shutdown issues, with a questionnaire requesting names of people in the home.

It's hard to read how many people are really new citizens, and how many may have feared telling government surveyors that they are not citizens.

The change in reported naturalized citizens, 1.3 million, outstrips the 870,000 new naturalizations reported by USCIS between mid-2024 and mid-2025, according to Stateline calculations.

Lloyd Potter, Texas state demographer, said it's likely some people were afraid to report their true status this year.

"We had a change in administration and kind of an uptick in terms of detention and deportation of unauthorized immigrants," Potter told Stateline. "I think probably that created a situation where people who were noncitizens might say, on a survey, 'Yeah, I'm a citizen.'"

About 11% of Texas voters were naturalized citizens in 2024, according to the Pew Research Center report.

Christopher Dick, a consultant for the University of Florida's state-funded Bureau of Economic and Business Research, said it's also possible more noncitizens didn't respond at all to the survey, which would make it seem like a larger proportion of immigrants were citizens, distorting the survey.

As far as the cutbacks in new citizen numbers before the midterms, Steven Camerota, director of research for the Center for Immigration Studies – a think tank that favors less immigration – said it's part of a pattern of extreme presidential power seen in recent decades. He maintains that Democratic presidents have also used their powers to influence immigration policy and that a divided Congress has not used its powers to halt the pattern.

"We're in a period here of executive dominance," Camerota said. "When you have a situation where Congress is willing to surrender all its powers, this is the result."

Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at thenderson@stateline.org.

text:
HOUSTON, Texas -- A federal immigration officer charged with aggravated assault after he ran over a Mexican man with his car in Houston has turned himself in.

ABC13 video showed Mario Alberto Morales, a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer, walking inside the courtroom with his legal counsel on Monday morning. Cameras were not allowed inside. According to court records, Morales posted a non-arrest bond after a judge set his bond at $30,000.

Morales is accused of hitting Miguel Parra Hernandez, a 48-year-old construction worker, with his unmarked SUV on Oct. 10, as he chased Parra Hernandez through a parking lot.

A grand jury indicted Morales on Friday on a felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. On Monday, Morales appeared before a judge to answer that charge.

SEE ALSO: ICE agent indicted after running over man with vehicle, Harris County officials announce

Morales's attorney, David Lindenmuth, previously told The Associated Press that Morales planned to turn himself in on Monday.

Lindenmuth also told the AP that the incident was "clearly just an accident" and that local officials had "invented a crime out of thin air."

Prosecutors, on the other hand, said that the hit was intentional, arguing that Morales crossed a median and aggressively turned the wheel to strike Hernandez.

Michael Wynne, another Morales representative, questioned the case's timing and said the grand jurors were "presented with one side of the story."

"A side that Sean Teare decided to present, for whatever reason, on the last day of early voting... to make a certain news cycle," Wynne said.

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said, "As in every case that we prosecute in this courthouse, things need to come forward in a courtroom. Not at a podium. We don't litigate these cases in the media or in the public. We do it in front of, eventually, a jury of the defendant's peers."

Wynne told ABC13 they will push to move the case to the federal level as soon as possible.

"We'll press this case and litigate it the way the framers designed it, and that is in a federal forum," Wynne said.

Teare said this is something they're prepared for.

"We are fully anticipating that. We've been in preparation to combat that. We believe this case will eventually be tried in a Harris County Courthouse," Teare said.

A lawyer not connected to the case, Kent Schaffer, told ABC13 that if the case moves to federal court, Morales could get immunity if his defense attorneys argue he acted within the scope of his employment as an ICE agent.

"If the judge finds that's the case, then the case could be dismissed, but if the judge finds that the agent or officers' actions were not necessary to enforce federal law, then the case is going to go to trial," Schaffer said.

Morales is due back in court on Dec. 2.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: “Offensive Driving”: ICE's Deadly Weaponization of Vehicles Against Civilians
description:
The government said the man was not struck, but video released by the New York Times showed the ICE vehicle swerving into the bicycle.
As the Trump administration ramped up deportations over the last year, federal agents have effectively turned their cars into massive, deadly blunt objects.
In December, ICE agents in Elgin, Illinois, chased a Venezuelan man until his car and the ICE vehicles crashed.
Ramming Pedestrians ICE agents’ vehicles are not just recklessly pursuing and ramming vehicles driven by who they thought were targets for immigration enforcement.
When ICE agents brought a detainee to a Brooklyn hospital after a violent arrest in May, hundreds protested outside the hospital.
text:
As Miguel Parra Hernandez, a Mexican national, was fleeing from U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement on foot last month, he turned into a parking lot. An unmarked government vehicle came screaming into the lot after him and struck him.

When a grand jury in Harris County, Texas, charged the U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement officer behind the wheel last week, the indictment pointed to a broader pattern in the Trump administration’s crackdown on immigrants and activists. The charge was assault with a deadly weapon; the weapon was the vehicle.

The Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, claimed Parra Hernandez ran in front of the government vehicle; surveillance footage of the incident shows him running away from the car moments before he is hit. (An attorney for the ICE officer accused of assault against Parra Hernandez told The Associated Press his client had not committed any crime.)

In the same month, an unmarked ICE vehicle speeding the wrong way down a one-way street in Long Beach, California, struck a bicycle ridden by Ricardo Gonzalez, whose daughter later said he was a U.S. citizen. An agent immediately drew their gun on Gonzalez, who was later hospitalized for his injuries. The government said the man was not struck, but video released by the New York Times showed the ICE vehicle swerving into the bicycle.

Three days later after the collision in Long Beach, Antonio Moreida stood in the street in Woodland, California, outside Sacramento, documenting an unmarked ICE vehicle when the black Chevy Tahoe accelerated toward him. When the SUV hit him, Moreida told a meeting at Woodland City Hall last week, he was knocked to the ground — and the driver of the Tahoe did not stop to check on him.

The Department of Homeland Security said Moreida jumped onto the hood of the unmarked car, but when video of the incident showed him standing in place, local police and the mayor publicly disputed ICE’s account.

Weaponized Vehicles

In the national conversation about ICE’s heavy-handed crackdown on immigrants across the country, much has been made of the Department of Homeland Security’s claims that immigrants and activists “weaponized” their vehicles against federal agents. After immigration officers shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, who was targeted by ICE, and community defender Renée Good in separate incidents, the government said the civilians had used their cars to attack agents — allegations that have not been borne out in criminal charges, or were called into question by witness accounts and video analysis.

What happened to Parra Hernandez, Gonzalez, and Moreida, however, was the opposite of what the government said about Good and Salgado Araujo: It was ICE agents who weaponized their vehicles against civilians.

As the Trump administration ramped up deportations over the last year, federal agents have effectively turned their cars into massive, deadly blunt objects. Common tactics, known collectively as “offensive driving techniques,” include ramming the cars of immigrant targets and activists; “brake-checking” volunteers trying to observe ICE activity; and, in some cases, outright driving into civilians. The Intercept reviewed two dozen cases of ICE using vehicles against civilians in these ways, including multiple incidents where victims were hospitalized or even died from their injuries.

“Vehicles are another tool ICE agents are using with unchecked force, just like their guns, Tasers, and pepper spray,” said Hannah Stauss, co-director of Hands Off NYC, a group that opposes ICE’s presence in New York City. “ICE’s deranged use of vehicles effectively weaponizes them against our immigrant neighbors and rapid responders, and will continue to kill people. We are witnessing in real time the results of a federal agency being allowed to operate with impunity, in secrecy, and with unfettered violence.”

In a statement to The Intercept that compiled past responses to the incidents in this article, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said, “ICE is instituting additional training including, crowd control measures, additional training for high-risk vehicle stops, a live-fire cover course for officer safety, and medical training.”

The spokesperson did not respond specifically to allegations about the incident involved Parra Hernandez; said Gonzalez was not struck by an ICE car; and blamed Moreida for the accident because he was in the roadway.

“Offensive Driving Techniques”

In federal policies and memos, the maneuvers used in the incidents reviewed by The Intercept, along with testimony from rapid responders, are referred to by federal agents as “offensive driving techniques.” They are part of a wider patten of aggressive driving by law enforcement officers across the country, but especially by federal agents with little accountability and nearly blanket backing from the Trump administration.

Last October, Leo Martinez was monitoring immigrations agents’ activity as a volunteer with VC Defensa, a community defense group in Ventura County, California, when an unmarked ICE car rammed his pickup truck. ICE agents arrested Martinez and later released him without charge.

In March, they did it again: Three unmarked government vehicles rammed Martinez’s car as he sought to reverse away from them. The federal agents broke his window and dragged him out. Martinez, who was hospitalized from his injuries, was again released without charge. (The Department of Homeland Security spokesperson did not respond specifically to questions about the incidents involving Martinez.)

“They run stop signs, red lights, they’ll cut off complete intersections, and they rarely turn on their lights,” Martinez told The Intercept. “They’ll slam on their brakes in the middle of the freeway, in the middle of the street. Sometimes they’ll do sudden U-turns in the middle of nowhere and cut off traffic in both directions.”

When activists are monitoring federal agents, one of the most common ways for ICE to leverage their vehicles as physical threats is the “brake check,” a move where a car suddenly breaks to cause the car behind it to slow down — or slam into its rear bumper.

“Brake-checking” doesn’t appear in official guidelines as an “offensive driving technique” with good reason: It is considered to be illegal in all 50 states, covered by various statutes like reckless driving or other anti-road-rage laws. Yet VC Defensa volunteers, who like Martinez monitor ICE activity, said that when they follow ICE vehicles to alert the community with horn-honking, they keep a distance of two to three car lengths because federal agents so frequently brake-check volunteers.

Federal agents use “offensive driving techniques” so often in Ventura County that VC Defensa volunteers sometimes identify the unmarked cars by the body damage that characterizes them.

Customs and Border Protection, another agency that, like ICE, is under the umbrella of the Department of Homeland Security, expanded its agents’ discretion and ability to use these techniques during abduction operations after President Donald Trump took office for a second term.

A previous 2023 Customs and Border Protection pursuit policy largely prohibited officers from boxing in vehicles or making vehicle contact with another vehicle in motion. A partially redacted 2025 CBP directive gives officers broader discretion to use offensive driving techniques and ignore traffic laws.

“Most federal agencies are not well trained in police-citizen interactions, traffic stops, and pursuits,” said Geoffrey Alpert, a criminology and criminal justice professor at the University of South Carolina who helped Customs and Border Protection rewrite their car-chase policy under the Biden and Obama administrations.

In December, ICE agents in Elgin, Illinois, chased a Venezuelan man until his car and the ICE vehicles crashed. State investigators found the ICE agents likely conducted an “unskilled precious immobilization technique (‘PIT maneuver’) and lost control of the vehicle.” (The Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said the target of the raid rammed an ICE vehicle into a tree.)

In January, Christian Molina, a U.S. citizen, was preparing to pull over for an ICE traffic stop in Minneapolis when the agents rammed the back of his car, injuring his back. The agents said they would pay for the damage, but left without providing contact information. (The Department of Homeland Security spokesperson did not respond specifically to questions about the incident involving Molina.)

In June, agents conducted a high-speed chase through a residential neighborhood of Chicago, blowing through intersections until finally ramming their target’s car. (The Department of Homeland Security spokesperson blamed the target of the immigration enforcement action for the accident because he fled from ICE.)

“It’s disheartening to see some sort of federal agents or law enforcement driving so aggressively in a residential area,” one neighbor told Block Club Chicago. “I have a kid who’s two and we go out for walks all the time. We could have been crossing the street when they came through the intersection.”

High-Speed Chases

Following the killings of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in July, the Department of Homeland Security ordered a temporary halt to traffic stops.

The day the directive was issued, ICE chased a group of roofers in Texas, blowing through a stop sign and over a speed bump without sirens. A mother driving her son to the theater was forced to swerve into a ditch to avoid a collision.

“They speeded right next to me,” the mother told the Texas Observer. “They hit the speed bump so bad that, when they got in front of me at high speed, I had to go to the right.”

If she had not swerved, she said, “they would have hit me.”

Some of these car chases have turned deadly in the very places where local police are restricted from chasing suspects because of the attendant dangers.

In February, agents undertook a high-speed chase in pursuit of Oscar Vasquez Lopez outside of Savannah, Georgia. Vasquez Lopez’s car struck a teacher, killing her.

The Savannah Police Department only allows pursuits when the suspect has committed or is attempting to commit a forcible felony, and the risk of not capturing someone outweighs the risk of the chase. Vasquez Lopez had no criminal record, only a civil deportation order from 2024.

Two immigration car chases in New Jersey, where police face similar restrictions at the statewide level, resulted in hospitalizations. (In the Texas case, the Georgia case, and the New Jersey case, the Department of Homeland Security spokesperson blamed the target of the immigration actions for causing unsafe conditions by fleeing.)

“They are not required to follow local agency policies (the same as other agencies), but they must be held responsible for their actions under state and federal law,” Alpert, the criminology professor, said. “The failure to evaluate these behaviors in a full, complete and transparent manner leaves us all in the dark.”

Earlier this month, the AP reported on an internal memo to ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations division that banned agents from conducting high-speed car chases. The directive still allows trained agents to make traffic stops and undertake offensive driving maneuvers.

Ramming Pedestrians

ICE agents’ vehicles are not just recklessly pursuing and ramming vehicles driven by who they thought were targets for immigration enforcement. In multiple filmed interactions, agents have driven into pedestrian rapid responders and protesters.

In Woodland, California, ICE agents crashed into Moreida as he sought to collect their license plate information. After a major workplace raid in Los Angeles in June 2025, a news helicopter filmed the moment a protester walked in front of several ICE vehicles. One slowly sped up until it knocked him to the ground.

“It’s a disproportionate use of force. An individual is not going to win a fight with a vehicle,” Alpert, the criminology professor, said. “I’ve never seen any state or local law enforcement ever use a vehicle properly to hit or to run into a civilian.”

In other incidents, federal agents have weaponized their vehicles against crowds of activists. (Asked about the protests incidents mentioned in this article, the Department of Homeland Security spokesperson blamed “anti-ICE agitators.”)

In the aftermath of an ICE shooting this month in the New York City neighborhood of Marble Hill, immigration agents were seeking to move a man with a gunshot wound — whose car, with his 5-year-old son in the back, smashed into a concrete barrier during the incident — from a hospital to a detention facility. As government vehicles left the hospital in a speeding caravan, a bicycle was nearly hit by an federal agent in a black vehicle, which honked its horn, according to video of the incident. In another social media post, an ICE agent in an unmarked vehicle continued driving even with six protesters walking in front of it.

In July 2025, in San Francisco, after ICE clashed with protesters while moving detainees from the immigration courthouse to unmarked vehicles, several protesters clung to the hood of the car until they were physically thrown off when the vehicle sharply accelerated.

“I absolutely worry about ICE agents hurting people or killing people with these aggressive driving maneuvers,” said a New York rapid responder. “In order to avoid having their movements in vehicles documented, ICE agents will dramatically accelerate far beyond safe speeds for a dense urban environment like New York City.”

The organizer, who requested anonymity to avoid retaliation from the government, reported that agents drive at high speeds into oncoming traffic, run red lights, and abruptly turn without signaling. They rarely use emergency lights or sirens. These tactics align with the pattern of behavior described by Martinez in California — but in a city where rapid responders and neighbors are more often on foot or riding bicycles, not in their own vehicles.

When ICE agents brought a detainee to a Brooklyn hospital after a violent arrest in May, hundreds protested outside the hospital. One TikTok video from the night captured the moment an unmarked ICE vehicle drove into several gathered people, accelerating sharply until they leapt out of the way.

“Given the frequency with which these agents are engaging in aggressive maneuvers to try and lose rapid responders or prevent documentation of their movements,” the organizer said, “it is honestly only a matter of time until an ICE agent seriously injuries or kills a cyclist or pedestrian in New York City.”

title: Ex-Chicago FBI chief says he was ousted over a failed protesters case, sues Justice Department
description:
Douglas DePodesta, a 24-year veteran of the FBI, says in the suit against top Justice Department officials that federal prosecutors pushed “politically motivated prosecutions” against Chicago’s demonstrators before gathering evidence.
The FBI and the Justice Department, which are both named in the suit, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Federal prosecutors brought charges against around 30 protesters during the Chicago immigration enforcement operation, called Operation Midway Blitz.
According to DePodesta’s lawsuit, Boutros faced pressure from the Justice Department throughout the crackdown to charge protesters with felonies.

text:
CHICAGO (AP) — The former head of the FBI's Chicago field office says he lost his job after being wrongly blamed for prosecutions that fell apart against six people who protested the federal immigration crackdown in the city, according to a lawsuit he filed Monday.

Douglas DePodesta, a 24-year veteran of the FBI, says in the suit against top Justice Department officials that federal prosecutors pushed “politically motivated prosecutions” against Chicago’s demonstrators before gathering evidence. He says his superiors told him that FBI Director Kash Patel wanted him fired, and he stepped down against his will this summer.

"I saw the writing on the wall,” DePodesta told The Associated Press on Monday.

He accused the top federal prosecutor in Illinois, Andrew Boutros, of starting a “campaign within the Department of Justice to blame” him after the so-called “Broadview Six” case dramatically fell apart earlier this year.

Boutros’ office declined to comment. The FBI and the Justice Department, which are both named in the suit, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Hours after DePodesta filed the suit, U.S. District Judge April Perry ordered Boutros and three of his assistant attorneys to testify under oath on Nov. 16 in the failed case against the protesters.

“There is more than an adequate factual basis for the Court to pursue an inquiry as to whether willful false statements were made to the court,” Perry wrote in the order.

Federal prosecutors brought charges against around 30 protesters during the Chicago immigration enforcement operation, called Operation Midway Blitz. Many of those charges have been dropped or dismissed.

According to DePodesta’s lawsuit, Boutros faced pressure from the Justice Department throughout the crackdown to charge protesters with felonies.

“Boutros sent DePodesta emails demanding that DePodesta open FBI investigations into individuals with political views or affiliations in opposition to the Trump administration,” DePodesta’s attorneys wrote.

Boutros often pressured attorneys under him in the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Illinois to press charges “before investigating the objective evidence,” and he wanted felony charges when assisting attorneys “favored misdemeanors or no charges at all,” the suit alleges.

The office last October charged six people with conspiring to obstruct a federal officer, a felony, for their actions during a protest at a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in the Chicago suburb of Broadview.

Transcripts turned over to the court, which a judge ordered Boutros' office to remove redactions from, later revealed that a grand jury twice refused to indict the six, despite prosecutors' urgings and a highly unusual speech Boutros gave to jurors. Boutros dropped all charges against the six in May as the court moved to investigate possible prosecutorial misconduct.

Boutros “repeatedly complained to his superiors in Washington” that the failure was DePodesta's fault “to deflect attention from his own malfeasance,” DePodesta's attorneys wrote in the suit. DePodesta denied Boutros’ accusations to his superiors at the FBI, and they conceded that he was only being forced out because of the “political pressure Boutros created,” according to the suit.

The suit alleges Boutros told Justice Department leadership that DePodesta and his sister-in-law Nancy DePodesta, who is an attorney representing one of the six former defendants, “conspired to destroy” the case.

Nancy DePodesta, who represents Michael Rabbitt, one of the former defendants, confirmed to the AP that she is Douglas DePodesta's sister-in-law.

“There is no one at the FBI who took their oath of office and their ethical and moral responsibilities more seriously than Doug,” Nancy DePodesta said in a statement to the AP. “It is both heartbreaking and shameful that he was forced out of his position based on what appear to be utterly false rumors spread by” Boutros, she added.

In late September, one of the prosecutors on the “Broadview Six” case abruptly resigned, writing in a scathing resignation letter that Boutros had “scapegoated and publicly vilified” her. She filed a motion asking the court to treat her as an independent party going forward.

The former defendants have asked Judge Perry to appoint a special counsel to look into possible misconduct by prosecutors. At an Oct. 1 hearing, Perry ordered further “fact-finding” about communications between Boutros’ office and Justice Department leadership.

Wisconsin ICE arrestee’s case heads to US Supreme Court. Federal immigration authorities asked the U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday to hear the case of a Mexican national whom agents arrested last year in Racine. The petition is the latest escalation in a legal fight over the Trump administration’s mandatory detention policy for immigrants facing deportation. The justices’ decision will determine whether tens of thousands of immigrants currently in federal detention can seek release on bond. “The question of mandatory detention thus boils down to one question: Can we lock up noncitizens without giving them a day in court first?” said Jenifer Bizzotto, the Wisconsin attorney representing Jaciel Cirrus Rojas, the man at the center of the case. “The stakes could hardly be higher.”. Arrested as ‘collateral’. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents turned up at then-24-year-old Cirrus Rojas’ apartment in June 2025 in search of a prior tenant. They instead arrested Cirrus Rojas, who entered the U.S. in 2018 without a visa, as “collateral.” Wisconsin court records show no criminal convictions under his name. He spent most of the next nine months in custody at the Dodge County Detention Center in Juneau, entangled in a new White House policy barring ICE detainees from posting bond — a departure from decades of precedent. The 1996 Immigration Reform Act requires immigration authorities to detain — without bond — anyone found crossing the U.S. border without authorization. Prior administrations applied that rule narrowly, allowing many immigrants arrested in the country’s interior to seek a bond hearing in immigration court. The Trump administration bucked that approach in July 2025, when ICE Director Todd Lyons issued a new legal interpretation requiring detention without bond regardless of where immigrants are arrested. The Board of Immigration Appeals, a panel of judges who set the rules for the federal immigration court system, later signed off on the interpretation. With bond off the table, tens of thousands of immigrants in ICE custody turned to a backup option: filing habeas corpus petitions in federal district courts to challenge their detention. Unlike immigration courts, which are part of the U.S. Department of Justice, federal district courts belong to the judicial branch and, therefore, are technically independent of the White House. When a federal district court grants a habeas petition, it generally orders an immigration court judge to hold a bond hearing. Wisconsin’s Western and Eastern District courts have received more than 100 habeas petitions over the past year. A federal appeals court split. The 7th Circuit ruled 2-1 in Cirrus Rojas’ favor in July, joining appellate courts based in New York, Cincinnati, Denver, Atlanta and San Francisco in rejecting the policy.“If Congress had indeed demanded — but not funded — no-bond detention for all unlawful entrants, that may well have thrown the nation’s immigration system into chaos,” Judge Joshua Kolar, whom Joe Biden appointed to the court, wrote in the court’s majority opinion. “Immigration authorities might have found themselves quickly overwhelmed by a colossal unfunded mandate to arrest and detain millions.” Judge Diane Sykes, a George W. Bush appointee, dissented alone. “At this point, only the Supreme Court can bring uniformity and settle this question once and for all,” she wrote. “I anticipate that it will do so soon.”. Cirrus Rojas left custody earlier this year after a federal district court judge in California vacated the mandatory detention rule. The San Francisco-based 9th Circuit Court of Appeals stayed that decision less than a month later. The 7th Circuit allowed his case to move forward because federal authorities plan to re-detain him. Supreme Court could have final say. “Nothing, absent our intervention, stops the government from making good on its promise,” Kolar wrote.The U.S. Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, is now asking the Supreme Court to step in. The court agreed to take up another mandatory detention dispute earlier this month. That case involves a Brazilian national arrested during a traffic stop in Massachusetts last September. DHS asked the justices to hold Cirrus Rojas’ case until they decide the Massachusetts case. In Bizzotto’s view, both cases “offer the Supreme Court the opportunity to affirm that the Constitution means what it says.”. A ruling against the mandatory detention policy would open the door for thousands of ICE detainees — at least those within circuits that side with the Trump administration — to request bond hearings in immigration court. It would not require immigration court judges to grant their bond requests. The Supreme Court also quietly declined this week to revive a Biden-era policy that allowed immigration court judges to pause deportation proceedings for immigrants seeking humanitarian visas or other forms of legal status. Federal immigration authorities asked the U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday to hear the case of a Mexican national whom agents arrested last year in Racine. The petition is the latest escalation in a legal fight over the Trump administration’s mandatory detention policy for immigrants facing deportation.

The justices’ decision will determine whether tens of thousands of immigrants currently in federal detention can seek release on bond.

“The question of mandatory detention thus boils down to one question: Can we lock up noncitizens without giving them a day in court first?” said Jenifer Bizzotto, the Wisconsin attorney representing Jaciel Cirrus Rojas, the man at the center of the case. “The stakes could hardly be higher.”

Arrested as ‘collateral’

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents turned up at then-24-year-old Cirrus Rojas’ apartment in June 2025 in search of a prior tenant. They instead arrested Cirrus Rojas, who entered the U.S. in 2018 without a visa, as “collateral.” Wisconsin court records show no criminal convictions under his name.

He spent most of the next nine months in custody at the Dodge County Detention Center in Juneau, entangled in a new White House policy barring ICE detainees from posting bond — a departure from decades of precedent.

The 1996 Immigration Reform Act requires immigration authorities to detain — without bond — anyone found crossing the U.S. border without authorization. Prior administrations applied that rule narrowly, allowing many immigrants arrested in the country’s interior to seek a bond hearing in immigration court.

The Trump administration bucked that approach in July 2025, when ICE Director Todd Lyons issued a new legal interpretation requiring detention without bond regardless of where immigrants are arrested.

The Board of Immigration Appeals, a panel of judges who set the rules for the federal immigration court system, later signed off on the interpretation.

With bond off the table, tens of thousands of immigrants in ICE custody turned to a backup option: filing habeas corpus petitions in federal district courts to challenge their detention.

Unlike immigration courts, which are part of the U.S. Department of Justice, federal district courts belong to the judicial branch and, therefore, are technically independent of the White House. When a federal district court grants a habeas petition, it generally orders an immigration court judge to hold a bond hearing.

Wisconsin’s Western and Eastern District courts have received more than 100 habeas petitions over the past year.

A federal appeals court split

The 7th Circuit ruled 2-1 in Cirrus Rojas’ favor in July, joining appellate courts based in New York, Cincinnati, Denver, Atlanta and San Francisco in rejecting the policy.“If Congress had indeed demanded — but not funded — no-bond detention for all unlawful entrants, that may well have thrown the nation’s immigration system into chaos,” Judge Joshua Kolar, whom Joe Biden appointed to the court, wrote in the court’s majority opinion. “Immigration authorities might have found themselves quickly overwhelmed by a colossal unfunded mandate to arrest and detain millions.” Judge Diane Sykes, a George W. Bush appointee, dissented alone.

“At this point, only the Supreme Court can bring uniformity and settle this question once and for all,” she wrote. “I anticipate that it will do so soon.”

Cirrus Rojas left custody earlier this year after a federal district court judge in California vacated the mandatory detention rule. The San Francisco-based 9th Circuit Court of Appeals stayed that decision less than a month later.

The 7th Circuit allowed his case to move forward because federal authorities plan to re-detain him.

Supreme Court could have final say

“Nothing, absent our intervention, stops the government from making good on its promise,” Kolar wrote.The U.S. Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, is now asking the Supreme Court to step in.

The court agreed to take up another mandatory detention dispute earlier this month. That case involves a Brazilian national arrested during a traffic stop in Massachusetts last September.

DHS asked the justices to hold Cirrus Rojas’ case until they decide the Massachusetts case.

In Bizzotto’s view, both cases “offer the Supreme Court the opportunity to affirm that the Constitution means what it says.”

A ruling against the mandatory detention policy would open the door for thousands of ICE detainees — at least those within circuits that side with the Trump administration — to request bond hearings in immigration court. It would not require immigration court judges to grant their bond requests.

The Supreme Court also quietly declined this week to revive a Biden-era policy that allowed immigration court judges to pause deportation proceedings for immigrants seeking humanitarian visas or other forms of legal status.

text:
A federal judge on Nov. 2 determined that Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers repeatedly violated an existing court order restricting warrantless immigration arrests in Oregon and expanded it, requiring the federal administration to provide new documentation to show it is complying with the order.

In a sharply worded opinion that opens with a quote from Tim Snyder's "On Tyranny," which says that to abandon facts is to abandon freedom, U.S. District Judge Mustafa Kasubhai said ICE officials in Oregon continued making warrantless arrests without first making an individualized assessment of whether a person was likely to escape before a warrant could be obtained.

Kasubhai also determined an ICE deportation officer intentionally fabricated details in an official arrest report to make an arrest appear lawful.

“The judge found that ICE has been making warrantless arrests that don’t comply with the law or his order. Now ICE has to turn over evidence and footage for every arrest its agents make in the state,” said Jordan Cunnings, legal director at Innovation Law Lab. “The people who have been unlawfully taken from their families, pulled out of their cars on their way to work, or had their windows smashed deserve to know ICE is being held accountable.”

The ruling expands the documentation ICE must provide to attorneys representing immigrants in Oregon, requiring the agency to disclose records for all civil immigration arrests, regardless of whether ICE characterizes an arrest as warrant-based.

"What they claim to be warrant-based arrests in this record are simply not. And no amount of insistence or table-pounding will make them so. Defendants, through their own conduct, have lost trust," Kasubhai wrote. "Both warrant-based and warrantless arrests documents are now subject to this preliminary injunction, because Plaintiffs have shown that many of Defendants' warrant-based arrests are in fact warrantless."

Opinion related to lawsuit against warrantless immigration arrests

The order follows a two-day evidentiary hearing in Portland in September on a motion brought by lawyers for Innovation Law Lab, who claimed the federal government is "routinely, openly and brazenly" violating a preliminary injunction prohibiting warrantless immigration arrests in the state.

The organization sued the Trump administration after Operation Black Rose began, a monthslong federal immigration enforcement campaign conducted by the Department of Homeland Security that started in late September 2025 and resulted in more than 1,500 arrests statewide.

On Feb. 4, Kasubhai granted a preliminary injunction largely barring ICE from conducting warrantless arrests.

The government has "not halted their illegal warrantless arrest policy and practice," wrote lawyers with Innovation Law Lab in a motion filed Sept. 4. "In fact, the Defendants have doubled down on their illegal policy or practice by issuing instructions to their agents that blatantly violate the Court's injunction with respect to the subclass."

Four immigrants testified during the hearing and described being boxed in by vehicles, handcuffed, searched, and transported before federal agents even confirmed who they were.

Officer admitted to inaccurate report under oath, troubling Oregon judge

Kasubhai was particularly troubled, he said, about the arrests involving an ICE officer identified only as J.G.

The government called the officer as a witness during the trial, who said he currently works out of the Medford office and has been with ICE for 11 months. According to his testimony, he is a former Grants Pass police officer and former officer with the Department of Veterans' Affairs.

J.G. testified about being physically present in two encounters involving men identified as HDGH and CJVM.

CJVM, a Medford McDonald's employee, filed a declaration saying two vans boxed him in around 4:05 a.m. on June 13 as he arrived for work.

CJVM, who said he no longer works for the restaurant, remembered five men and one woman surrounding his vehicle. He said he reached over to the passenger seat to grab his cellphone to record as officers began shouting. He estimated 30 seconds passed before agents broke the driver-side window.

CJVM said agents forcibly grabbed his arm and handcuffed him. He was released with an apology after agents discovered he had an active asylum application and was complying with release terms.

HDGH, a 22-year-old who has lived in Medford since 2021, spoke about being arrested alongside a friend, MTM, after they were followed by ICE officers for 30 minutes from a Walmart parking lot to Emigrant Lake on July 26.

The deportation officer testified that officers that morning were running license plates of cars in the Medford Walmart lot at random to find cars whose owners were unlawfully present in the country. They discovered the registered owner of the car HDGH was reportedly in the country unlawfully.

HDGH said agents handcuffed both men and identified them only after they were taken to the Medford ICE office.

In the arrest of HDGH, J.G testified that officers followed the vehicle to Emigrant Lake because ICE has instituted a policy barring vehicle stops. That policy came in the wake of two fatal ICE shootings in Maine and Houston.

In court, J.G. acknowledged that the ICE report known as an I-213 he authored about HDGH's arrest described a different sequence of events than what actually occurred, claiming officers had identified HDGH before approaching the vehicle and obtained an arrest warrant before placing him in handcuffs.

"The I-213 for H-D-G-H-’s arrest describes a series of events that Officer J.G. now admits never occurred," Kasubhai said.

J.G. acknowledged he wrote the report as if he "already knew who the person was, but I did not" on the stand and said he "did not even know" HDGH existed.

Kasubhai said "it defies logic" that "consequential errors" in the I-213 forms, like those made in HDGH's arrest, are "merely a 'mistake'" and cited the deportation officer's more than decade of law enforcement experience.

"Officer J.G. is well-versed in law enforcement practices. This Court finds that he did not make a mistake in the I-213. He lied in an official record to facilitate the impression he was conducting a lawful warrant-based arrest. The I-213 form that Officer J.G. crafted for H-D-G-H- demonstrates intentional, coordinated falsification that would in all likelihood never have been uncovered but for this evidentiary hearing," Kasubhai said.

Two other arrests improper, Oregon judge finds

Kasubhai said JCCV's arrest was also improperly classified and lacked a valid warrant. He again referenced a copy of his I-213 form submitted to the court at the evidentiary hearing where agents incorrectly described JCCV's vehicle. The form listed a Toyota Camry, but he was driving a 2010 Toyota Corolla and had the wrong license plate. It also misstated the arrest location as Napa, California, rather than Hood River.

Kasubhai also rejected the government's explanation for why it shifted from characterizing JCCV's arrest as warrantless to warrant-based. The government was maintaining that a three-year-old warrant issued in April 2023 provided a legal basis for JCCV's rearrest.

The 2023 warrant states that an ICE officer served it on JCCV in Texas. JCCV testified about being detained by ICE for eight days that year. ICE's lawyers argued that the same warrant allowed officers to rearrest JCCV in 2025. Kasubhai said defendants had ignored a "key detail": an attorney general must first revoke a bond or parole to do so.

Kasubhai wrote that no evidence of revocation was presented and noted that lawyers instead argued that the I-213 form for JCCV indicated "there was an intention to revoke the bond or parole.”

"Intention does not constitute revocation, and the Court admonishes counsel that they are expected to make good faith arguments as officers of the court. Real people’s lives and liberties are at stake and they should remember that. Evidentiary hearings are not first-year law school examinations where one can score points with a scattershot strategy," Kasubhai added.

He found a third arrest report also "unreliable." The arrest involved a man identified as HFMJ, a Eugene resident.

HFMJ said he works as a landscaper to support three children. He and his roommate were traveling to work on July 3 when ICE vehicles began following their car. HFMJ said agents arrested his coworker and then approached the car. HFMJ said agents then arrested him without showing him any paperwork.

Kasubhai said the arrest report narrative "differs significantly" from HFMJ's testimony. Kasubhai noted narratives for HFMJ and his arrested coworker "are nearly identical." Kasubhai said he was "skeptical" that both men received identical information so promptly, given HFMJ's testimony that he never even gave officers his name before being arrested.

New order expands documentation required around Oregon arrests

Kasubhai referred to evidentiary hearings as "essential tools to ensure that a rigorous record of something closer to the truth is preserved, and to hold liars to account," and added that the federal government has tried to circumvent compliance with the law and preliminary injunctions.

In his order, Kasubhai said both warrant-based and warrantless arrest documents are now subject to his preliminary injunction. He also ordered the government to disclose documents and body-worn camera footage related to all civil immigration arrests in the state.

I-213s alone, he explained, do not accurately reflect the facts of warrantless arrests and said Innovation Law Lab presented "copious evidence" of the federal government's violations in Oregon.

"There is no telling how many other agents in Oregon engaged in similar misconduct, which calls into question the veracity of all I-213 forms completed by ICE officers in Oregon," reads part of Kasubhai's order and opinion. "Based solely on the evidence presented in this case, Defendants have clearly violated the Court's preliminary injunction order."

Under Kasubhai's new order, ICE must retransmit the injunction to relevant officers, employees, and contractors every 30 days. He also ordered the agency to provide previously disclosed records without redactions.

The agency must also provide body camera footage for arrests made on or after Sept. 1.

Kasubhai rejected the government's argument that modifying the order would improperly interfere with immigration enforcement.

He said other district courts have also found it necessary to enforce or modify prior orders against ICE officials in light of repeated violations.

"The presumption of regularity directs the courts to assume, unless clear evidence indicates differently, that government officials have properly discharged their duties, acted in good faith and followed required procedures. This presumption no longer holds for Defendants," Kasubhai said. "The evidence in this case proves as much. Defendants are held to the same expectation as any other litigant before this Court. One must earn credibility by acting with integrity."

This story may be updated.

text:
Standing at a podium to tout the Trump administration’s “fraud task force” achievements on Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told a reporter that it would be a “waste of our time” to investigate ICE’s recent purchase of a prison from a private company for hundreds of millions of dollars over a prior asking price.

Bessent responded sternly when a reporter suggested at a press conference in Minnesota on Friday that the Trump administration look into a recent, questionable $496 million purchase of a prison by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

“If the administration has declared war on waste and fraud, could you explain the 420 million overpayment for a prison in Appleton, Minnesota, when the company offered it to the state of Minnesota for 75 million?” a reporter asked the treasury secretary.

“I don’t know anything about that. What we are here to do is prosecute criminal fraud and any question like that that deflects away from it, I think, is a waste of our time,” Bessent responded.

The reporter was referring to an investigation by local outlet KARE 11 last week that found that, in August, ICE spent nearly half a billion dollars for a vacant prison in Appleton, Minnesota, being sold by major private prison company and ICE contractor CoreCivic. Communications obtained by KARE 11, however, showed that CoreCivic had offered to sell the facility to the state of Minnesota for $75 million in May 2025, which the state declined.

This means that the administration may have overpaid $420 million for the facility. CoreCivic, a major Trump donor, is one of the top contractors tapped by the Trump administration in its mass deportation campaign. The company swiftly announced the new ICE contract for CoreCivic to run the prison for an expected profit of $75 million a year.

The Department of Homeland Security responded to the investigation by saying that the purchase price was set through a different process than the company’s offer to Minnesota.

“The 1,600-bed site gives ICE immediate capacity to detain and remove those who have no legal right to remain, protecting American communities and restoring the integrity of our borders without waiting years for new construction,” the agency said. CoreCivic’s offer to Minnesota “was not based on replacement-cost analysis and did not reflect the intervening rise in construction costs or federal operational standards,” it added.

Bessent’s dismissal of the question is ironic considering the press conference that took place immediately beforehand. The secretary and other officials like FBI Director Kash Patel announced in a lengthy presser that the administration is taking even further action to insert the federal government in the state’s investigation of the welfare fraud scheme, as part of its supposed “war on fraud.” For over a year, the administration has used this scheme to justify a wide range of actions against Minnesota and its Democratic leaders, including Operation Metro Surge and President Donald Trump’s open attacks on Somali immigrants.

Standing in front of a sign that read, “the vice president’s fraud task force,” the officials made lofty statements about the administration’s supposed work on the issue.

“President Trump has made clear that the war on fraud is not the work of one department, but a mandate that we must carry across the entire administration,” said Bessent. “That is why I visited Minnesota in January to make clear that the U.S. Treasury is employing every tool to bring an end to this egregious, unchecked fraud and hold perpetrators to account.”

“This FBI follows the money. This FBI will put in prison anyone who commits fraud anywhere in the world against any American citizen,” said Patel.

text:
In July 2025, the Trump administration suddenly adopted a new radical misinterpretation of immigration law, declaring that anyone who entered the country without inspection must be detained without any individualized bond hearing. The administration’s mandatory detention policy does not take into account a person’s family or community ties or how long they have lived in the country.

Millions of immigrants are affected, including people who were previously released by the government, people who are eligible for legal status, as well as those with long-pending immigration applications who have been waiting years due to administrative backlogs.

This policy is cruel, inhumane, and illegal. That’s why it’s been repeatedly rejected by the federal courts, with hundreds of federal district judges ruling on thousands of related habeas petitions. Nine out of 10 of those judges have ruled that the administration’s misinterpretation of the law is illegal. When the government appealed those rulings, the ACLU and partners defended those decisions at the courts of appeals, where nine out of 11 circuits agree that the administration’s new policy violates the law.

Our client in this case, Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, has been living in the United States for over 20 years, has two U.S. citizen children, owns a home and a business, and has had an application for legal status pending since 2016 and permission to work legally in the U.S. Nonetheless, in September 2025, the Department of Homeland Security detained him under the government’s new no-bond policy.

A district court judge found this unlawful and ordered a bond hearing. An immigration judge then found that Mr. Barbosa da Cunha was not a flight risk or a danger to the community and ordered his release.

The Second Circuit unanimously affirmed the district court’s decision and agreed that the administration’s new policy violated existing immigration law. The vast majority of federal appeals courts have ruled against the policy, including the ruling at the center of this case.

The law is clear: Try as it might, the government cannot lock up immigrants for months or even years without giving them the basic protection of a bond hearing.

About Cookies

Cookies and related technologies (herein “Cookies”) are small text files that a website saves on your computer when you visit the site. Cookies the University sets are called first-party Cookies. The data collected might be about you, your device, your preferences, or your login information. See the for more information.

Strictly Necessary Cookies - Always Active

Strictly Necessary Cookies are first-party Cookies that are necessary for the website to function. They can be either permanent or temporary and are usually only set in response to actions made directly by you that amount to a request for services, such as logging in or filling in forms. For example, we use Strictly Necessary Cookies to handle user registration and login. Some sites require the use of Strictly Necessary Cookies to access the site, such as University websites requiring University credentialed authentication. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, you may not be able to access the site or some parts of the site will not work.

Performance Cookies - Always Active

Performance Cookies allow us to count visits and traffic sources so we can measure and improve the performance and effectiveness of University websites. Performance Cookies also help the University understand which webpages are the most and least popular, see how visitors move around the site, and determine whether webpage content is relevant to user interests. Performance Cookies may be first-party or third party, permanent or temporary, and do not personally identify individual visitors. Some Performance Cookies are “analytics” Cookies (e.g., Google Analytics), using third-party software tools, which help us understand more about how our websites are used and where visitors come from by collecting and aggregating anonymous information on the pages visited and any advertisements viewed. The University does not take responsibility for the collection, use, and management of data by any third-party software tool provider unless required to do so by applicable law. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, some site services and functionalities may not work.

Functional Cookies - Always Active

Functional Cookies enhance the performance and functionality of our websites but are non-essential to their use. These permanent Cookies allow our website to remember information from your previous visits, such as details you submitted before or your previously stated preferences. These Cookies may also be used to provide services you request, such as newsletters or publications. They may be first- or third-party Cookies that enable services we have added to our webpages. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, some or all of these services may not function properly.

Targeting Cookies - Always Active

Targeting Cookies are used to deliver content tailored to your interests and may be temporary or permanent. They may also be first-party or third-party Cookies. Targeting Cookies are based on uniquely identifying your browser and device; they do not store information such as your name. The University may use targeting Cookies prepared by the University, its third-party contractors, or advertising partners to provide you with personalized University display advertising and promotional material about the University and its programs. text:
Three immigrant and labor groups in Washington state say efforts by the federal government to set aside the ballots of more than 400 state residents federal officials claim are noncitizens is an act of voter intimidation.

OneAmerica Votes, the Latino Community Fund of Washington, and the United Food and Commercial Workers International Union filed a lawsuit Friday in Seattle federal court accusing the Trump administration of violating the Constitution and other federal voting laws.

“[The] Defendants’ list is not evidence of anything,” the suit argues, “and their deeply chilling threats of federal penalty for elections officials and others who fail to conform to their demands are baseless.”

A week ago, two Trump-appointed U.S. attorneys held a press conference where they claimed to have found more than 400 non-citizens on Washington’s voter rolls who they believe illegally voted in past elections. Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs issued a letter two days later in response to the claims and said the submitted list was “not reliable.”

Other states like California have faced similar federal requests and refused. California officials said the Department of Justice did not provide information about its data or methodology, and federal demands were going against state and federal law.

“Immediately, serious and significant problems with and errors in the DOJ's list began to come to light,” according to the Washington lawsuit. “Los Angeles County reviewed a sample of the listed voters with Los Angeles addresses and found that more than a quarter of the sampled entries listed a place of birth in the United States, and that more than 40% concerned registrations that had already been cancelled.”

The lawsuit filed Friday said the federal claims are part of a larger effort to intimidate voters and suppress voter turnout.

“ The federal government is ramping up attacks in the final weeks leading up to the midterm elections to intimidate the public and suppress the vote — our vote,” said Roxana Noruzi, executive director of OneAmerica Votes. She said it’s an effort to keep U.S. citizens, immigrants, and their communities in a state of constant fear and crisis “to consolidate power and move an authoritarian agenda.”

“The Trump administration directly threatened Washington's elections by demanding the state set aside the ballots of voters that they deemed suspicious with absolutely no evidence to back this,” Noruzi said. “We know what this is. The administration is setting itself up to deny election results they won't like, and once again, making immigrant communities their scapegoat.”

The lawsuit asks the court to rule federal prosecutor’s actions unlawful, and block federal officials from interfering with Washington state’s ongoing elections, calling it an attempt to disqualify U.S. citizen voters.

text:
A federal judge ruled Monday that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers have continued to make arrests in Oregon without warrants.

Attorneys with Innovation Law Lab originally filed a class action lawsuit against ICE last year, arguing that the agency could not arrest someone without a warrant.

U.S. District Judge Mustafa Kasubhai issued a preliminary order earlier this year that ICE could only make a warrantless arrest if the person is likely to flee, and the agency must send documentation of those arrests to Innovation Law Lab.

Lawyers for Innovation Law Lab had said ICE was not complying with that order. They argued that ICE has continued to conduct hundreds of warrantless arrests since the judge’s order went into effect. Attorneys for the federal government have denied those claims.

In his new order, Kasubhai is now requiring the federal government to provide all arrest documents to Innovation Law Lab.

ICE must also produce all body-worn camera footage for arrests conducted on or after Sept. 1, 2026.

During a hearing in September, four immigrants — all arrested by ICE in 2026 — testified that they were each arrested without a valid warrant. An ICE deportation officer testified that, in two of the arrests, agents used license plate readers to identify the people detained.

In his order Monday, Kasubhai found that ICE has continued to conduct warrantless arrests and failed to properly document those instances, both in violation of his February order.

False and incorrect information found in reports, judge finds

The judge was particularly critical of an ICE deportation officer, identified as J.G. During the September hearing, J.G. testified that, while arresting a man in Medford last July, he had written false information in an arrest report, known as an I-213.

In the report, the agent attested that he knew the detainee’s immigration status before making the stop. On the witness stand, he admitted that was not true.

Innovation Law Lab argued that the warrant was invalid because it was issued after the arrest occurred.

Kasubhai said in the Monday ruling it was clear the agent had fabricated details, and had not simply made a mistake.

“It defies logic that such consequential errors in the I-213 form are merely a ‘mistake,’” he wrote. “The Court finds that he did not make a mistake in the I-213. He lied in an official record to facilitate the impression he was conducting a lawful warrant-based arrest.”

ICE did not immediately respond to OPB’s requests for comment Monday.

Kasubhai also wrote, “There is no telling how many other agents in Oregon engaged in similar misconduct, which calls into question the veracity of all I-213 forms completed by ICE officers in Oregon.”

The judge also admonished the “sloppy work” found in some reports. Other I-213s contained incorrect information, with one saying that an arrest took place in California when it was actually in Oregon. Also, many reports of different arrests contain nearly identical language, evidence ICE was using boilerplate language in arresting documents, he said.

“ICE agents’ boilerplate repetition of their ‘unawareness’ of community ties is a clear example of their failure to conduct simple law enforcement investigative duties. This is sloppy work,” Kasubhai wrote.

The judge also called into question the federal government’s own figures about the number of warrantless arrests. In documents provided to Innovation Law Lab, the government had said only 13 arrests were conducted without a proper warrant.

Kasubhai wrote that number is highly unlikely, since so many of the warrants used by ICE were invalid.

“The Court finds that ICE officers conducted significantly more than 13 warrantless arrests in Oregon between February 2026 and August 2026,” he wrote.

The order was issued as Kasubhai considers a similar case in federal court in Eugene. During an evidentiary hearing Monday, a man identified as L.A.M.A testified that he was arrested in a Walmart parking lot in Albany on June 18.

After saying they would drive him to the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, the agents eventually left him on the streets of Portland. L.A.M.A told the judge that his son had to drive from Albany to pick him up.

He said he was never shown a warrant during his arrest. Clearly emotional, he told the court in Spanish the experience left him feeling, “Anguish, quite a bit of it. Anguish, frustration — how your life can change in 24 hours.”

text:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Monday threatened the Trump administration with legal action over federal immigration agents’ use of city parking lots to stage raids, which the Democratic elected official said amounted to “unlawful commandeering” of public property.

“This use of city property in furtherance of federal immigration enforcement is unauthorized and is therefore illegal, endangers city residents, and sows fear among those who seek to access city property,” Mamdani wrote in a letter addressed to U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) acting director, David Venturella.

Mamdani’s letter notes that ICE agents have “reportedly parked their vehicles and conducted meetings in several city-owned, unstaffed parking lots” — including ones near a park and a city-run preschool.

“ICE has not secured any authorization from the city to use these lots for immigration enforcement. To be clear: the city does not authorize ICE using its property in this manner,” Mamdani wrote. “Parking lots connected to city parks are reserved for the safe use and enjoyment of New Yorkers and visitors who wish to use our parks. Use of these lots for other purposes, including ICE’s reported use of these lots, amounts to unauthorized activity on City property. Accordingly, you must immediately issue guidance to your agents prohibiting them from using any City lots to stage or conduct enforcement operations.”

Mamdani’s letter comes weeks after a plainclothes ICE agent shot a Dominican immigrant in the Bronx while his 5-year-old son was in the car, infuriating community members and intensifying pressure on the mayor to do everything in his power to remove the rogue agency from New York City.

“We know that ICE is rotten to its core,” Mamdani said after the shooting. The mayor has called on President Donald Trump to end all ICE operations in New York City and has demanded abolition of the agency, saying it is “making a mockery of what law and order is supposed to be.”

In mid-October, Mamdani and more than 100 other elected New York officials called on private parking lot owners to bar ICE agents from using their property.

text:
In the months leading up to the 2026 midterm elections, congressional Republicans and federal prosecutors have targeted dozens of local officials in cities and counties across the country that have adopted some sanctuary policies. The investigations have increasingly focused on prosecutors and law enforcement officers, many of whom have publicly announced plans to go after Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents who commit crimes in their jurisdictions or refuse demands to cooperate with federal immigration policing.

In total, 65 officials in 16 states have been targeted since January, according to a review of documents released by the House Judiciary Committee and the Department of Justice (DOJ), as well as interviews with senior officials who have direct knowledge of individual investigations. The House Judiciary Committee has issued subpoenas and other demands for testimony, documents, and records to more than 40 officials, 15 of them local prosecutors. Alongside that, the DOJ has initiated investigations into 50 local or state officials since 2025, including five involving local prosecutors. In all, 17 local prosecutors have been swept up in House Judiciary or DOJ investigations and lawsuits related to immigration policies.

House Judiciary Committee Chair Rep. Jim Jordan said in a recent report that “Democrats’ open-borders policies at the federal level and sanctuary policies at the state and local level allow millions of illegal aliens to pour into the country and ensure that criminal aliens, after encountered by local law enforcement, are released back into American communities,” echoing language the committee has commonly used in its investigations.

Many experts describe these investigations as unprecedented, and view the move as retaliation against local officials who refuse to cooperate with federal immigration agents or threaten legal action against ICE officers.

“These [prosecutors] are being intentionally intimidated by congressional and federal authorities,” said Mona Sahaf, the director of the Reshaping Prosecution initiative at the Vera Institute of Justice. “The use of [the] DOJ to target perceived political opponents is new. It’s busting norms, and it’s highly dangerous.”

The targeting of local prosecutors appears to be a matter of policy in the second Trump administration. “Sanctuary Jurisdictions Directives” issued by the attorney general’s office on February 5, 2025, held that the DOJ Civil Rights Division should “identify state and local laws, policies, and practices that facilitate violations of federal immigration laws or impede lawful federal immigration operations,” and “where appropriate, take legal action to challenge such laws, policies, or practices.”

The DOJ, in a June 18 press release announcing an investigation into local officials in Philadelphia — including District Attorney Larry Krasner — concerning a policy prohibiting federal agents from wearing masks, said that its “series of lawsuits brought by the Civil Division” targeted “illegal policies designed to thwart federal law enforcement across the country.”

Rebecca Roiphe, the Joseph Solomon Distinguished Professor of Law at New York Law School, said the investigations into local prosecutors represented “a wholesale abandonment” of the principle of separation between the DOJ and the political branches of government. “This administration has pretty openly suggested that it is normal and appropriate and even laudable for the political branches to have some degree of control over the Department of Justice,” she said.

Referring to the DOJ investigations, Roiphe said, “The bottom line is that these federal prosecutions can end up threatening local prosecutors to fall in line with federal priorities, and that’s illegitimate in our system.”

These overlapping investigations, reports, and the DOJ directives follow the Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025 threat to “initiate legal action against” prosecutors who refuse to adhere to the priorities of the Trump administration. For many of the targeted prosecutors, the political influence has become impossible to ignore.

Among the targeted is Parisa Dehghani-Tafti, the top prosecutor in Arlington, Virginia, who drew the ire of Representative Jordan’s committee on multiple occasions, including when she declined to charge an activist who handed out flyers containing the home address of Deputy White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, citing concerns over First Amendment-protected free speech.

In a July 1 letter to Dehghani-Tafti, Jordan described Dehghani-Tafti’s decision not to charge as “politically-motivated actions in a case involving a far-left agitator’s disturbing campaign to threaten, harass, and dox a senior White House official and his family” and accused her office of having “sanctuary policies that prioritize illegal and criminal aliens over American citizens.”

Dehghani-Tafti, who characterized the House Judiciary actions as “pathetic,” denies any wrongdoing and suggests that these investigations are the result of her political opponents’ inability to defeat her electorally.

“They can’t beat us at the polls, and so they’re being undemocratic about it and trying to undermine the voters,” she told Truthout.

In total, Jordan and the House Judiciary Committee have issued three letters and a subpoena to Dehghani-Tafti, in addition to writing an interim report on her in September, which was largely based on a July closed-door deposition. Following the report, the DOJ Civil Rights Division informed Dehghani-Tafti that she was under investigation following a referral from the House Judiciary, according to a senior official with direct knowledge of the investigation.

“None of this is normal,” Dehghani-Tafti said. “What they’re doing is taking mechanisms that are designed to uphold the rule of law and perverting them. And that is not normal, except for authoritarians.”

Dehghani-Tafti was not the only Northern Virginia prosecutor to be on the receiving end of both House Judiciary and DOJ investigations. The top prosecutor for Fairfax County, Virginia, Steve Descano, similarly received three letters and a subpoena, and was the subject of an interim report from Jordan’s committee. The report, “Fairfax County, Virginia: The Dangerous Consequences of Sanctuary Policies,” claims that a 2019 campaign promise to make “charging and plea decisions that limit or avoid immigration consequences” is discriminatory and violates federal law. The report goes on to accuse Descano’s office of “efforts to erase national borders and undermine immigration enforcement.”

Descano declined to comment for this story, citing the ongoing investigations. His chief of staff, Laura Birnbaum, directed Truthout to prior official statements issued by his office, including an October 20 response to the House Judiciary report. “This ‘report’ is nothing more than recycled Republican talking points put out weeks before the midterm elections as a desperate attempt to distract from widely anticipated Republican losses,” wrote Birnbaum.

Responding to the DOJ investigation, Descano’s office released a statement in May that accused the Trump administration “of misusing the Justice Department to launch partisan attacks.”

Both Dehghani-Tafti and Descano belong to a small coalition of prosecutors from cities across the U.S. that declared an intention to prosecute federal agents who commit crimes in their cities. The alliance — the Fight Against Federal Overreach — which intentionally takes its name from the slang acronym FAFO, formed in January in part as a response to the deadly ICE shootings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minneapolis that same month. Less than a year later, nearly half of the group’s founding members have found themselves under investigation by the DOJ.

“No other administration has ever done things like this,”said Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, who has been a target of DOJ investigators.

Moriarty, whose jurisdiction includes Minneapolis, made national headlines in January when she announced a state-level investigation into the shooting of Good by ICE agent Jonathan Ross. Just days later, the DOJ subpoenaed four Minnesota officials, including Gov. Tim Walz and Attorney General Keith Ellison, as part of an investigation into whether they impeded federal immigration agents during “Operation Metro Surge.” News reports initially incorrectly named Moriarty among the officials who received a subpoena, though it was later revealed that she did not receive one. Moriarty told Truthout she believes that her name was released intentionally by government officials to intimidate her.

Viewed in isolation, these actions may appear to be singular responses during an exceptional political moment, but taken together, the data suggest a wider attempt to punish officials who try to thwart federal immigration policies.

“The story is there — if you speak up and work to hold police accountable, we will come after you,” said Sahaf, referring to the House Judiciary and DOJ investigations. Sahaf, a former DOJ trial attorney, warned that should local prosecutors fear becoming a political target for investigating federal agents and police, “we’ll have no one … to deter this kind of conduct from happening again.”

Clarissa Delgado contributed additional reporting for this article.
